=== PAPER 1f8bcb9fc16e (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as enabling scalable, noise-resilient continual learning with variational quantum circuits for sequential signal-processing tasks, specifically ECG classification and financial time-series forecasting, where standard amplitude encoding is a bottleneck and conventional VQCs suffer catastrophic forgetting when tasks arrive sequentially. The authors motivate these challenges as key obstacles to deploying quantum learning in real-world signal-processing applications, including financial time-series prediction and ECG analysis.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-009, C-010]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The proposed method, CL-QAS, is a continual-learning quantum framework that combines TT-based amplitude encoding to compress high-dimensional inputs into low-rank quantum feature states, a bi-loop quantum architecture search where an inner loop trains VQC parameters and an outer loop uses a policy network to explore architectures based on validation-accuracy rewards with entanglement penalties, and EWC plus KL-divergence regularization to stabilize sequential updates and preserve prior-task knowledge. The approach assumes smoothness and bounded gradients for the per-task VQC losses, defines a joint objective over classifier and policy terms, and models noise via depolarizing, readout, and encoder-angle jitter, with experiments implemented as TTN+VQC hybrids and executed both in simulation and on IBM’s Heron r2 hardware.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-011, C-003, C-012, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-013, C-024, C-031, C-053, C-054, C-056]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors claim theoretical upper bounds on approximation error, trainability (via gradient-variance bounds), generalization (combining inner-loop and outer-loop terms), and robustness of the full objective under quantum noise, including per-task classifier robustness and policy-term robustness under noisy rewards. Empirically, CL-QAS is reported to achieve substantial gains in accuracy, balanced accuracy, F1 score, and reward on ECG signal classification and synthetic financial time-series forecasting, with polynomial scaling in sample complexity and gradient variance, strong forward and backward transfer, bounded degradation under depolarizing and readout noise, and improved robustness. Across simulated and hardware experiments on IBM Heron, CL-QAS is said to consistently outperform baselines on ECG and financial tasks, maintain the highest resilience under added noise, demonstrate the best mean performance on hardware while keeping circuit depth and gate count low, and show that TT encoding improves classification performance with less runtime overhead; the discussion notes that the observed degradation between noiseless and noisy runs is marginal, consistent with the robustness theory.
    [codes: C-005, C-014, C-017, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-006, C-007, C-018, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Relative to quantum and hybrid baselines such as naive fixed-architecture VQCs, QAS without continual-learning mechanisms, TTN+VQC, and differentiable QAS, CL-QAS is reported to consistently achieve higher accuracy, balanced accuracy, F1 score, and reward on the ECG benchmark and to attain the best overall performance on the financial time-series tasks in both noiseless and noisy settings. The authors also state that CL-QAS maintains its top performance when deployed on IBM Heron hardware and that TT-based encoding in their framework improves performance with less runtime overhead compared to the corresponding non-TT variants.
    [codes: C-037, C-039, C-040, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-053]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that their current work is focused on near-term NISQ-type simulation, indicating that stronger guarantees and broader validation remain open. They note that extending their theoretical analysis to explicitly incorporate stochastic quantum-noise models and imperfect measurements would be necessary to strengthen generalization guarantees, and that empirical evaluation on larger qubit systems, mixed-state datasets, and more extensive runs on real quantum hardware is required to better understand the practical scalability of CL-QAS.
    [codes: C-049, C-050, C-062]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future research directions proposed by the authors include extending the theoretical framework to handle stochastic noise models and imperfect measurements, empirically scaling CL-QAS to larger qubit systems, mixed-state datasets, and broader real-hardware deployments, and incorporating meta-learning or federated quantum updates to enable distributed continual adaptation across heterogeneous quantum devices. They also suggest investigating theoretical connections between their curvature-based continual-learning approach (via EWC) and quantum natural gradient methods.
    [codes: C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims as its primary novelty the introduction of CL-QAS, a continual-learning quantum framework that unifies TT-based amplitude encoding, bi-loop quantum architecture search, and EWC regularization to address amplitude-encoding costs and catastrophic forgetting in sequential tasks. Additionally, the authors state that they derive analytical bounds on representation capacity, trainability, generalization performance, and robustness under quantum noise—highlighting improved scalability and stability over conventional VQCs—and that they validate these properties with simulated and hardware experiments on ECG and financial datasets showing consistent gains in accuracy, generalization, and hardware efficiency.
    [codes: C-001, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper structures CL-QAS training as a two-stage per-task process with an inner-loop VQC training phase and an outer-loop policy-reinforcement phase optimized under a joint objective, with validation accuracy (and an entanglement-penalized reward) guiding architecture search and EWC plus KL regularization stabilizing policy updates. The theoretical analysis explicitly states smoothness and bounded-gradient assumptions and derives stability, trainability, generalization, and robustness bounds that are later linked in the discussion to observed controlled gradient dynamics, stable convergence, and marginal degradation between noiseless and noisy simulations. Experimentally, the ECG benchmark uses eight sequential tasks with TT-encoded inputs, applies an 80/20 stratified split preserving class balance, and reports consistent CL-QAS improvements; the financial dataset is synthetically generated to mimic asset prices with regime shifts, uses next-step direction labels, and is partitioned into eight chronological tasks with splits that avoid future–past leakage. The authors also describe their noise model in detail and report simulated and hardware validation on IBM Heron r2, emphasizing low depth and gate count as well as TT ablations showing better performance and lower runtime, which together speak to experimental rigor and resource awareness.
    [codes: C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-042, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-056, C-058, C-059, C-060, C-061]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper also surveys related work on differentiable quantum architecture search as a comparison point, and notes specific hardware characteristics of IBM’s Heron r2 processor such as improved connectivity, cross-talk suppression, and two-qubit gate fidelities, which contextualize the reported hardware results.
    [codes: C-055, C-057]

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as detecting modular/community structure in complex dynamic and stochastic networks, including financial graphs, where communities evolve over time and are hard to identify with existing methods. It emphasizes that community recognition in such dynamic settings remains challenging and motivates a unified spectral–stochastic–quantum framework for modular structure discovery in evolving networks, explicitly applying it to financial graphs as part of the evaluation scope.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-017, C-034]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The method is a quantum-walk-inspired but largely classical framework that constructs Fourier–Markov operators grounded in discrete-time quantum walk principles, lifting a Markov transition matrix to a unitary operator and sandwiching it in a graph Fourier basis to obtain a Fourier–Markov operator that encodes both spectral modes and quantum-inspired transition dynamics. Random walk processes are embedded into a quantum-inspired Hilbert space, with community partitions first initialized spectrally and then optionally refined via a QAOA-inspired search on a unitary operator implementable on quantum simulators, forming a hybrid workflow with classical alternatives such as simulated annealing and Lanczos-based spectral approximation for scalability.
    [codes: C-002, C-008, C-011, C-012, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that their QFM-CommNet framework uncovers latent modular structures with enhanced resolution and achieves superior community quality—modularity, normalized mutual information, adjusted Rand index, and temporal smoothness—on benchmark dynamic networks, including financial graphs. Quantitatively, they highlight best reported scores of modularity Q = 0.561, NMI = 0.739, ARI = 0.671, and temporal smoothness TS = 0.593, while also claiming that the method’s runtime scales polynomially and remains efficient on graphs up to 100K nodes, with the Lanczos-based approximation shown to be effective for large dynamic graphs.

  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper claims that QFM-CommNet surpasses state-of-the-art community detection baselines in terms of community quality metrics and reports that it consistently outperforms classical spectral and random-walk-based techniques across all evaluation parameters. At the same time, the authors state that its computational efficiency is comparable to classical spectral and random walk approaches and that its polynomial runtime scaling remains competitive even for 100K-node networks, positioning the method as quality-improving rather than dramatically faster than classical baselines.
    [codes: C-004, C-013, C-035, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly identify that existing spectral methods are often sensitive to noise and tend to neglect temporal correlations, while Markovian and random-walk-based methods, although modeling temporal behavior, often miss fine-grained frequency-domain structural details; these points motivate their unified framework rather than being limitations of their own method. For their approach, the main acknowledged constraint is that it is currently evaluated using quantum simulators with QAOA-inspired refinement and classical approximations, implying that practical deployment on real quantum hardware and in more complex multimodal or heterogeneous dynamic networks remains future work rather than a demonstrated capability.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-009, C-016, C-032, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper points to future research on hybrid implementations of the framework on quantum hardware and on extending the method to multimodal and heterogeneous dynamic networks, indicating plans to move beyond simulator-based studies and to broaden applicability beyond the current set of dynamic graph benchmarks, including financial networks.
    [codes: C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim novelty in proposing a unified operator-theoretic framework that integrates spectral graph theory, Markovian dynamics, and quantum walk principles for modular structure detection in dynamic networks, addressing an underexplored combination of quantum walks, Fourier operators, and Markov processes for community detection. They articulate three main contributions: the construction of a family of Fourier–Markov operators grounded in discrete-time quantum walks, a hybrid embedding that maps random walks into a quantum-inspired Hilbert space to capture both frequency-domain and probabilistic evolution for interpretable and scalable partitions, and empirical validation on synthetic and real-world dynamic networks demonstrating superior modularity, stability, and robustness versus state-of-the-art baselines.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-016, C-017]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper grounds its framework in a precise dynamic network representation with time-indexed graphs and Markov transition matrices aggregated over snapshots to form an average stochastic flow operator, then transformed via a unitary lift and Fourier–Markov construction. The authors emphasize interpretability by relating low-frequency modes to coherent communities, high-frequency modes to boundaries and anomalies, and superposition effects to overlapping community memberships, and they approximate spectral decomposition with Lanczos iteration to ensure tractability on large graphs. For evaluation, they use diverse synthetic, social, biological, and financial benchmark datasets under the QFM-CommNet label, claiming diversity and reproducibility in the dataset design, and present the operator FQ as a rigorous yet physically intuitive spectral lens on modular dynamics.

They further note that systematic integration of quantum walks, Fourier operators, and Markovian dynamics for community detection remains underexplored, which they use to motivate their framework.

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames a risk-management problem in a supply-chain digital twin where predictive uncertainty must be quantified because failing to analyse uncertainty can lead to optimistic predictions, financial losses, and operational problems; the study specifically aims to quantify predictive uncertainty in hybrid quantum–classical models, understand how quantum circuit configurations affect uncertainty propagation, and analyse the impact on a financial-style target (cost efficiency).
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-037]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a hybrid quantum–classical approach in which selected classical features are angle-encoded into qubits via single-qubit RX, RY, and RZ rotations, followed by entangling CY gates, and then measured to obtain Pauli-X/Y/Z expectation values as transformed features for downstream regression models. The quantum circuit is trained by minimising a cost function that combines mutual information loss with a diversity penalty, and the resulting quantum-transformed features are fed into Bayesian ridge, quantile regression, random forest, and neural network models to form hybrid variants.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across all model families, hybrid quantum–classical models achieve predictive accuracy comparable to classical baselines (e.g., R²≈0.79, RMSE≈0.78, MAE≈0.75) but exhibit notably different uncertainty characteristics, including narrower uncertainty bounds and a higher number of outliers detected. The authors report that quantum feature transformation affects uncertainty propagation, with hybrid models often showing a positive uncertainty–error correlation and statistically significant differences in uncertainty (but not errors) relative to classical counterparts; increasing the qubit count changes uncertainty distributions and reduces outlier counts without affecting errors, and qubit scaling also alters risk-adjusted cost efficiency (RACE), especially for HQRF and HQNN, while HQBRR and HQQR remain robust.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-039, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The study directly compares classical BRR, QR, RF, and NN models with their hybrid-quantum counterparts and finds similar predictive errors but systematic differences in uncertainty behaviour. Classical BRR shows a stronger uncertainty–error correlation than HQBRR, while hybrid models like HQQR and HQNN exhibit positive correlations; quantum models tend to have narrower uncertainty bounds yet identify more outliers, and statistical tests (Wilcoxon Signed-Rank) confirm significant differences in predictive uncertainties but not errors for BRR and QR.
    [codes: C-018, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that although quantum circuit configurations and qubit counts lead to significant differences in uncertainty, these changes are not directly correlated with prediction error, which complicates the interpretation of uncertainty improvements.     [codes: C-042, C-043]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work will investigate hybrid quantum models where quantum circuits perform direct prediction rather than only feature transformation, explore whether there are qubit-count thresholds beyond which adding qubits no longer improves results, and extend the proposed UQ frameworks to more complex datasets for broader validation.

The authors further employ nonparametric statistical tests (Wilcoxon Signed-Rank and Kruskal–Wallis) and introduce a risk-adjusted cost efficiency metric (RACE) to link uncertainty to financial-style performance, although all experiments are conducted on a simulator with synthetic data, limiting direct real-world inference.

=== PAPER 20e9442a73f0 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) and explicitly aims to bring quantum machine learning (QML) methods into this setting by proposing the QuLTSF model. The forecasting problem is formulated under a channel-independence assumption, where each univariate time series channel is modeled separately over L time stamps and trained using mean squared error as the objective.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-010]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors introduce QuLTSF as a hybrid model that combines classical linear neural network layers with a variational quantum circuit (VQC) hidden layer. The classical input layer maps the L-length input sequence into a 2N-dimensional vector that is fed into a hardware-efficient ansatz with K layers and circular CNOT entanglement, from which Pauli-Z expectation values are measured and passed to a classical output layer mapping quantum features to the T-step forecast horizon. All quantum and classical parameters are trained jointly using MSE loss.
    [codes: C-002, C-012, C-013, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-010]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that QuLTSF outperforms state-of-the-art linear time series forecasting models and transformer-based LTSF models on the Weather dataset across multiple forecast horizons and sequence lengths. The authors emphasize that even though simple linear models can beat complex transformer architectures, adding a hidden quantum layer yields additional performance improvements over these strong linear baselines.
    [codes: C-003, C-027, C-028, C-005, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical comparisons include three state-of-the-art linear baselines (Linear, NLinear, DLinear) and transformer-based models, with the authors noting prior work where simple autoregressive linear models can outperform transformers for LTSF. Within this setup, QuLTSF is reported to consistently outperform all baseline linear models across the tested cases, and to achieve better error than the transformer baselines as well, although statistical and RNN-based baselines are explicitly excluded from the comparison.
    [codes: C-005, C-022, C-023, C-027, C-028, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations. Methodologically, QuLTSF uses a generic hardware-efficient ansatz rather than a problem-specific circuit, and they flag the choice of ansatz as a design caveat. From an implementation perspective, they state that deploying QML-based LTSF models on actual quantum hardware is challenging due to decoherence, noise, and the barren plateau phenomenon, where gradients vanish as system size or depth increases, making optimization of VQCs difficult at scale.
    [codes: C-029, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions include searching for optimal or improved ansätze tailored to QML-based LTSF and to different datasets, recognizing ansatz design as a standalone research problem. The authors also suggest exploring improved data preprocessing such as reverse instance normalization, and call for innovations in error correction, problem-specific circuit design, and alternative optimization strategies to achieve scalable, noise-resilient QML for LTSF.     [codes: C-001, C-005, C-012, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study fixes a channel-independence condition by forecasting each univariate series separately and trains using MSE loss. The quantum model’s key hyperparameters (e.g., number of qubits N=10, number of VQC layers K=3) and the use of the Adam optimizer are reported, signaling some degree of reproducibility, and baselines include multiple linear and transformer models, although statistical and RNN baselines are omitted by design.

=== PAPER 21611a37dd85 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses the challenge of generating privacy-preserving synthetic financial data in a setting where data integrity and privacy regulations hinder access to real data, focusing on oversampling an extremely imbalanced minority class of approved withdrawal requests in a Banco BV FGTS approval dataset. Synthetic data is framed as a way to protect sensitive training data while correcting class imbalance for downstream modelling. The authors also position their work within the broader question of whether near-term quantum generative models can handle complex real-world financial datasets.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-014]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study proposes and implements a hybrid quantum-classical GAN (HQGAN) where a resource-efficient quantum circuit acts as the generator and a classical neural network with one hidden layer serves as the discriminator. The quantum generator follows a Huang et al.-inspired design using angle-embedded QNNs with a feature map and parameterized ansatz, linear controlled-Z entanglement, and a split between data qubits for feature generation and ancilla qubits to introduce nonlinearity via partial measurement and dependence of the post-measurement state on the latent vector. Due to the 2^NG capacity constraint, the authors use NG=4 data qubits and NA=1 ancilla qubit, pad the feature space to 16 dimensions, and train the HQGAN with SGD and BCE loss in a simulator environment.
    [codes: C-002, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-031, C-033]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The HQGAN failed to reach sufficient accuracy to capture the complex patterns in the financial data, exhibiting erratic MSE behavior without clear convergence toward the real data distribution. In contrast, the classical GAN displayed typical loss dynamics and a consistent reduction in MSE that eventually stabilized, highlighting that in this case the hybrid quantum approach underperformed on the financial dataset. The authors reiterate in the conclusion that the HQGAN did not achieve adequate accuracy for the target financial application.
    [codes: C-004, C-034, C-036, C-037, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper explicitly compares the HQGAN against a fully classical GAN based on DCGAN, noting that the classical model has orders of magnitude more parameters and includes batch normalization, while the HQGAN has a much smaller parameter count and lacks such normalization. Empirically, the classical GAN shows typical adversarial training behavior with generator and discriminator losses remaining close and an MSE that improves and stabilizes, whereas the HQGAN's MSE is higher and erratic and does not show convergence. The authors thus report that, under their settings, the classical GAN is more effective for financial synthetic data generation than their HQGAN.
    [codes: C-003, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors highlight that their HQGAN could not achieve the accuracy needed to learn intricate financial patterns and generalize to the complex financial dataset, underscoring current limitations of quantum-inspired methods for such data. They point out a structural constraint in the quantum generator, whose data capacity is limited by the number of data qubits (2^NG), which forced padding of features and may restrict scalability to richer datasets. They also note that the patch strategy from the reference design was omitted due to the relatively small number of features, and they acknowledge that the absence of batch normalization in the hybrid model may cause unstable training, slower convergence, and inferior sample quality. More broadly, they frame the work within the open question of whether existing quantum devices can support real-world generative learning, implicitly noting that their results suggest current approaches are not yet adequate for this financial task.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-010, C-019, C-021, C-040, C-042]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors propose exploring new normalization mechanisms tailored to quantum models to address training instabilities, and investigating alternative hybrid GAN architectures in which the quantum component is placed in the discriminator or replaced by a fully quantum GAN. These directions aim to better exploit potential advantages of quantum generative models while mitigating the limitations observed in the present HQGAN design.
    [codes: C-041, C-043]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution centers on formulating and experimentally evaluating a hybrid quantum-classical GAN with a resource-efficient quantum generator for privacy-preserving synthetic oversampling in a real-world, highly imbalanced financial approval dataset, and on empirically assessing its capability relative to a strong classical GAN baseline. By implementing a Huang et al.-inspired QNN generator with ancilla-enabled nonlinearity and adapting it to tabular financial data with specific preprocessing and padding, the paper sheds light on the near-term feasibility and limitations of quantum generative models in financial services.
    [codes: C-002, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-014, C-018, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses a large, proprietary Banco BV FGTS approval dataset with severe class imbalance (~0.4% positives) and performs structured preprocessing including feature selection, removal of the target and time variables, ordinal encoding of a categorical feature, and min–max normalization, plus feature padding to satisfy quantum generator constraints. Both HQGAN and classical GAN are trained under a shared protocol with BCE loss, identical batch size and epochs, and performance is quantitatively evaluated using mean squared error between real and synthetic distributions. The authors also design a follow-up truncated training experiment to probe divergence behavior, indicating some effort to diagnose training instability and overfitting.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-021, C-022, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-039]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper notes that, because the dataset has relatively few features, the patch-based generator strategy from the reference quantum architecture was deemed unnecessary, which affects how directly their implementation aligns with prior quantum patch-GAN designs but is not central to the main findings.
    [codes: C-019]

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames mutual fund portfolio optimization as a computationally complex, often NP-complete/NP-hard problem requiring search over many candidate portfolios, with both convex and combinatorial formulations, and focuses specifically on mutual funds and their equity-market drivers as the application domain. The authors position this as part of a broader set of mutual fund optimization problems (e.g., liquidity management, benchmark tracking) and emphasize that human investors struggle to select future winners, motivating advanced computational approaches including classical ML and QML for portfolio construction, return forecasting, and risk modelling.

It also covers NISQ-targeted algorithms like quantum walk-based portfolio optimization, QCBM-based generative models, and quantum amplitude estimation for Monte Carlo tasks, highlighting hybrid schemes where quantum subroutines are combined with classical optimization.

  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The review reports that quantum portfolio optimization has shown experimental success in the literature, including dynamic portfolio optimization and finance-focused QML models, and notes that quantum annealer and QUBO-based approaches are emerging as de facto standards for NP-hard portfolio problems. It finds that most QML work is very recent (about 68% of papers from 2019–2023), that multilayer perceptrons are the dominant classical ML technique in existing portfolio construction studies, and that mutual-fund-specific QML applications remain underexplored. The authors also highlight claims from cited works that QAOA and related quantum approaches can provide quick, higher-quality solutions or speedups for Monte Carlo sampling, while at least one cited study reports that no dynamic portfolio framework yet outperforms the covariance model.

Across the broader literature, classical baselines often include heuristic or metaheuristic optimizers, and the review notes that traditional ML/dynamic frameworks sometimes fail to beat standard covariance-based models.

They note that quantum linear-algebra techniques are not universally applicable across financial use cases and that fundamental hardware issues such as error correction, coherence time, and qubit stability remain unresolved. On the classical side, portfolio optimization is NP-complete/NP-hard, many instances are non-convex and high-dimensional, and classical algorithms and ML/DL methods can suffer from the curse of dimensionality, time and cost constraints, and getting stuck in local optima. Methodologically, the review identifies a literature gap where many studies focus on stocks rather than mutual funds, and concludes that QML for mutual fund portfolio optimization specifically has received insufficient attention.

  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The study explicitly benchmarks quantum-enhanced models against classical machine learning, claiming higher accuracy, reduced training or simulation times, and better scalability on high-dimensional data. The authors position QML as tackling challenges that classical models find insurmountable, especially in large, complex feature spaces, and they structure a dedicated comparison between quantum and classical frameworks to showcase these benefits. Reported numerical comparisons include finance accuracy gains from 85% to 92%, healthcare accuracy from 88% to 94% with 50% shorter training, and climate simulations with higher accuracy and 20% runtime reduction.
    [codes: C-016, C-017, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-034, C-037, C-046, C-070, C-071, C-072, C-073]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several substantive limitations and challenges. On hardware, they stress that quantum computing is in its infancy: current NISQ devices have a limited number of qubits, qubits are highly sensitive and prone to decoherence, and quantum gates can introduce errors, with quantum noise degrading algorithm reliability. They note that quantum error correction is extremely resource-intensive, requiring many additional qubits and computational resources. Integration with classical systems is expected to persist, and building effective hybrid architectures is described as complex and optimization-intensive. Data-related constraints include the need for large-scale, high-quality data, the prevalence of sparse, noisy, or incomplete datasets, and the requirement to adapt classical preprocessing methods for quantum settings. Algorithmically, they concede that only a few quantum algorithms like QSVM and QNN are relatively mature, with many others still in early research stages, and they emphasize that practical, scalable, and efficient QML algorithms still need significant research and development.

  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the paper proposes advancing practical, scalable quantum machine learning algorithms and explores several domain-specific directions. In logistics and supply chain management, they suggest designing QAOA-based methods for optimizing supply chains. In healthcare, they foresee QNNs that integrate large-scale genomic and imaging data to revolutionize diagnosis, and they highlight quantum reinforcement learning for creating intelligent agents capable of optimized decisions in dynamic environments. They also propose that hybrid quantum–classical models could support large-scale analytics across finance, climate modeling, and marketing, and explicitly call for examining the societal and ethical implications of quantum-enhanced AI.

They argue that, compared with prior work, their distinctive contribution is the formulation and demonstration of this quantum-AI framework, its explicit integration into existing predictive systems, and its application across multiple real-world domains such as finance, healthcare, and climate modeling, accompanied by quantitative comparisons with classical approaches.
    [codes: C-002, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper states an intention to provide rigorous and reproducible experiments, including a dedicated section describing experimental setups and datasets from finance (market trends, risk data), healthcare (gene sequences and diagnostic imaging), and climate modeling (atmospheric simulations). The workflow is explicitly hybrid: classical tools are used for data cleaning, outlier removal, and sample-size reduction; then QML models such as QSVM and QNN are selected to match dataset characteristics, with hybrid quantum–classical architectures where quantum algorithms perform optimization and prediction. Evaluation compares quantum-enhanced and classical models using metrics like accuracy, computation or training time, and scalability, implemented via common quantum software frameworks (Qiskit, TensorFlow Quantum, PennyLane). However, the codes provided do not specify dataset names, sizes, or detailed experimental settings, so the claim of methodological rigor rests mainly on high-level descriptions.

It explains core quantum computing principles such as superposition, entanglement, and interference, highlighting quantum parallelism and the ability to explore many possibilities simultaneously as a basis for exponential computational power, particularly in high-dimensional feature spaces. It defines predictive analytics and quantum machine learning, emphasizing that QML aims to enhance productivity and accuracy while reducing cost, and positions quantum-enhanced AI as a transformative but still emerging approach that will complement rather than replace classical computing. The authors also emphasize that hybrid quantum–classical models can leverage the strengths of both paradigms across application areas like finance, healthcare, marketing, and logistics.

=== PAPER 26d9ab80fc82 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles stock market trend prediction in the context of rapidly growing financial data and increasing model complexity, positioning quantum finance as a domain where quantum machine learning could offer advantages over traditional methods. It formulates the problem as forecasting discrete market trend regimes (e.g., bullish/bearish/range-bound) for 15 Chinese stock indices using a hidden quantum Markov model that operates on discretized time-series data. The authors motivate this with the need for innovative solutions that can better handle complex, high-dimensional market dynamics than classical HMMs, which they say overlook some influencing factors.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-016, C-021, C-022]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study employs a Hidden Quantum Markov Model (HQMM), where conditional observation probabilities are defined via Kraus operators acting on a density matrix, allowing the model to retain historical information and quantum coherence. Multiple Kraus operators can be associated with different market conditions or trading patterns, and the quantum state is evolved and optimized under a Stiefel-manifold constraint while constructing a likelihood function from historical observations. Because HQMMs require discrete inputs, the authors develop two preprocessing pipelines—an even discretization baseline and a GMM–MVTF pipeline that transforms 30‑day windows of continuous OHLCV data into six discrete states—followed by HQMM training and prediction using a rule based on minimizing a cost Jn.
    [codes: C-011, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-023, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-036]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that HQMM training, measured by description accuracy (DA), converges quickly—DA increases rapidly within five iterations and stabilizes after about 40. In backtests on 15 SSE/SZSE stock indices, the HQMM with GMM–MVTF discretization achieves the highest average capital (1,404,827 CNY) and the highest reported comparative growth rate (4.96%), while the HQMM with even discretization yields 1,362,922 CNY and 1.59%, and the classical HMM yields 1,390,860 CNY and 3.73%. They also highlight that the HQMM approaches require 12 minutes versus 40 minutes for the classical HMM, and claim a computational complexity of O(T n w) for HQMM compared with O(T n²) for HMM.
    [codes: C-033, C-034, C-035, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The HQMM variants are explicitly benchmarked against a classical HMM trained under distinct preprocessing schemes to highlight the benefits of quantum coherence. While the classical HMM attains a 3.73% average comparative growth rate and 40‑minute runtime, the HQMM with even discretization underperforms in growth (1.59%) but matches the HQMM with GMM–MVTF in runtime (12 minutes). The GMM–MVTF‑discretized HQMM is presented as superior overall, combining the fastest computation, the highest comparative growth rate (4.96%), and the largest resulting capital versus both the classical HMM and the HQMM using even discretization.
    [codes: C-011, C-013, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that their HQMM-based algorithm can currently only handle discretized time-series data, meaning continuous financial time series cannot be modeled directly. They also note that straightforward even discretization may severely distort the original data and harm model effectiveness, motivating their more elaborate GMM–MVTF pipeline. In the conclusions, they state that data preprocessing becomes a bottleneck for high-frequency markets, implying scalability and latency concerns for real-time or intraday use. Beyond technical aspects, they caution that financial institutions adopting such quantum-inspired algorithms should establish validation protocols to ensure algorithmic transparency.
    [codes: C-016, C-023, C-024, C-046, C-047]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The conclusion indicates that future research should further enhance model performance and develop more mature benchmarks, suggesting continued optimization of the HQMM framework and associated preprocessing pipelines. They specifically point to several directions for improvement, although these are not detailed in the extracted codes, and link future work to both algorithmic refinement and more robust evaluation standards.
    [codes: C-045]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in applying Hidden Quantum Markov Models to stock prediction, stating that prior work has not implemented HQMMs in this domain because continuous data discretization remained an unsolved challenge. To address this gap, they introduce a GMM–MVTF discretization pipeline and a hybrid quantum computing model for stock trend forecasting, and argue that this combination enables HQMMs to demonstrate quantum-coherence-related advantages over classical HMMs in financial forecasting.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-018, C-019, C-020]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses real daily OHLCV data for 15 indices from the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges, with a clear temporal split into training, validation, and testing periods to reduce look-ahead bias. The authors detail two discretization procedures—an even-threshold scheme and a GMM–MVTF approach with specified parameter choices (e.g., six clusters and five Gaussian components) and provide explicit formulas such as the MVTF weighting and DA metric interpretation, as well as optimization on a Stiefel manifold. They also describe a simple trading simulation rule mapping predicted states to long/short positions to translate predictions into capital outcomes and highlight robustness of the initial density matrix across different K values, which together enhance transparency and potential reproducibility of their experiments.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-015, C-021, C-022, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors extrapolate potential real-world applications, suggesting that their HQMM-based model could support real-time signal generation for bullish, bearish, or range-bound regimes, thus enabling dynamic portfolio adjustments, optimized risk controls, and data-driven allocation shifts. They further claim that validating quantum advantage in financial forecasting opens the door to practical deployment of quantum-inspired prediction models by investors and institutions, including enhanced quantitative strategies with automatic stop-loss triggers and drawdown control.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-019, C-020, C-043, C-044]

=== PAPER 2849bbcb864e (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets credit-risk assessment, where models must balance predictive accuracy with interpretability to satisfy regulatory and institutional demands for transparent, auditable reasoning. It formulates default prediction on the Taiwan credit card dataset as a supervised binary classification problem with 23 input attributes and a markedly imbalanced label distribution (~22.1% defaults).
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-015, C-016, C-017]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a single-qudit variational quantum neural network in which both data features and trainable parameters are co-encoded into a unitary generated by the full su(d) Lie algebra, enabling exploration of the entire d-dimensional Hilbert space. The circuit uses a compact Hamiltonian where trainable weights appear as linear coefficients of input features, with data re-uploading across multiple layers to enhance nonlinearity and feature cross-talk, and all data and variational parts condensed into a single unitary operator. Training employs a bounded nonlinear remapping of x_j w_j, cross-entropy loss with L2 (ridge) regularization, and the Adam optimizer; su(d) generators are constructed algorithmically in symmetric, antisymmetric, and diagonal sets and implemented in matrix form.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the Taiwan credit card default dataset, the qudit QNN achieves a macro-averaged F1-score of about 0.667 with 384 parameters, consistently outperforming logistic regression and closely matching a classical neural network while reaching random-forest-level macro-F1. Its edit distance in feature ranking relative to LR (~20.9) is statistically indistinguishable from that of RF, despite using far fewer parameters (384 vs. 3927 for RF). Under feature poisoning (selected inputs replaced with noise), the QNN attains the highest classification performance, exhibiting superior robustness and competitive accuracy while maintaining moderate interpretability according to the introduced metrics; the authors argue these findings suggest quantum approaches may uncover complex financial patterns that may elude conventional methods.
    [codes: C-005, C-008, C-011, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-044, C-047]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The QNN is benchmarked against logistic regression, random forest, and a classical neural network. It consistently outperforms LR and reaches or closely matches RF and NN in macro-F1, while using substantially fewer parameters than RF. In feature-ranking interpretability, the QNN’s edit distance from LR’s ranking is similar to RF’s, and poisoning-based metrics (BIS/WIS) indicate RF preserves the strongest alignment with the LR reference, whereas the QNN attains the best poisoned-data F1 but only moderate interpretability. The authors also note that although the classical NN slightly exceeds the QNN’s F1 on clean data, it lacks an intrinsic feature-ranking mechanism, whereas LR and the QNN provide explicit parameter–feature relationships.
    [codes: C-005, C-010, C-018, C-019, C-033, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-044, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: A key methodological limitation acknowledged by the authors is that parameter-shift rules connecting partial derivatives to circuit observables are not yet established for their specific single-qudit Hamiltonian encoding, constraining gradient estimation techniques for hardware implementations. In terms of trade-offs, they characterize the QNN as offering only moderate interpretability relative to RF under poisoning tests, and as slightly lagging classical NNs in accuracy on uncorrupted data, indicating the approach does not dominate classical baselines on all criteria.
    [codes: C-027, C-042, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose extending their architecture to multi-qudit implementations as a direction for future work, presumably to increase expressivity and explore scalability beyond a single qudit setting.
    [codes: C-048]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is framed as a compact, single-qudit QNN that co-encodes data features and trainable parameters via the full su(d) generator set, thereby exploring the entire Hilbert space while preserving a transparent correspondence between learned weights and input feature importance. They emphasize an interpretability mechanism where feature importance is inferred from learned coefficient magnitudes, supported by multilayer expansions in which weights add linearly at first order and cumulative weight size relates to influence. Additionally, they introduce two custom interpretability metrics—edit distance between model and LR feature rankings, and a poisoning-based Weighted Interpretability Score—to quantitatively assess how faithfully a model’s learned weights focus on informative features.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-006, C-007, C-013, C-014, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: The study uses the well-known Taiwan credit card default dataset with 30,000 records, 23 attributes, and a 22.1% default rate, providing a realistic imbalanced benchmark. The QNN ansatz is rigorously specified via the full su(d) generator construction, categorized into symmetric, antisymmetric, and diagonal sets and implemented in matrix form, and the training pipeline is clearly described (nonlinear remapping, cross-entropy plus ridge regularization, Adam optimizer). Interpretability is operationalized through two explicit metrics: edit distance to LR’s feature ranking and a poisoning-based Weighted Interpretability Score in which models are expected to downweight corrupted features. The authors also analyze how multilayer weight accumulation affects feature influence, arguing that small cumulative weights indicate negligible effect while large weights signal strong contributions, thereby grounding their feature-ranking procedure in the circuit’s series expansion.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors argue that finance applications, particularly credit risk, require models that reconcile strong predictive performance with explicit, auditable reasoning, and suggest that quantum approaches may have the potential to uncover complex patterns in financial behavior beyond conventional techniques. They further observe that increasing the number of QNN layers systematically enhances classification performance, indicating a depth–performance relationship in this qudit-based architecture.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-011, C-014, C-047]

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets credit risk assessment for loan default prediction, using a real-world Kaggle credit risk dataset with 24 normalized features and binary default labels, and frames it as a supervised binary classification problem suitable for a hybrid quantum–classical pipeline. Each latent feature is angle-encoded onto a single qubit using RY gates, forming a four-qubit product state that is processed by a VQC composed of Hadamard and trainable unitary U(θq) gates, with only the quantum parameters optimized while the classical extractor remains fixed; measurement in the computational basis produces expectation values that are fed into a final sigmoid output layer for classification. The quantum circuit is implemented in PennyLane as a 4‑qubit VQC, trained with binary cross-entropy loss and the Adam optimizer on an 80/20 stratified split of the credit dataset.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets fraud and anomaly detection in IoT-assisted financial transaction networks, framed as a need for a pipeline that combines anomaly detection with verifiability and auditability rather than optimizing a single accuracy metric. It formulates the problem as ensuring that fraud detection outcomes are cryptographically verifiable, resistant to identity-correlation and replay attacks, and grounded in a trustworthy end-to-end channel between enrolled devices and on-chain decisions.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-005, C-020]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The quantum component uses GHZ–θ quantum state verification followed by a quantum support vector classifier/variational circuit that encodes fraud features via a ZZFeatureMap and a trainable ansatz composed of RY, RZ, and CX gates under a four-qubit constraint. GHZ fidelity checks with a threshold (F < 0.5 leads to rejection) are integrated before learning, and accepted samples are processed by the QSVC/VQC-style classifier with a fraud decision threshold at score ≥ 0.75.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-013, C-016, C-019, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-032]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, classical baselines such as Random Forest and XGBoost achieve balanced accuracy above 77%, whereas the QSVC alone attains about 42.1 ± 2.8% balanced accuracy under the stated NISQ-era constraints. Ablation studies suggest that amplitude encoding with angle re-uploading at moderate variational depth (L ≈ 6–8) improves discrimination before saturating, and SMOTE-ENN yields the highest recall under extreme class sparsity. Despite lower balanced accuracy, QuanFraud attains the maximum composite Trust Score and is presented as prioritizing verifiability and security over raw BA.
    [codes: C-003, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors report that strong classical baselines (Random Forest and XGBoost) outperform QSVC in balanced accuracy, exceeding 77% BA compared to around 42% for QSVC under comparable, leakage-safe settings. They emphasize that while classical models win on discrimination metrics, QuanFraud is distinguished by its integration of GHZ/θ verification, DIDs, kernel privacy, audit trail, and calibration, which classical-only baselines lack.
    [codes: C-003, C-029, C-011, C-038]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations of its quantum classifier: the QSVC is restricted to roughly four qubits, limiting feature expressivity and entanglement depth, which impairs separability of the fraud classes. Variational layers are susceptible to barren plateaus, leading to vanishing gradients that impede training. Device or simulator noise is noted as disturbing kernel estimates and margins, with mitigation and depth control only partially reducing drift. The authors also state that identity mechanisms alone cannot stop attacks from legitimate but compromised devices, so detection and additional controls remain necessary, and they call for further validation using n-fold (10-fold) schemes beyond their current analysis.
    [codes: C-021, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work is described as focusing on improving QML accuracy without sacrificing verifiability by investigating stronger quantum neural architectures, richer feature embeddings with re-uploading, and tuned hybrid quantum–classical models with calibrated thresholds. The authors also explicitly call for additional validation through extended n-fold (10-fold) validation mechanisms to further substantiate their findings.
    [codes: C-035, C-040]

The authors argue that prior work has focused either on predictive accuracy or on blockchain immutability alone and has generally lacked the combination of verification, governance, and trust scoring that QuanFraud offers.

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum computing as both an opportunity and a risk for the financial system: it examines how quantum algorithms might improve stress testing, macroeconomic analysis, risk management, payments and portfolio optimisation, while also analysing how quantum-capable adversaries could undermine widely used cryptography and thereby financial stability. It emphasises that while quantum computers are still experimental, their future impact on financial institutions, infrastructures and macroeconomic outcomes could be profound, and highlights specific channels such as online/mobile banking, payment transactions and VPN communications as particularly vulnerable to quantum-enabled attacks.

Throughout, they stress that quantum and classical computers are expected to complement each other, with redundancy via additional qubits used to address noise and error correction challenges.

Cited examples include quadratic speedup expectations for some risk-management algorithms, a stylised VaR example where a quantum computer could compute risk for a one‑million‑asset portfolio in about 30 minutes, potential improvements in Monte Carlo-based risk assessment, and liquidity savings of roughly CAD 240–276 million in a quantum-optimised payment system study. The authors further cite work showing that a quantum annealer solved a real business cycle dynamic programming problem in about 3% of the classical computation time and discuss synergies with AI, including expected acceleration in reinforcement learning and deep learning training. On the risk side, they quote model-based estimates that a successful quantum-enabled cyberattack on financial infrastructures could generate expected GDP losses of about 0.1% within five years, rising to over 1% within 15–20 years, and report from Project Leap that post-quantum cryptography increased VPN setup latency, with implications for time-critical services such as instant payments.

For risk management, they describe anticipated quadratic speedups and illustrate classical intractability in systemic network-risk problems where classical computation would exceed the age of the universe. In macroeconomic modelling, they cite evidence that a quantum annealer solved an RBC dynamic programming problem in 3% of the classical runtime (around a 33x speedup), and in Project Leap they compare the latency of legacy versus post-quantum cryptography in VPN setup, finding additional overhead for the quantum-safe schemes.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper stresses numerous limitations and caveats. Technically, practical quantum computers do not yet exist and it is impossible to know if or when they will; current devices are noisy, with fragile qubits requiring strong isolation and substantial redundancy, and there is no consensus that quantum supremacy has been achieved. Quantum computing is suitable only for a narrow class of tasks, and data loading and read‑out steps can become bottlenecks, so real‑life use cases with practical quantum advantage are expected to be few, with initial gains mostly modest speedups. Even where gains exist, classical supercomputers may remain more cost‑effective economically. The authors also highlight major obstacles to integrating quantum with AI, such as costs and technical limitations. On the security side, they emphasise that migrating to quantum‑safe cryptography is complex, time‑consuming and resource‑intensive; post‑quantum schemes can introduce latency that strains time‑critical use cases like instant payments; and quantum key distribution, though promising, currently faces scalability and integration challenges. In addition, they underline the harvest‑now‑decrypt‑later threat: data already being intercepted can be decrypted once a cryptographically relevant quantum computer—whose arrival is highly uncertain but possibly within 5–30 years—is available, making the cyber threat imminent even though functional quantum advantage in finance may be delayed.

=== PAPER 2a0770a1a995 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames financial forecasting as two supervised learning problems at Itaú Unibanco: predicting which customers will churn in the next three months based on the previous six months of behavior, with an operational focus on high‑precision intervention, and estimating SME credit default probabilities using a large tabular risk dataset evaluated via Gini score.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-017, C-019, C-039, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The work explores two quantum‑inspired/quantum approaches: (i) a DPP‑enhanced Random Forest that replaces uniform subsampling with Determinantal Point Process sampling, including a novel batched DPP-RF procedure and corresponding quantum circuits for DPP sampling with theoretically favorable gate complexity, and (ii) quantum neural networks using orthogonal and compound layers built from RBS‑based orthogonal circuits, compound matrices acting on fixed Hamming‑weight subspaces, and custom data loaders (unary, RY, H) plus an expectation‑per‑subspace loss to compress exponential output. For hardware experiments, the churn DPP pipeline is made hardware‑ready via PCA and small batches, while QNNs are trained classically and then deployed as quantum inference circuits on IBM hardware using the trained parameters.
    [codes: C-006, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-016, C-026, C-028, C-031, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-047]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: For churn prediction, the DPP‑RF model improves precision at low recall from about 71.6% to 77.5% (about a 6% absolute increase) and yields modest gains in withdrawals captured and maximum possible withdrawals captured relative to the baseline Random Forest. For credit risk, orthogonal and compound‑layer networks achieve Gini scores comparable to a classical residual baseline while using far fewer trainable parameters. On quantum hardware, the IBM processor reproduces classical/simulator DPP performance only for very small matrix dimensions, and for QNNs the OrthoResNN’s hardware Gini is close to the noiseless simulation and can be brought even closer with error mitigation, whereas the compound model’s hardware performance degrades substantially.
    [codes: C-002, C-007, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-029, C-036, C-043, C-044, C-049, C-050, C-052]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors report that classical DPP‑enhanced Random Forests outperform a standard Random Forest baseline on precision, efficiency, and business bottom‑line KPIs for churn, despite higher training time. For credit risk, the OrthoResNN with orthogonal layers matches the baseline residual network’s Gini with substantially fewer parameters, and OpenML benchmarks show only small performance differences between orthogonal/quantum‑inspired architectures and standard feed‑forward networks, suggesting parity rather than clear dominance. Quantum hardware results are compared mainly to classical/noiseless simulations rather than to separate classical baselines.
    [codes: C-007, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-043, C-044, C-046, C-029, C-049, C-050]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations. Classical DPP sampling remains computationally costly, with naive methods taking exponential time, and even practical batched DPP‑RF training is much slower than a standard Random Forest and sensitive to batch size choices. Quantum DPP hardware experiments require strong problem reduction (PCA to very low dimensions and small batches), and the IBM processor matches simulator performance only for very small matrices; as dimensions grow, hardware noise leads to degraded classifier performance. For QNNs, hardware inference was limited to a small subsample of 300 test points, and orthogonal versus compound layers show different robustness, with the compound architecture performing much worse on hardware. The authors also stress that error‑mitigation techniques, while helpful for OrthoResNN, add overhead, rely partly on heuristics, and may not scale efficiently to larger circuit sizes.
    [codes: C-014, C-021, C-022, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-048, C-050, C-053]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that quantum‑inspired methods already offer benefits as classical ML enhancements but anticipate greater impact as quantum hardware improves. They highlight that quantum DPP sampling can in principle achieve lower complexity than classical methods and that their quantum circuits for DPPs have favorable gate counts and depths, implying potential future runtime advantages once hardware noise and scale constraints are addressed. More broadly, they expect these quantum or quantum‑inspired architectures to run faster and achieve better forecasting performance with more advanced devices.
    [codes: C-004, C-015, C-026, C-054, C-055]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is positioned as demonstrating how quantum machine learning ideas—specifically DPP‑based sampling and orthogonal/compound QNN layers—can improve real‑world financial forecasting tasks at a major bank. Methodologically, the authors introduce quantum algorithms for DPP sampling coupled with a novel batched DPP-RF training procedure, and propose quantum neural architectures with orthogonal and compound layers that reduce redundancy, mitigate vanishing gradients, and, via a pyramid circuit, exactly represent the special orthogonal group while using significantly fewer parameters than classical layers. They further claim empirical evidence that these quantum‑inspired models can match or modestly improve classical performance on finance use cases and benchmarks, and that orthogonal layers are particularly NISQ‑friendly based on hardware experiments.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-009, C-010, C-012, C-016, C-032, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-043, C-051, C-054]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: The study uses large, realistic proprietary datasets for churn (304k points, 153 features) and SME credit risk (~141.5k observations, 32 features), with clearly described temporal splits and business KPIs such as precision at low recall, withdrawals captured, and Gini scores. The authors explore multiple model architectures (residual, orthogonal, compound) and report results across internal use cases and public benchmarks, including ROC‑AUC comparisons that show small differences, suggesting careful benchmarking. For hardware experiments, they transparently describe dimensionality reduction via PCA, batch sizing, and the constrained test subsample of 300 points, as well as the hybrid setup where models are trained classically and then run on quantum processors with error mitigation. These details indicate attention to experimental realism and to making the methods feasible under current NISQ constraints.
    [codes: C-005, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-025, C-028, C-031, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-052]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper emphasizes structural properties of its circuits: RBS‑based orthogonal layers preserve Hamming weight, compound layers act blockwise on fixed Hamming‑weight subspaces, and orthogonality is claimed to reduce redundancy and help avoid vanishing gradients; the expectation‑per‑subspace loss is motivated as a way to capture information about the output distribution despite exponential Hilbert space size. The authors also interpret the hardware results as evidence that orthogonal layers are more NISQ‑friendly than compound layers.
    [codes: C-032, C-034, C-035, C-038, C-051]

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses bank account fraud detection as a critical issue for corporate sustainability and loss minimization, emphasizing that fraud patterns evolve over time and are inherently challenging to detect, causing substantial revenue losses and severe harm to organizations. The authors frame fraud as a Devastating Evolutionary Dynamic Entity (DEDE), characterized by evolutionary, increasingly effective methods and large financial impact, and highlight technical challenges such as strong class imbalance and high‑dimensional, non‑normal data. Fraud detection is thus formulated as a difficult, dynamic classification problem where quantum machine learning might eventually offer benefits despite current practical constraints.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-007]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study uses a Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) with a quantum kernel built via angle encoding, mapping eight selected, scaled features to eight qubits after removing columns with high missingness and dropping remaining missing values. Due to hardware constraints, the quantum part operates in a hybrid quantum‑classical setting on a reduced, balanced sample of 750 instances (250 fraud, 500 non‑fraud), with the quantum model trained and evaluated over six repeated runs to obtain key performance indicators. The authors attribute their quantum design choices—including feature reduction to eight qubits and stringent preprocessing—to limitations of current quantum hardware and QSVMs’ difficulty handling missing data.
    [codes: C-002, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-031, C-034]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Classical state‑of‑the‑art models, specifically XGBoost, achieve high ROC‑AUC scores between 89% and 95% on the synthetic bank‑fraud datasets. The quantum model underperforms XGBoost but is described as doing a fair job or achieving a reasonable level of performance given the restricted number of qubits, limited samples, and quantum kernel limitations. Across the biased dataset variants, KPI metrics such as F1, ROC‑AUC, precision, and recall decrease relative to the base variant, with Variant 1 showing a slight drop, Variants 2 and 3 a more significant decline, and Variants 4 and 5 recovering somewhat yet still below the base and Variant 1.

The authors explicitly state that under current hardware limitations the hybrid quantum‑classical method does not outperform classical methods and that the quantum model underperforms compared to XGBoost, though they regard its constrained performance as moderately good. This comparison underscores that, for this fraud detection task and current resources, classical methods remain superior while quantum models are still exploratory.
    [codes: C-003, C-017, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors repeatedly emphasize hardware constraints as the biggest limitation, noting that current quantum computers and quantum kernels restrict the number of qubits and usable samples, and generally require substantial computational resources and large datasets to reach performance levels comparable to classical models. These constraints forced them to remove columns with over 25% missing values, reduce the feature set to eight qubits, and work with a small, balanced sample of 750 instances, which they argue contributes to weaker generalization and lower KPIs for the quantum model. They also acknowledge that repeated kernel runs and limited samples introduce additional overhead and likely impair performance, and more broadly that quantum computing is promising but currently impractical for widespread corporate deployment due to resource demands and hardware limitations.

For methodological refinement, the authors recommend using synthetic data without missing values in future studies to better assess the full potential of quantum‑enhanced methods without heavy preprocessing constraints. They further propose exploring a broader range of quantum algorithms for fraud detection beyond the specific QSVM‑based approach used in this study.
    [codes: C-037, C-039, C-040]

On the technical side, they present their work as an early demonstration of a hybrid quantum‑classical fraud detection pipeline using quantum encoding and a quantum SVM on a bias‑aware synthetic bank account fraud dataset, arguing that the observed moderate quantum performance under stringent resource constraints is promising evidence of quantum computing’s potential in this domain.

=== PAPER 2a9cd8a96604 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets anomaly detection formulated as a one‑class, unsupervised learning problem, where the goal is to characterize normal data despite limited label information. It adopts the support vector data description (SVDD) perspective of enclosing normal data within a minimum‑volume hypersphere in feature space.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose Quantum Support Vector Data Description (QSVDD), which replaces classical SVDD’s feature map with a quantum feature map implemented via amplitude encoding, a variational QCNN circuit, and a final embedding/measurement stage. The QCNN ansatz is chosen for its shallow depth, logarithmic parameter scaling, trainability (including avoidance of barren plateaus), parameter sharing, and pooling that halves the number of active qubits at each stage; the hypersphere center is typically fixed at zero and the regularization term on circuit parameters is omitted. The measurement plus last convolution layer are interpreted as a parameterized measurement, and the latent feature-space dimension (number of Pauli observables) is treated as a tunable hyperparameter, ultimately fixed at nine in experiments to balance performance and computational cost.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-005, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the authors report that setting the hypersphere center to zero is practical and effective, and that QSVDD’s performance improves as the latent-space dimension increases up to nine, after which gains saturate. On MNIST, QSVDD achieves a mean AUC of 83.13%, outperforming QAE (70.54%) and DSVDD (70.32%), and on Fashion‑MNIST it achieves a mean AUC of 80.59% versus 76.69% (QAE) and 76.05% (DSVDD). Across tasks, QSVDD shows lower standard deviations than the baselines, and the authors emphasize its logarithmic growth in circuit depth and parameter count as an efficiency and stability advantage over QAE-based approaches.
    [codes: C-003, C-011, C-013, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-038]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classically, SVDD and Deep SVDD (DSVDD) are used as conceptual and empirical baselines: DSVDD replaces the kernel map with a neural network but still suffers from kernel‑matrix or network scaling issues. The authors argue that kernel methods incur poor O(m^2) scaling and memory requirements, and that QSVDD, with fewer parameters, nonetheless outperforms DSVDD in most cases. They also compare to a QAE-based quantum baseline, configuring QSVDD, QAE, and DSVDD with similar parameter budgets (75, 78, and 92 parameters respectively) and noting that QAE’s parameter and depth scaling is worse than QSVDD’s. The reported mean AUCs on MNIST and Fashion‑MNIST consistently favor QSVDD over both QAE and DSVDD.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that classical kernel-based SVDD methods suffer from poor computational scaling and memory usage, motivating alternatives such as deep or quantum feature mappings. They also note that increasing the latent-space dimension raises computational time due to the larger number of Pauli observables to be measured, which leads them to cap the latent space at nine dimensions in practice. Furthermore, they stress that shallow circuits are imperative given NISQ devices’ limits on reliably executable circuit size, implicitly limiting the depth and complexity of their approach.
    [codes: C-006, C-020, C-021, C-029]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors suggest that QSVDD’s advantage may become more pronounced on inherently quantum data, indicating an intended shift from classical image benchmarks to quantum-native domains. They also call for further optimization of data encoding, VQC architecture, measurement design, and classical optimization algorithms to better tailor QSVDD to specific applications. Methodologically, they propose exploring more general quantum measurements, such as POVMs, beyond projective measurements, and investigating classical-to-quantum transfer learning as an additional extension.
    [codes: C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The core contribution claimed is the introduction of Quantum Support Vector Data Description (QSVDD), an unsupervised anomaly‑detection framework that combines SVDD’s minimum‑volume hypersphere principle with a compact, shallow QCNN-based quantum feature map, whose parameter count scales logarithmically with the number of input qubits. The authors position this as a compact, trainable, and near‑term‑oriented alternative to both kernel‑based SVDD and quantum autoencoder approaches for one‑class anomaly detection.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-005, C-007, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-028, C-031]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper grounds QSVDD in the classical SVDD and Deep SVDD formulations and clearly specifies circuit design choices such as amplitude encoding, QCNN structure, and measurement as a parameterized readout. The authors explore the impact of varying latent feature dimension, then fix it at nine for subsequent experiments due to computational overhead from additional observables; they also ensure comparable parameter budgets across QSVDD, QAE, and DSVDD to support fair comparison. In benchmarking, they simplify the QAE anomaly detector by omitting decoding, arguing it is unnecessary for AD, and provide complete numerical QSVDD simulation results in an appendix to support reproducibility claims.
    [codes: C-005, C-007, C-008, C-012, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-029, C-036, C-038]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors emphasize that the compact circuit and parameter design of QSVDD—enabled by QCNN depth and parameter scaling—makes it especially suitable for implementation on near‑term quantum devices with limited resources. They also reiterate the practical importance of shallow circuits for NISQ hardware and highlight that lower variability in QSVDD’s performance compared to the baselines may be beneficial in applications requiring stable anomaly detection performance.
