=== PAPER 2abf80ef91e3 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses multivariate time-series forecasting, including stock price prediction, electricity load, and weather, formulating it as predicting future target values over a forecasting horizon from historical feature vectors and training via a mean squared error loss. The authors motivate this by arguing that traditional methods like ARIMA and exponential smoothing, as well as deep models such as LSTMs and Transformers, struggle with complex nonlinear patterns, high dimensionality, and long-term dependencies, and propose a hybrid quantum-classical model using PQCs to better capture such patterns.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-028, C-034]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The quantum method is a NISQ-oriented variational gate-based approach where time-series features, compressed by a classical encoder to match the qubit count, are angle-encoded into a parameterized quantum circuit composed of stacked layers of single-qubit rotations and entangling two-qubit gates. The PQC outputs expectation values (e.g., Pauli-Z) on each qubit, which are then passed to a classical decoder; the whole hybrid model (encoder–PQC–decoder) is trained end-to-end with gradient-based optimization using the parameter-shift rule, implemented in a PyTorch–PennyLane framework with simulator and optional IBM Qiskit/Amazon Braket backends and hyperparameters such as 4–12 qubits, depth 1–5, and standard learning-rate and batch-size ranges.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across electricity load, stock price, and weather forecasting datasets, the authors report that the hybrid quantum-classical model achieves lower MSE and MAE and higher R² than classical baselines, with example hybrid performance figures of MSE=0.008, MAE=0.072, R²=0.94 for electricity load; MSE=0.014, MAE=0.088, R²=0.90 for stock prices; and MSE=0.01, MAE=0.075, R²=0.92 for weather. Robustness experiments indicate resilience to moderate quantum noise and varying circuit depth, while an ablation study suggests that including quantum components improves the forecasting metrics relative to a purely classical version of the same architecture.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-038]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The hybrid model is compared against state-of-the-art classical baselines including LSTM, Transformers, and ARIMA, using common forecasting metrics (MSE, MAE, R²) under a shared cross-validation protocol. The authors claim that the hybrid quantum-classical architecture consistently outperforms these baselines on all evaluated datasets, particularly in regimes with nonlinear dynamics and low signal-to-noise ratios, and that a hybrid variant with quantum components also outperforms an otherwise similar architecture without quantum components in ablation studies.
    [codes: C-003, C-006, C-007, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-038]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The main acknowledged limitation is that the model’s performance degrades significantly when quantum noise levels are high and when circuits become too deep, indicating sensitivity to current NISQ hardware constraints on noise and circuit depth. The authors’ discussion of robustness to only moderate noise and their positioning of the work as NISQ-oriented implicitly bound the demonstrated performance to relatively shallow, low-noise settings.
    [codes: C-036, C-037, C-005]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose exploring alternative quantum circuit architectures and training strategies to further improve performance and scalability of hybrid models, and they identify the investigation of error mitigation techniques as a key future direction to enhance robustness under quantum noise. These directions are framed as necessary steps to address the current sensitivity to hardware noise and depth constraints.
    [codes: C-039, C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The claimed contribution is an end-to-end trainable hybrid quantum-classical forecasting architecture that integrates a classical encoder, a PQC-based quantum processor, and a classical decoder to capture complex temporal patterns in multivariate time series, positioned as bridging the gap between earlier theoretical quantum models and practical forecasting applications. The authors also highlight the provision of a comparatively comprehensive empirical evaluation—across multiple datasets, classical baselines, robustness analysis, and ablation studies—as a response to prior work that focused mainly on theory with limited empirical validation, and they frame the work as showcasing the potential of NISQ-compatible hybrid approaches.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-032, C-038, C-005]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study defines a clear MSE training objective and uses standard optimizers (Adam or RMSProp with learning-rate scheduling) within a PyTorch–PennyLane implementation, specifying hyperparameter ranges for qubits, circuit depth, learning rate, and batch size. The evaluation uses multiple benchmark datasets (electricity load, stock prices, weather), a 5-fold cross-validation protocol with a defined train/validation/test split, and standard forecasting metrics (MSE, MAE, R²), and includes robustness and ablation analyses that vary noise and quantum components. The paper notes support for both simulator and real-hardware backends (IBM Qiskit or Amazon Braket), though the codes emphasize simulation and do not detail full hardware results.
    [codes: C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-036, C-038]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors argue that hybrid quantum-classical models can mitigate current quantum hardware limitations—such as noise and limited qubit coherence—by combining quantum and classical strengths, and they present the work as an illustration of the potential of such NISQ-era approaches for complex forecasting tasks. They also explicitly identify that prior quantum time-series studies have mainly emphasized theoretical aspects and lacked comprehensive empirical evaluation, which motivates their applied focus.

=== PAPER 2ae3455aa47b (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) as a key strategy to harness NISQ-era devices for solving classically intractable problems across domains, including finance modelling and specific financial tasks such as portfolio optimization and risk analysis. Financial use cases are formulated mainly as combinatorial optimization (Markowitz mean–variance) and sampling/estimation problems (risk analysis, derivative pricing), to be mapped into Hamiltonians or variational circuits within a hybrid quantum–classical framework.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-044, C-063, C-064, C-070]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors review several VQA families—VQE, QAOA, and QNNs—as hybrid quantum–classical algorithms built from parameterized quantum circuits with shallow-depth ansätze motivated by NISQ constraints. They detail how VQE relies on the Rayleigh–Ritz variational bound with an ansatz U(θ), QAOA uses a problem-specific alternating operator ansatz for combinatorial optimization, and QNNs are treated as parametrized circuits with specific layer structures and data-encoding schemes; optimization typically uses gradients via the parameter-shift rule or alternative optimizers, and noise is addressed through shallow circuits, error mitigation, and QEC methods such as QVECTOR.
    [codes: C-003, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-046, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-068, C-069]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The review reports that cited VQE experiments achieve chemical accuracy on small molecules such as H2, LiH, and BeH2, including a hardware H2 demonstration with dissociation energy error within chemical accuracy. For QAOA on MaxCut, the authors report an approximation ratio of ~0.755 at p=1 and above 0.9 at p=2 under ideal simulation, surpassing the Goemans–Williamson bound. They also cite QNN-based results, including 94.3% accuracy in thoracic CT classification, improved Sharpe ratios in quantum portfolio optimization, a benchmark table of QNN performance on molecular energy prediction, and NISQ-era VQA benchmarks across domains; further claims include strong ML correlations in material-science pipelines, significant error reduction via mitigation, polynomial scaling–driven screening efficiency, and high-fidelity quantum generative models with faster convergence. In finance specifically, they reference QAOA-based Markowitz optimization within 92% of classical solutions, 40% variance reduction in risk analysis relative to Monte Carlo, improved Sharpe ratios from quantum trading QNNs, and 30% Sharpe-ratio improvements from quantum portfolio optimization via efficient sampling.
    [codes: C-004, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-032, C-033, C-039, C-040, C-042, C-043, C-055, C-056, C-057, C-058, C-059, C-061, C-062, C-063, C-064]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Throughout the survey, the authors contrast VQAs with classical baselines, typically reporting that cited quantum methods match or improve upon classical performance metrics on small instances. They note that higher-depth QAOA can exceed the classical Goemans–Williamson approximation ratio under ideal conditions, QNNs in clinical imaging outperform classical CNNs in accuracy with far fewer parameters, and quantum portfolio optimization and trading strategies achieve better Sharpe ratios than classical Markowitz models and classical trading counterparts. In risk analysis, they report that quantum approaches can reduce variance versus classical Monte Carlo, and in materials and chemistry they emphasize polynomial scaling of VQAs compared to exponential scaling of classical methods, presenting these as indications of potential practical advantage rather than definitive speedups.
    [codes: C-004, C-023, C-032, C-033, C-039, C-040, C-055, C-058, C-061, C-062, C-063, C-064]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper highlights several fundamental limitations of VQAs: barren plateaus arising from highly expressive ansätze that lead to exponentially vanishing gradients, substantial optimization overhead and highly non-convex landscapes with many local optima, and measurement overhead due to repeated sampling for expectation-value estimation. Hardware-related constraints are emphasized, including high error rates, short decoherence times, and limited qubit connectivity that restrict feasible circuit depth and motivate shallow circuits. In the context of QNNs, the authors point to practical difficulties with error mitigation and preserving qubit coherence. They also note broader efficiency issues around measurement frugality and explicitly acknowledge that for financial applications, current gate error rates (>10⁻³) limit circuit depth and require more robust error-mitigation techniques to ensure reliable decision-making.
    [codes: C-005, C-014, C-016, C-019, C-041, C-048, C-065, C-067]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Looking ahead, the authors discuss the trajectory from NISQ-era VQAs toward fault-tolerant quantum computing and emphasize that understanding the interplay between quantum noise models and variational parameter optimization is an open question with major implications for scalability and generalizability. They propose future innovation in noise-sensitive ansatz design, adaptive and problem-motivated circuit construction, and novel classical optimization heuristics as promising pathways to overcome current limitations and to enable more scalable, robust VQAs.
    [codes: C-007, C-071, C-072]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is presented as a comprehensive, NISQ-focused synthesis of variational quantum algorithms, comparing key variants (VQE, QAOA, QNNs) in terms of noise robustness, ansatz architecture, and hybrid optimization strategies across diverse application domains, including finance. The authors claim to highlight benchmarks suggesting potential practical quantum advantage, systematically analyze fundamental limiting factors such as barren plateaus and hardware constraints together with mitigation strategies like adaptive ansätze and QVECTOR, and to articulate how the hybrid quantum–classical paradigm offers, in principle, a practical route to tackling classically intractable chemistry, optimization, and machine-learning problems.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-043, C-053, C-054, C-055, C-070]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper is a survey that summarizes experimental and simulation benchmarks from the literature rather than presenting a single unified experimental protocol, and it aggregates results across physics, chemistry, machine learning, and finance. It formalizes VQA components such as cost functions, ansätze, and optimization rules with mathematical detail, and includes benchmark tables (e.g., for QNN molecular energy prediction and selected NISQ VQA applications), but does not itself provide dataset specifications or reproducible pipelines for the cited financial case studies; instead, it relies on previously published benchmarks.
    [codes: C-015, C-020, C-042, C-043, C-055, C-056]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors repeatedly draw explicit analogies between VQAs and classical machine learning, describing variational circuits as quantum versions of ML models, defining cost functions as loss-like quantities, and presenting QNNs as a cross-domain approach with three fundamental quantum advantages and broad potential in nuclear, particle, and materials sciences. They also stress that VQAs’ hybrid architecture and shallow, noise-aware ansätze inherently help manage noise while exploiting NISQ hardware limitations.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets a credit sales risk classification task: determining a customer’s reliability (whether goods can be issued or sales should be blocked) from selected decision variables, posed as a two-class problem that also contains additional subgroups of samples in each class and is not well separated in the original feature space.
    [codes: C-001, C-010, C-019]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a hybrid variational quantum eigensolver (VQE)–based classifier for credit sales risk, in which classical data samples are first normalized and amplitude-encoded into normalized quantum states, then a parameterized ansatz circuit is trained via a VQE-style expectation minimization to produce class-specific pattern states, and finally a SWAP-Test–based similarity measurement plus a decision rule based on high |0⟩ probabilities on three qubits is used for classification. The method emphasizes suitability for NISQ-era hardware, using structurally simple VQA circuits, a low-complexity SWAP-Test, and ansatz designs explicitly constructed to recreate the entanglement structure observed in the encoded data, including a compact nine-qubit register layout with ancilla, VQE, and data sub-registers and two ansatz variants (a standard and a simplified, data-structure-aware circuit).
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that their VQE+SWAP-Test classifier achieves high training-set accuracy on the proprietary credit-risk dataset, with best performance reaching 100% classification efficiency when classification thresholds are properly tuned. They find that the three-qubit amplitude encoding of eight features (with one padded zero feature) not only reduces the number of qubits but also speeds up the optimization process compared to an eight-qubit encoding. Analysis of the encoded samples shows that in most cases all three qubits are entangled, with distinct entanglement partitions for the two classes, and the authors claim the overall algorithm has polynomial complexity and requires only a logarithmically increasing number of qubits in the feature dimension.
    [codes: C-005, C-016, C-017, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Using classical exploratory analysis, the authors observe that although correlations between variables are weak and the raw classes are not well separated, PCA reveals class-based clustering. They further report that several classical classifiers can fit the same training data extremely well, with some models attaining 100% fit but being described as quite complex, which they implicitly contrast with their compact, logarithmic-qubit quantum representation.
    [codes: C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors caution that the choice of acceptance threshold—the boundary distance from a class center to its most distant elements—is critical: if set too high it may cause class overlap and degrade classification quality. They also implicitly delimit the scope of their optimization findings by noting that the barren plateaus problem has not been observed for this problem instance, which should not be generalized beyond the studied setting.
    [codes: C-033, C-041]

    [codes: C-037]

The authors perform classical exploratory analyses (correlations, separability, PCA) before designing the quantum ansatz to match observed entanglement, and they note that barren plateaus were not observed in their optimization runs. === PAPER 30582038a7ba (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles unsupervised anomaly detection in temporal (seasonal) time series, formulating it as a one-class learning problem where anomalies are identified via a quantum kernel that incorporates seasonality structure. The authors emphasise suitability for settings with scarce labels and the need for kernels that treat recurring time steps with similar behaviour equivalently.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-010, C-025]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The method is a quantum-kernel SVM for temporal anomaly detection that first encodes each time-step vector via a static feature map into a 2‑qubit state, then applies a time-dependent unitary evolution generated by a Hamiltonian to preserve temporal dependencies while embedding seasonality through a periodic unitary construction. Periodicity is enforced by choosing integer (coprime) Hamiltonian eigenvalues so that the time-evolution unitary has a period aligned with the dataset seasonality, and temporal kernels are combined using periodic weights to ensure translation invariance over periods; multiple kernel learning is performed classically after quantum kernel computation.
    [codes: C-002, C-007, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-016, C-017, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-027, C-028]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Embedding seasonality directly into the quantum kernel improves the performance of quantum kernel-based SVMs, with the 7-period Hamiltonian model—whose period matches the weekly seasonality—achieving a balanced accuracy of about 81.6% and an F1-score around 73.3%, outperforming both a random Hamiltonian and a 1-period Hamiltonian whose performances are similar. The authors also note that random parameter selection in related kernels can perform comparably to optimized parameters, supporting the use of non-optimized periodic Hamiltonians.
    [codes: C-003, C-019, C-029, C-030, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Compared with classical baselines, the best classical RBF kernel SVM attains the highest precision (~94.1%) and balanced accuracy (~86.9%), outperforming all quantum kernels, while Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), designed for temporal dynamics, reaches a balanced accuracy of 85% and F1-score of 80.2%. The seasonal 7-period quantum model is described as competitive with DTW in precision and balanced accuracy, but it does not surpass the RBF kernel, which suggests that this dataset’s anomaly detection task may not be strongly dependent on temporal correlations.
    [codes: C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors highlight several limitations of learning or optimizing Hamiltonians for temporal quantum kernels: parameterized Hamiltonian learning has notable drawbacks, including that gradient computation may be infeasible on noisy hardware or with limited measurement shots, and that such learning typically requires a supervised setting, which conflicts with anomaly detection scenarios where labeled anomalies are scarce. They further argue that Hamiltonian optimization may be impractical for their target anomaly-detection use case because it relies on efficient gradient computation and supervised data, motivating their use of fixed or randomly parameterized periodic Hamiltonians instead of fully trained ones.
    [codes: C-013, C-014, C-015, C-018]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper suggests that the proposed periodic unitary encoding could be applied beyond anomaly detection to other tasks where seasonality or periodic temporal structure is relevant. They also propose investigating whether their approach can outperform other quantum models on tasks that are more deeply connected to time-related properties than the NYC taxi anomaly dataset used in this study.
    [codes: C-036, C-037]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The central contribution is a novel quantum kernel for unsupervised temporal anomaly detection that directly embeds seasonality via a periodic unitary encoding, constructed so that time instants equivalent under the series’ period are treated consistently. The model is framed within a newer class of quantum machine learning approaches that are seen as more scalable and hardware-efficient than earlier paradigms, and it is explicitly designed to work in unsupervised settings while integrating prior knowledge about task periodicity without requiring gradient-based training on quantum hardware.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-006, C-007, C-017]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Experimentally, the study uses the public NYC Taxi Request time series, defining anomalies as weeks containing specific known anomalous days and dividing the data into 7-day windows, with models trained only on non-anomalous data and hyperparameters tuned via validation balanced accuracy. Quantum kernels are computed using 2‑qubit noiseless simulations in Qiskit, with periodic Hamiltonians instantiated by random integer eigenvalues, and the temporal structure is carefully analyzed—showing that naive permutation-invariant averaging destroys temporal dependencies while their time-dependent kernel preserves them—before combining instantaneous kernels with heuristically chosen periodic weights and optimizing those combinations via classical multiple kernel learning.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors note that RBF’s strong performance, despite not modeling temporal correlations, suggests that their specific anomaly detection task may not heavily depend on temporal information, and they observe more generally that random parameter selection in related quantum kernels can perform comparably to optimized parameters, which informs their design choices but also indirectly contextualizes the limits of their improvements.

The authors summarize that adding qubits and quantum layers generally reduces loss and that RMSprop performs marginally better than alternative optimizers on this hybrid setup.

=== PAPER 317e6bb03bfa (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets generative modelling of financial return or volatility-related distributions, motivated by the prospect that quantum techniques may offer exponential advantage over classical counterparts in such tasks and by instabilities in classical GAN training (e.g., vanishing gradients and mode collapse) [C-001, C-004]. Concretely, it formulates a distribution-learning problem where a quantum generator must learn a discrete distribution derived from option prices and implied volatility, with particular focus on modelling the SVI-based volatility distribution on a discretized grid [C-003, C-026, C-028, C-029].
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-026, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors construct a fully quantum generative adversarial network in which both generator and discriminator are quantum circuits, unlike earlier QuGANs that used a quantum generator with a classical discriminator [C-005, C-006]. The core building block is a non-linear quantum neuron that encodes classical data into quantum states, computes a quantum inner product via phase-encoded controlled rotations, and applies a quantum activation function implemented using phase estimation techniques [C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-012]. The discriminator is instantiated as a quantum perceptron with a sigmoid activation acting on measured output qubits to distinguish target from generated states, while the generator is an inductively constructed circuit of controlled rotations that produces wavefunctions encoding discrete probability distributions; training is posed as a min–max game optimized via stochastic gradient ascent/descent with gradients obtained using the parameter-shift rule and heuristic weight initialization [C-013, C-014, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023].
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Methodologically, the authors show that their quantum inner-product procedure behaves like quantum phase estimation, and that the corresponding activation circuit realizes the intended non-linear map within the neuron [C-010, C-012]. For the adversarial setup, they state that an optimal quantum discriminator would almost surely separate fake and real states and emphasize that their discriminator uses only three parameters, thereby avoiding over-parameterisation relative to typical classical counterparts [C-015, C-016]. In the financial experiment, they report that the fully quantum GAN "manages to overall learn" the target SVI distribution when monitored via fidelity and KL divergence metrics, although convergence of the KL proxy does not reach a neighborhood of zero [C-031, C-032, C-033, C-035].
    [codes: C-010, C-012, C-015, C-016, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-035]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper positions its work against classical GANs by noting that classical GAN training can suffer from instability, vanishing gradients, mode collapse, and potential non-convergence of the min–max optimization [C-004, C-024]. It further claims that prior quantum GAN approaches enhanced accuracy by introducing quantum components, but typically retained a classical discriminator, whereas this work proposes a fully quantum discriminator with only three parameters, implicitly contrasting its compactness with more heavily parameterized classical models [C-005, C-006, C-015].
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-006, C-015, C-024]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: Several limitations are explicitly acknowledged. On the algorithmic side, the authors note that making the generator circuit too deep risks untrainability due to the barren plateau phenomenon, leading them to restrict network depth [C-019]. Training hyperparameters, including weight initialization, are chosen heuristically, which may affect robustness and reproducibility [C-023]. They recognize that, as in classical GANs, the min–max optimization may fail to converge, which also appears in their experiments where the KL divergence proxy does not converge near zero and may reflect getting stuck at saddle points [C-024, C-035]. For the financial application, they stress that their uniform discretization of the SVI distribution ignores the underlying probability mass structure and should ideally be refined via one-dimensional quantization, and that performance is constrained both by the limited number of available qubits and by the expressivity of their network architecture [C-030, C-034].
    [codes: C-019, C-023, C-024, C-030, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose future research on understanding the geometry of the QuGAN optimization landscape induced by the shape of the target distribution and on developing strategies to avoid saddle points responsible for non-ideal convergence behavior [C-036]. They also indicate that refining the discretization of the SVI distribution using quantization rather than a uniform grid would be a natural methodological extension [C-030].
    [codes: C-030, C-036]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main claimed contribution is the development of a fully connected quantum generative adversarial network tailored to learning discrete distributions, with a specific application to mathematical finance and volatility modelling [C-002, C-003]. This architecture departs from earlier QuGANs by implementing both generator and discriminator as quantum circuits, including a quantum perceptron with a QPE-based non-linear neuron, and by emphasizing a compact discriminator with only three parameters that is applied to SVI-based implied volatility distributions [C-006, C-007, C-010, C-013, C-015, C-017, C-028].
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-006, C-007, C-010, C-013, C-015, C-017, C-028]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper specifies the mathematical finance background, including Black–Scholes and the definition of implied volatility, and adopts the market-standard SVI parameterization as the source of a synthetic target distribution [C-026, C-027, C-028]. The SVI-derived density is discretized on a uniform grid to define the training target, and the authors explicitly discuss that this uniform discretization is a simplification, suggesting quantization as a more faithful alternative [C-029, C-030]. Training is monitored using fidelity and KL divergence, and gradients are obtained analytically via the parameter-shift rule, with stochastic gradient ascent/descent optimization and stated learning-rate and initialization schemes, which adds transparency to the experimental setup though these choices remain heuristic [C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-031, C-032].
    [codes: C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032]

=== PAPER 33968c404556 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies quantum generative modeling of discrete binary datasets using a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) that aims to represent joint distributions over bitstrings, including a small benchmark BAS image dataset and a financial dataset of Japanese government bond (JGB) interest-rate movements encoded in binary form. The core problem is how to design and extend parameterized quantum circuits under limited resources so that they capture dataset-specific correlations while avoiding known trainability issues of generic, randomly initialized circuits. In the financial setting, the task is formulated as learning the distribution of quantized, differenced JGB rates across maturities within a 12-qubit basis encoding.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-006, C-009, C-011, C-024, C-025, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is a QCBM where the target distribution is encoded in an n‑qubit parameterized state, trained via gradient-based optimization of the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) loss using parameter-shift gradients. The circuit is first pretrained as a linear-connectivity ansatz obtained from a classically optimized matrix product state (MPS) via a DMRG-like negative log-likelihood minimization, with truncation and analytical decomposition transferring the MPS to a quantum circuit. A greedy, metric-based extension heuristic then adds SU(4) two-qubit gates between qubits whose corresponding classical features are deemed similar according to a chosen distance metric (Hamming distance for BAS, variation of information for JGBs), with a similarity threshold—selected via an elbow rule—controlling the number of added gates and hence the inductive bias.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the BAS dataset, the metric-based extension adds 10 extra connections versus 28 for an all-to-all extension, yet achieves better performance than randomly extended circuits with the same parameter count and even outperforms the all-to-all extension on the test set, where the latter shows clear overfitting; the authors interpret this as hinting at better generalization of the metric-based design. For the JGB interest-rate data, restricting to 12 qubits and using variation of information, the metric-based heuristic produces a circuit with 13 additional gates that tend to connect bits within the same feature and yields lower training MMD than the linear baseline and random extensions, although the separation on the test set is less clear. Across both tasks, the heuristic substantially reduces the number of parameters needed compared with an all-to-all connectivity pattern while still improving model performance over naive extensions.
    [codes: C-010, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-036, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The main classical ingredient is MPS-based pretraining: an MPS is trained with a DMRG-like algorithm to obtain a high-quality classical generative model that is then decomposed into a linear quantum circuit, which serves as a strong baseline before any metric-based extension. The paper does not report direct performance comparisons against purely classical generative models on BAS or JGB data, but instead compares different circuit-connectivity strategies (linear, nearest-neighbor, random, metric-based, all-to-all) that all build on the same MPS-pretrained initialization.
    [codes: C-005, C-015, C-017, C-029, C-041]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors state that problem-agnostic all-to-all circuit extensions, while showing promising gradient behavior, become infeasible to train on hardware with limited resources as problem size grows, motivating more parsimonious designs. They acknowledge that in the JGB experiment the improvement of the metric-based extension on the test set is not clearly separated from baselines, limiting the strength of generalization claims. They further emphasize that they did not establish a mathematical connection between classical feature similarity, the entanglement capacity of the resulting circuits, and inductive bias, and that they did not investigate the impact of circuit depth, in particular repeating the extension layers, leaving open how depth interacts with their heuristic.
    [codes: C-007, C-042, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions implied by the discussion include formally characterizing the relationship between classical feature similarity metrics, the entanglement capacity of the extended circuits, and the resulting inductive bias, as well as systematically exploring the role of circuit depth by repeating extension layers for different design strategies. Addressing hardware resource constraints for larger problem sizes by further optimizing connectivity patterns is also a natural continuation suggested by their resource-focused limitations.
    [codes: C-007, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims as its main contribution a metric-based extension heuristic for quantum generative modeling that designs problem-informed circuit extensions using classical feature similarity, thereby introducing inductive bias under limited resources and avoiding drawbacks associated with Chow–Liu-tree-based designs. This heuristic is demonstrated on both a toy BAS dataset and a real financial JGB interest-rate dataset, where the extended circuits empirically outperform randomly extended circuits with the same number of parameters, and in some cases even all-to-all extensions, while using fewer parameters.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-043]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses QCBMs trained with an implicit MMD loss and parameter-shift gradients, with circuits initialized from classically optimized MPS solutions using a specified truncation cutoff and analytical decomposition. The metric-based extension heuristic is implemented greedily, with a tunable similarity threshold (chosen via the elbow rule) balancing parameter count and inductive bias; Hamming distance is used for binary BAS data, and variation of information is used for noisy, nonlinearly correlated financial time-series data. The BAS experiment uses the full small dataset of 14 images with a defined train/test split and trains on the full training set each iteration, while the JGB experiment preprocesses daily bond yields via differencing and binary quantization, restricts to 12 qubits, and reports separate train and test behavior, though test curves for JGBs are only discussed qualitatively. The choice of SU(4) gates as extension units and explicit reporting of the number of added gates for each design provide some transparency on parameter counts and resource usage.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all verified codes were incorporated into dimensions 1–8.
    [codes: —]

=== PAPER 342ce43a11d1 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames Monte Carlo sampling as a core computational bottleneck in many numerical economic applications, including policy-relevant stress testing and dynamic macroeconomic models, which remain computationally infeasible under classical limitations for high accuracy. It formulates three economic use cases—bank stress testing with credit shocks and fire sales, a neoclassical investment problem, and a realistic macro model solved with deep neural networks—as expectation‑estimation tasks amenable to Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) and amplitude estimation. The stress testing problem is reduced to computing a polynomial operator of random default rates, while the macro deep-learning problems are expressed as expectations of (linear) random variables within Bellman‑error loss functions.
    [codes: C-004, C-008, C-027, C-029, C-030, C-034, C-036, C-038, C-041]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use the Quantum Monte Carlo (amplitude estimation) algorithm, which theoretically offers quadratic speedup in query complexity for expectation estimation compared with classical Monte Carlo, encoding the expectation value into the probability of an ancilla qubit and then applying phase estimation. They implement QMC by variationally preparing the underlying probability distribution with a parameterized circuit optimized to approximate the target distribution, exploiting product distributions to decompose multidimensional encodings, and constructing a controlled oracle Q without needing a controlled version of the underlying unitary F. The algorithm is simulated using PennyLane, including a template implementation for a simple example and resource tracking (gate depth, qubit counts) that is later mapped to physical runtime.
    [codes: C-005, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-016, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-047]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that QMC retains its quadratic query‑complexity scaling relative to classical Monte Carlo, with oracle calls scaling as 1/ε, and in simulations the observed error exponents (≈−0.64 for an approximate encoding and ≈−1.0 for an exact encoding) both outperform classical Monte Carlo’s −0.5 scaling. In the bank stress‑testing use case, the QMC estimate of two‑period system‑wide loss (1.622% of assets) closely matches the theoretical value (1.618%), and even with only two estimation qubits the fractional error remains modest. For the more complex DSGE consumption‑saving model, the authors report very slow classical error scaling (≈−0.22), extreme sample requirements to reach 10⁻⁸ error, and claim that QMC’s quadratic speedup persists with multiple random variables, finding that additional variables do not fundamentally compromise scaling (within the small simulated range). Using their gate‑depth‑to‑runtime mapping, they further report that, at an assumed 1 ns gate time, the approximate QMC implementation can reach a computational error of 10⁻⁸ about 5.6 times faster than a strong HPC cluster accessible to an average researcher, and that under idealized noise‑free conditions high accuracy can be achieved with relatively few qubits.
    [codes: C-003, C-005, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-015, C-016, C-020, C-025, C-031, C-032, C-037, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-054, C-055, C-056]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors explicitly contrast QMC with classical Monte Carlo, noting that classical error scales as 1/√N (samples inversely proportional to the square of target error), whereas QMC requires only O(1/ε) oracle calls, yielding a quadratic theoretical speedup in expectation estimation. They benchmark physical runtimes by comparing QMC’s gate‑depth‑derived runtimes against classical Monte Carlo on a strong HPC cluster and show that, at an error of 10⁻⁸ and under optimistic gate‑time assumptions, QMC can be 5.6 times faster, with the advantage increasing as tighter error tolerances are demanded. For classical deep‑learning solutions of DSGE models, they emphasize that Monte Carlo sampling remains a major bottleneck—classical Bellman‑error convergence can be extremely slow and require astronomically many draws—while their observed QMC scaling exponents in both simplified and multivariate macro settings surpass the classical −0.5 rate.
    [codes: C-003, C-005, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-015, C-016, C-020, C-034, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-056]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper stresses that QMC’s quadratic speedup only holds if the decomposition of the core unitary operators is efficient; otherwise gate overhead can negate the theoretical advantage. Discretization of continuous distributions introduces an additional error term that must remain below the target Monte Carlo error, and some reparameterizations (such as renormalizing the payoff function to avoid a bimodal phase‑estimation output) reduce accuracy. The authors note that encoding Monte Carlo problems into quantum circuits without amplitude estimation yields no speedup, and that quantum arithmetic operations and the associated ancilla registers are costly in terms of gates and qubits, posing challenges for both hardware and simulators. They also report a fundamental hardware limitation: current quantum devices are noisy, with noise dominating outcomes after roughly 100 gates in their stress‑testing scenario, and emphasize that fast gate times, longer coherence, and sufficient qubit counts are essential for realizing any practical quantum speedup. Finally, they acknowledge that their multivariate simulations are limited to three random variables due to classical simulation constraints, so scalability claims beyond this regime remain untested.
    [codes: C-006, C-017, C-019, C-023, C-026, C-033, C-045, C-049, C-050]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that QMC could be integrated more deeply into deep‑learning pipelines for solving DSGE models by accelerating the Monte Carlo averaging over future shocks, thereby improving convergence of neural‑network–based solution methods. They argue that approximate QMC implementations requiring fewer quantum resources are likely to be realized first in practice, but highlight that further research is needed to optimize quantum arithmetic and amplitude‑estimation subroutines and to extend variational distribution‑encoding techniques from single distributions to encoding entire economic problems. They present these as open technical challenges and research directions that must be addressed before QMC can be deployed at scale in realistic macroeconomic and stress‑testing applications.
    [codes: C-035, C-048, C-051, C-052]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to be the first to study the potential runtime improvements of Quantum Monte Carlo for economic applications and to systematically examine the associated challenges, and more broadly the first to apply the QMC algorithm to economics and among the earliest applications of quantum computation in this field. It also positions itself as presenting methodological innovations in benchmarking QMC, including direct physical runtime comparisons with classical algorithms on HPC resources and new circuit‑design elements such as variational probability‑distribution encoding and a construction of a controlled Q oracle without a controlled F.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-009, C-012, C-013, C-054]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study encodes three different economics use cases into quantum circuits, demonstrating how to translate stress‑testing models and deep‑learning–solved macro models into QMC‑compatible expectation‑estimation problems. The authors rely on PennyLane simulations to implement QMC, monitor performance as the number of qubits scales, and compute circuit depth, which they then convert into estimated computational time under different gate‑time assumptions, enabling explicit time‑to‑solution benchmarking. They also use a simple numerical example implemented with PennyLane’s QuantumMonteCarlo template to validate the basic QMC simulation pipeline and to study estimator behavior (such as bimodal phase distributions), while their variational distribution‑encoding approach includes an explicit cost function minimizing distance to a target distribution, indicating an attempt at systematic, if simulator‑based, experimental design.
    [codes: C-002, C-012, C-014, C-018, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-030, C-036, C-038, C-047]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper situates itself in a broader context by noting the overall scarcity of quantum computing applications in economics and by emphasizing that stress testing and DSGE‑style macro models represent particularly policy‑relevant domains where Monte Carlo speedups could have impact. It also observes that in the absence of noise, quantum simulations achieve high accuracy even with relatively few qubits, an idealized regime that contrasts with current noisy hardware conditions.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-029, C-055]
[SILO OVERLAY]
  SILO_RELEVANCE: This paper matters for quantum_ml_finance because it shows how quantum Monte Carlo can accelerate expectation estimation inside finance-adjacent learning pipelines, especially where model training or inference depends on repeated sampling. Its most relevant contribution is the circuit-level and benchmarking evidence that quantum methods may reduce the cost of Monte Carlo-heavy financial prediction/classification workflows, though the paper itself focuses on stress testing rather than direct classification tasks.
    [silo_relevance_score: medium]

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames a general supervised classification problem and proposes a hybrid quantum–classical model, quantum‑enhanced kernel logistic regression (QEKLR), as a practical alternative to deep quantum models affected by barren plateaus, aiming in particular at real‑world datasets such as Statlog Heart Disease and Ecoli rather than only toy benchmarks.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-011, C-050]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The quantum component uses a shallow‑depth ZZFeatureMap with at most four qubits and up to two repetitions with full entanglement to map classical feature vectors into quantum states, then constructs a fidelity‑based quantum kernel (inner products of quantum states) whose values lie in [0,1] with diagonal elements fixed to 1, and feeds this kernel into a classical logistic regression model trained by gradient descent for prediction. The design explicitly leverages entangling operations to capture nonlinear feature interactions while keeping circuit depth and qubit count NISQ‑compatible.
    [codes: C-002, C-008, C-010, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across four datasets (synthetic, Iris, Statlog Heart Disease, Ecoli), QEKLR reports headline accuracies of 100%, 100%, 94.87%, and 71% respectively, with especially strong performance on Statlog Heart Disease where the best variant achieves 94.87% accuracy, MCC 0.88, and AUC‑ROC 0.98, and a complementary variant attains 100% sensitivity at slightly lower MCC. On the Ecoli dataset, the authors report 70.97% accuracy, noting this is comparable to strong classical baselines and that classification is harder due to more complex distributions and class characteristics; kernel similarity visualizations show diagonally dominant matrices with most pairwise similarities concentrated around 0.4–0.6.
    [codes: C-003, C-014, C-041, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053, C-054]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors benchmark QEKLR against multiple classical machine‑learning models (including RF, LR, CART, and KLR) and quantum baselines (VQC, QSVC), claiming that QEKLR surpasses these models on the Statlog Heart Disease dataset in terms of accuracy, MCC, and AUC‑ROC, while on the Ecoli dataset it matches the accuracy of RF and exceeds LR and CART. For simpler synthetic and Iris problems, QEKLR reaches 100% accuracy, which the authors also describe as superior to several recent classification approaches on Iris, though they acknowledge that such datasets are linearly separable and relatively easy.
    [codes: C-015, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly acknowledges several limitations of current quantum machine learning that motivate and constrain QEKLR: NISQ hardware noise and limited qubit counts, lack of interpretability in many QML models, and barren plateaus/vanishing gradients in deep parameterized circuits. At the algorithmic level, the authors note that quantum kernel methods face scalability challenges as dataset sizes and qubit numbers grow, including kernel stability problems where large datasets cause exponential concentration so kernel values cluster in a narrow range, which can degrade discrimination power.
    [codes: C-006, C-008, C-010, C-055, C-056]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors plan to improve quantum kernel techniques for medium‑ to large‑scale datasets by integrating more advanced hybrid quantum–classical optimization schemes, exploring more effective feature maps, and leveraging quantum transfer learning (QTL) to mitigate current scalability and kernel stability issues.
    [codes: C-057]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main claimed contribution is the introduction of the QEKLR method, a hybrid quantum‑enhanced kernel logistic regression model that uses a shallow ZZFeatureMap with ≤4 qubits and a fidelity kernel to provide an operational and reliable substitute for deeper quantum models affected by barren plateaus, while offering moderate interpretability through the logistic regression layer. Additional contributions include demonstrating QEKLR on four benchmark (including real‑world) datasets and conducting comparative analyses against classical ML, existing QML, and recent classification methods.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-015]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper describes a fairly detailed classical preprocessing pipeline involving IQR‑based outlier detection and removal, PCA for dimensionality reduction, and MinMax scaling to the range [−1,1], noting how this changes dataset sizes (e.g., Statlog from 270 to 192 and Ecoli from 336 to 306). Experiments are run in a controlled simulator environment using Qiskit (1.0 SDK, Machine Learning 0.7.2, Algorithms 0.3.0, Python 3.9), with an 80/20 train–test split across all datasets and multiple evaluation metrics (accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, F1, MCC, and AUC‑ROC for Statlog). The authors also provide background on the quantum components (feature maps, kernels, VQC training loops, and classical LR/KLR behavior) and visually inspect quantum kernel matrices, which show diagonal dominance and mid‑range similarity concentration, supporting their interpretation of how the kernel behaves.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper includes general background explanations of quantum computing concepts such as entanglement, superposition, and interference, emphasizing how interference can amplify correct answers and cancel incorrect ones, and introduces quantum feature maps as a core component of QML for encoding classical data into quantum states; these sections serve primarily as conceptual framing rather than methodological or result‑oriented content.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses fraud detection in large-scale, real-time payment (RTP) systems where transactions occur in milliseconds and conventional machine learning and rule-based systems struggle with high-velocity, highly imbalanced data, leading to delayed detection and losses. The authors motivate quantum approaches as a way to explore many candidate fraud patterns in parallel and to handle weak, nonlinear anomalies in massive transaction streams. Implementations use Qiskit and Amazon Braket in a hybrid setup, with angle encoding feature maps (including ZZFeatureMap) on small (≈4-qubit) circuits, leveraging superposition and entanglement in large Hilbert spaces to evaluate multiple fraudulent patterns simultaneously. Transactions are modeled as graphs where nodes are accounts and edges are transactions for QGNN, and the models are trained and evaluated via Qiskit Aer simulation and deployment on Rigetti hardware through Amazon Braket, with platform-level QaaS comparisons noted.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-010, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-021, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029]

=== PAPER 35da1ebe30e2 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames complex optimization problems in domains such as logistics, finance, and AI as NP-hard and computationally challenging for traditional gradient-based and evolutionary algorithms, motivating exploration of quantum machine learning (QML) as an alternative. In finance specifically, portfolio optimization and asset allocation are cast as combinatorial optimization problems over large solution spaces that might benefit from quantum parallel exploration and search. The authors emphasize that existing work typically examines single QML algorithms in isolation, leaving a gap for an integrated view of how these methods address such hard optimization tasks.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-010, C-064, C-065]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: Rather than implementing one specific algorithm, the paper conducts a systematic literature review and qualitative comparative analysis of several QML approaches for optimization: QAOA, VQE, QNNs, QSVMs, Grover’s search, QPCA, and quantum k-means. It details core algorithmic structures, including QAOA’s hybrid quantum–classical design with alternating problem and mixer Hamiltonians, VQE’s parameterized quantum circuits optimized via classical optimizers to minimize Hamiltonian expectation values, and QNNs and QSVMs that use quantum circuits for feature mapping and neural architectures exploiting superposition and entanglement. The methods section describes the review protocol (databases searched, keyword strategy, comparison criteria) rather than experimental implementation on hardware.
    [codes: C-002, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-023, C-024, C-030, C-037, C-041, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors conclude that QML algorithms show substantial potential to explore large solution spaces in parallel, achieve faster convergence, and improve optimization performance relative to classical approaches, although most evidence is prospective or drawn from cited studies. In their comparative synthesis, QAOA and VQE are portrayed as particularly effective for combinatorial and energy optimization, with reported strengths such as high-quality solution sampling, near-term suitability on NISQ hardware, parameter transferability, and noise-resilient shallow variants, while VQE is cited as converging faster and achieving improved energy estimates in molecular problems. Learning-oriented methods like QNNs and QSVMs are said to perform strongly in learning-based optimization and classification tasks, with reported gains from residual connections, hybrid quantum–classical neural architectures, quantum kernel acceleration, and quantum k-means speedups in clustering; Grover’s algorithm is highlighted for its quadratic search speedup, and QPCA for efficiently extracting principal components. The concluding section reiterates that, across reviewed work, QML methods demonstrate significant promise in improving optimization efficiency and may shorten processes such as drug discovery and enable more efficient portfolio search and routing optimization.

For security, they specify lattice‑based cryptography grounded in SVP and LWE, detailing an LWE‑style encryption c = As + e + m and highlighting homomorphic properties for secure computation on encrypted financial records. QAOA is claimed to improve portfolio optimization with a 10–15% Sharpe ratio uplift and 25% faster optimization, including a reported Sharpe ratio of 1.45 for a 50‑asset portfolio and an example allocation of 45% equities and 30% bonds. QPCA is reported to reduce dimensionality by ~90% while preserving around 95% variance (e.g., 95.2% variance retained on S&P 500 indicators), and QBM is said to increase forecasting accuracy by about 5–10% with 30% faster convergence, achieving roughly 88–88.5% stock‑price prediction accuracy. For security, lattice‑based cryptography is claimed to provide 99.9% security against classical and quantum attacks with roughly 10–15% extra execution time, yet still securing financial transactions with minimal overhead in their examples. The conclusion summarizes that all quantum‑enhanced components yield substantial gains in computing efficiency, predictive accuracy, and security.

=== PAPER 3c1b7774da65 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles discrete Black–Litterman (BL) portfolio optimization, where selecting a fixed number of assets under constraints turns the task into an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem with an exponentially growing search space. The authors frame BL as more practically appealing than classic Markowitz mean–variance (MPT) and cast the discrete, budget-constrained BL portfolio selection as a QUBO/Ising problem amenable to quantum optimization subroutines. They also formalize investor views as a classification problem that can be handled with quantum machine learning.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-009, C-010, C-011]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is a hybrid quantum pipeline: quantum machine learning (QML), specifically QSVM and a QNN classifier, is used to predict investor views, and a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) then solves the resulting BL combinatorial optimization problem. The authors implement a 12‑qubit proof-of-concept instance selecting 6 assets from 12, with heuristic VQE and QAOA ansätze compared, and emphasize using very few final measurement shots after variational optimization because the optimized heuristic ansatz yields a probability distribution concentrated on high-quality eigenstates. They also execute the optimized 12‑qubit heuristic VQE circuits on the IBM Auckland device using only 5 hardware shots for final sampling.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-035]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that VQE solutions achieve high approximation ratios and that even near-optimal solutions (high AR) perform about as well as exact optima in backtesting. Backtests indicate that the BL model with quantum-generated views consistently outperforms several common portfolio models, including MPT, in terms of pure return and mean certainty-equivalent return (CER) over a long walk-forward period from 2008–2021. For the view-prediction stage, QSVM with a simple, non-entangling embedding is found to deliver higher testing accuracy than alternatives such as a Pauli feature map, leading the authors to adopt QSVM-predicted views in their main backtests. Real-device runs on IBM Auckland reproduce the simulator’s best solution within only 5 shots in 6 out of 9 cases, supporting the claim that few final samples suffice when the ansatz distribution is well concentrated.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-012, C-021, C-022, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper compares its quantum-enhanced BL approach against classical baselines on both the machine learning and portfolio performance sides. For investor views, QSVM was chosen over other methods because its quantum kernel achieved higher accuracy than classical alternatives, and simple feature maps outperformed more complex entangling Pauli maps. In portfolio backtests, the BL model (including the quantum-generated views and approximate quantum optimizer) is reported to outperform the classical MPT model and several other portfolio constructions in terms of pure return and mean CER over a long continuous period.
    [codes: C-005, C-012, C-021, C-022, C-033]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors highlight several limitations and practical caveats. Penalty parameter tuning is delicate: λ must be large enough to enforce discrete constraints but not so large that it dominates the Hamiltonian, which can hurt solution precision. QAOA is reported as more difficult to work with in this setting: it requires fully connected entanglement reflecting the fully connected problem structure, its optimization results vary tremendously with the choice of initial parameters, and the resulting circuits tend to be much deeper and still spread probability mass over many eigenstates, making them ill-suited to current noisy hardware. These issues motivate the preference for shallower heuristic VQE ansätze in the NISQ regime.
    [codes: C-024, C-027, C-031, C-037]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that larger problem instances may better reveal the potential of quantum computing for BL portfolio optimization, arguing that the required qubit resources grow only linearly with problem size, in contrast to the exponential growth of the classical search space. This scaling argument underpins their expectation that quantum methods could become more advantageous as asset universes grow.
    [codes: C-007, C-008]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper presents itself as a practical demonstration of integrating NISQ algorithms into the Black–Litterman framework by enhancing subroutines with quantum components: using QML (QSVM) to generate investor views and VQE-based quantum optimization to solve the discrete BL allocation problem. It also advances the idea that, with an appropriately chosen heuristic ansatz producing a highly concentrated solution distribution, one can—and should—use only a minimal number of final measurement shots to obtain high-approximation-ratio portfolios in a realistic backtesting setting.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-006, C-012, C-013, C-030, C-032]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study specifies several financial-modeling and data-processing choices: it uses log returns, arguing they are preferable for optimizing buy-and-hold strategies; defines market-implied returns via reverse optimization to make the market-cap-weighted portfolio optimal in the BL prior; and sets view uncertainty proportional to each asset’s variance. The risk-aversion parameter γ is adjusted via an effective γeff = γ/B to account for the discrete budget constraint. For QML, the authors describe a structured feature preprocessing pipeline (including labeling, moving averages, normalization, PCA, and label-based filtering of ambiguous feature vectors) and note that simple embedding maps without entanglement suffice for good performance. They design a walk-forward backtest from 2008–2021 with a 260-week training and 52-week testing window, and empirically choose the penalty λ = 1.0 based on inspection of Hamiltonian eigenvalues, while emphasizing that λ must balance constraint enforcement and objective fidelity.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-034]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: No additional relevant content beyond what is already captured in dimensions 1–8.
    [codes: —]
[SILO OVERLAY]
  SILO_RELEVANCE: This paper is highly relevant to quantum_ml_finance because it combines quantum classification for predicting investor views with a quantum optimization step for portfolio construction, making it a direct end-to-end example of QML in a financial decision pipeline. Its strongest silo value is the use of QSVM-based view prediction and the empirical comparison of quantum classifiers and ansätze in a finance-specific backtesting setting.
    [silo_relevance_score: high]
  KEY_POINT 1: Quantum machine learning is used to predict investor views that feed directly into the Black-Litterman pipeline.

=== PAPER 3f8ab7317ca4 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies quantum runtime scaling for several combinatorial optimization problems relevant to finance and data analytics—specifically portfolio optimization, feature selection, clustering, and weighted MaxCut—by reformulating all of them as quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) instances, with portfolio constraints incorporated via penalty terms in the cost function.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-013]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors employ a linear-ramp variant of QAOA in which the optimal parameters exhibit smooth increasing/decreasing patterns and are compressed into a schedule with only two free parameters, implemented as a specific parametrized quantum state. To circumvent costly high-dimensional variational optimization, they propose an extrapolation-based parameter estimation strategy that learns these two parameters on small random subinstances via grid search (with a log-scale parameter grid and a multivariate skew-Gaussian fit) and extrapolates them on a log–log scale to larger instances, then choose the QAOA depth p by minimizing a total-depth runtime metric.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-018, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the extrapolated linear-ramp parameters agree well with those obtained from direct optimization on larger instances, supporting the validity of the extrapolation scheme. For portfolio optimization, the authors report that the quantum runtime scaling exponent is smaller than the classical one and interpret this as an indication of potential quantum scaling advantage, while for feature selection the results suggest a quantum disadvantage relative to classical methods. In clustering, they observe instability with outliers exhibiting extremely large total depths, but show that using universal parameter scaling across instances both improves scaling coefficients and keeps success probabilities for the optimal solution on average above 0.1, which they argue would, if constant, imply algebraic (subexponential) median quantum runtime.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-026, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Quantum runtime scaling is explicitly compared against several classical optimization baselines, including commercial solvers (CPLEX and GUROBI), the MQLib/Burer2002 heuristic, and the Goemans–Williamson algorithm, with classical scaling quantified via the slope of fitted models. The authors ultimately select the MQLib/Burer2002 algorithm as the main classical reference for detailed comparison, against which they report superior scaling for portfolio optimization and inferior performance for feature selection.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors caution that their runtime comparisons implicitly assume that suitable LR-QAOA circuit parameters are already known or can be efficiently found, even though the computational effort for their parameter-search and extrapolation procedure itself grows with problem size. They also highlight instability in some applications—notably clustering—where outliers with extremely large total depth values appear, indicating that the extrapolation and parameter-scaling strategies may not behave uniformly well across problem instances.
    [codes: C-031, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors argue that to substantiate or refute the observed scaling indications, future studies must cover a broader range of problem sizes beyond N = 28. They additionally call for more elaborate statistical analyses that go beyond median runtime and examine the scaling behavior of multiple runtime percentiles to better characterize performance variability.
    [codes: C-036, C-037]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims as its core contribution an extrapolation-based method that estimates suitable linear-ramp QAOA parameters for larger problem sizes using only optimizations on smaller subproblems, thereby reducing the parameter-search burden while leveraging a two-parameter linear schedule informed by observed parameter patterns. It further positions the work as providing an evaluation of quantum runtime scaling on a simulator across four QUBO-formulated applications and as demonstrating, in the portfolio case, empirically superior scaling compared to classical runtimes, albeit as a potential rather than definitive quantum advantage.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study standardizes all considered problems via QUBO reformulations, including explicit handling of portfolio constraints through penalty terms, and models clustering as a MaxCut problem, which supports comparability across domains. Classical baselines are carefully selected and their scaling quantified by fitting slopes to runtime data, while on the quantum side the authors define runtime in terms of total circuit depth D and empirically validate their parameter extrapolation by comparing predicted parameters to optima from direct grid search on larger instances. They also introduce a universal parameter-scaling scheme and report success probabilities and median runtime implications, indicating attention to both optimization landscapes and performance metrics, though all evidence is obtained on a simulator rather than hardware.
    [codes: C-002, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-016, C-018, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-032, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None.
    [codes: —]

=== PAPER 41d2d7bb257a (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets credit risk prediction, arguing that accurate assessment is essential for financial health, default minimisation, and regulatory compliance, and that current credit models struggle with nonlinear relationships in high-dimensional data and poor recall on the minority (defaulter) class. It formulates the task as a binary loan default classification problem on a real-world credit risk dataset, aiming to improve AUC and minority-class recall via a quantum-assisted model. The work is framed within a broader move from traditional risk models, whose shortcomings were highlighted in the 2008 crisis, toward machine learning and quantum-enhanced approaches in financial risk management.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a hybrid quantum–classical transfer learning model in which a classical neural network compresses 24-dimensional input features into a 4-dimensional latent representation that is then encoded into 4 qubits via angle encoding with RY gates. The quantum component is a parameterized variational circuit comprising an embedding layer, entanglement (e.g., CNOT) layer, and trainable rotation gates; this circuit, together with the classical feature extractor and output layer, is co-trained end-to-end with binary cross-entropy loss using PennyLane’s TorchLayer inside a PyTorch pipeline. Only a selected subset of computationally significant features is encoded into quantum states, addressing data-encoding inefficiency, and all parameters (classical, quantum, and output) are updated jointly via backpropagation through the hybrid architecture.
    [codes: C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The co-trained hybrid QTL model is reported to achieve an AUC of 0.9134 and a test accuracy of 91.17%, with substantially improved recall for the minority defaulter class (0.73) compared to baselines. It demonstrates strong ROC performance and high overall classification accuracy, reaching its best performance at epoch 8, and the authors emphasise that it significantly boosts minority-class detection while maintaining strong metrics on the majority class. An additional empirical finding is that training on the original unbalanced dataset, rather than SMOTE-resampled data, yields higher accuracy, which the authors attribute to overfitting in synthetic samples.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-012, C-013, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-035]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The hybrid co-trained QTL model is compared against a standalone QNN baseline and a conventional classical neural network, with the co-trained model claimed to significantly outperform these baselines. Relative to the standalone QNN, the hybrid model shows higher accuracy (0.9117 vs 0.8097), higher AUC (0.9134 vs 0.7446), and much better minority-class recall (0.73 vs 0.16). The standalone QNN, trained directly on raw credit data with limited preprocessing, is said to suffer from poor recall and unstable convergence, while also requiring nearly twice the training time of the hybrid model, leading the authors to describe the hybrid as both more accurate and more time-efficient.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-012, C-013, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-050, C-051]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors note several limitations: at the field level, QML is constrained by hardware limits such as qubit count, coherence time, and noise, as well as data encoding inefficiencies, generalization gaps between theory and practice, and scarce benchmarking on real datasets. At the implementation level, they highlight that data encoding inefficiency is a critical barrier and that quantum circuit simulation, especially parameter-shift gradient computation on a CPU-based simulator, is the dominant computational bottleneck. For the standalone QNN, they report poor recall, unstable convergence, high computational demands, and the need to restrict training data to 1,000 samples because of parameter-shift overhead. For the hybrid model, they acknowledge higher computational cost due to joint training of classical and quantum layers and more variable convergence behaviour, which they attribute to non-convex circuit training and high-variance gradients, explicitly stating that this variability calls for careful optimization strategies.

    [codes: C-052, C-049]

The authors argue that this end-to-end co-training enables mutual adaptation between classical representations and the quantum circuit, improves minority-class detection and AUC, and demonstrates that quantum-assisted learning can be feasibly integrated into financial decision pipelines under current simulator and hardware constraints. They further position hybrid architectures as a meaningful near-term path that balances performance gains with existing quantum technology limitations.

  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses a public Kaggle credit risk dataset with 24 features and 32,580 instances, applies EDA and Min–Max normalization, and considers SMOTE to address class imbalance, ultimately opting for the unbalanced dataset after observing SMOTE-induced overfitting. The experimental setup includes a stratified 80/20 train–test split for the hybrid model; the standalone QNN baseline is trained on a reduced subset of 1,000 samples due to computational overheads. The hybrid architecture is implemented with PennyLane’s TorchLayer inside a PyTorch pipeline, trained using binary cross-entropy loss and the Adam optimizer, and evaluated with standard metrics including accuracy, ROC/AUC, precision, recall, and F1-score, with convergence behaviour and epoch-level performance explicitly reported.
