=== PAPER 470b798927ef (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies quantum optimization for three combinatorial problems reformulated as QUBOs: a constrained portfolio optimization problem with the budget constraint enforced via a quadratic penalty term, a feature selection task that balances feature–target relevance against inter-feature redundancy, and a clustering task reduced to a Max-Cut problem on a dense graph (including applications to financial/credit data). The overarching framing is to understand how QAOA runtime scales with problem size on these QUBO-encoded tasks, with portfolio optimization as the main finance use case.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a linear-ramp variant of QAOA (LR-QAOA) where the many variational parameters of standard QAOA are reduced to two global parameters Δγ and Δβ that define linearly ramped angles across layers, motivated by observed smooth patterns in optimal QAOA parameters and an interpretation of QAOA as a discrete adiabatic schedule. They define the LR-QAOA quantum state and parameterization explicitly, and avoid full variational optimization by fixing these ramp schedules and then optimizing only the circuit depth p via minimizing an estimated total circuit depth D. A key methodological contribution is an extrapolation scheme that learns suitable Δγ, Δβ from optimized solutions on small random sub-instances, iteratively refining them via grid search and skew-Gaussian fitting and then extrapolating their scaling with N under an assumed linear log–log relation.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-034]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: For portfolio optimization, the authors report that LR-QAOA with extrapolated parameters achieves a smaller fitted exponential runtime scaling exponent (α ≈ 0.22) in total circuit depth than the chosen classical heuristic baseline, and that the success probability of obtaining the optimal solution remains approximately independent of problem size within the studied range, consistent with an earlier conjecture. In contrast, for feature selection the quantum runtime scales worse than classical (≈ 2^0.46N vs ≈ 2^0.2N), and for clustering LR-QAOA also fails to outperform classical baselines (α ≈ 0.25 vs α = 0.061), though the extrapolated parameters generally match those found by full grid search except for some outliers at particular sizes. The paper thus finds problem-dependent behavior, with an indicative scaling advantage only for portfolio optimization in the simulated regime.
    [codes: C-004, C-008, C-031, C-035, C-037, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Quantum runtime is explicitly benchmarked against several classical solvers whose runtimes on the same QUBO instances are empirically fitted to exponential models, with MQLib/Burer2002 chosen as the main comparison baseline because other solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi, Goemans–Williamson) exhibit heterogeneous scaling, discontinuities, or frequent failures to find the optimum. The authors find that different classical methods have markedly different scaling behaviors across portfolio optimization, feature selection, and clustering, and they emphasize that for feature selection and clustering the tested classical methods still scale better than LR-QAOA, whereas for portfolio optimization LR-QAOA’s fitted exponent beats the MQLib/Burer2002 baseline but not all commercial solvers in all regimes.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-013, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-035, C-037, C-039]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations: some classical solvers like Goemans–Williamson often fail to find the optimum, and commercial solvers may change their search behavior unpredictably, complicating fair scaling comparisons. For the quantum side, the authors note that the extrapolation scheme is less stable for feature selection and exhibits outlier behavior for some clustering sizes, indicating fragility of the learned schedules on certain problem classes. Crucially, they state that the cost of finding optimized circuit parameters is not included in their quantum runtime metric, even though the extrapolation-based analysis still grows with problem size, and they position their study as assessing LR-QAOA potential under the assumption that good parameters are already known or can be found efficiently. They further highlight that their observations regarding success probability and conjectured polynomial scaling are based on relatively small problem sizes (up to N = 28), so the exponential-versus-polynomial scaling question remains unresolved.
    [codes: C-021, C-022, C-023, C-038, C-040, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors call for extending the analysis to larger problem sizes beyond N = 28 to clarify whether LR-QAOA can achieve polynomial-time scaling for some combinatorial optimization problems, explicitly flagging the broader open question of whether quantum optimization can yield polynomial-time solutions in such settings. They also propose that methods based on extrapolation and scaling of circuit parameters with increasing problem size are a promising direction for future research on QAOA parameter setting and should be further developed and tested.
    [codes: C-043, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s main contribution is the development of an extrapolation-based method to set the two parameters of a linear-ramp QAOA schedule using optimized solutions from small sub-instances, thereby largely avoiding expensive variational optimization while evaluating QAOA runtime scaling on multiple combinatorial problems. Building on observed smooth patterns in optimal QAOA parameters and a prior conjecture about constant optimal-solution probability under fixed linear ramps, the authors claim to systematically address the formerly unresolved problem of how to find suitable linear-ramp parameters and to demonstrate, in simulation, an indicative scaling improvement over a classical heuristic for portfolio optimization.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-005, C-006, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-035]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study defines quantum runtime as the median total circuit depth over all circuits needed to find the optimum, combining QAOA depth and required shots, and optimizes QAOA depth p by minimizing this estimated depth. The parameter extrapolation protocol is described in detail: random sub-instances of increasing size are sampled, grid search over Δγ and Δβ is iteratively refined via fitting a multivariate skew Gaussian to the success-probability landscape, and then the inferred optimal parameters are extrapolated under a linear log–log assumption. The classical benchmarking is also systematically designed, with multiple sampled instances per size, repeated runtime measurements, and robust log2-linear fits to estimate scaling exponents, while noting solver-dependent irregularities and failures. The authors frame their work as an exploration of LR-QAOA’s potential under an idealized assumption that suitable parameters can be efficiently obtained, and conclude that extrapolation and scaling-based parameter strategies appear promising but still require further validation.

=== PAPER 4715aa3cb8e4 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses credit card fraud detection under extreme class imbalance, focusing on improving minority-class (fraud) sensitivity rather than overall accuracy, which the authors argue can be misleading because trivial classifiers can reach ~99.8% accuracy by predicting all transactions as normal. They explicitly prioritize recall and PR-AUC as primary metrics to reflect real fraud-detection operational constraints such as changing attacker behavior and tight latency budgets.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-009, C-010]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a hybrid quantum–classical neural network where a variational quantum circuit (VQC) layer replaces a classical dense layer in an otherwise shared neural architecture, with the quantum layer implemented via a PennyLane TorchLayer that outputs expectation values as classical features. The circuit employs angle (RY) embedding with data re-uploading to expose all 30 features using 10–15 qubits, followed by a custom data-driven priority-entanglement scheme that entangles the most strongly correlated feature pairs and then a strongly entangling layer (SEL) composed of parameterized rotations and a ring of CNOTs to approximate global mixing. Entanglement is constrained by correlation-based priority-pair selection within feature chunks determined by the qubit count, and models are trained with class-weighted binary cross-entropy under a configurable decision threshold tuned toward higher recall.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The hybrid quantum–classical model is reported to achieve consistent gains in recall and PR-AUC over classical baselines under matched parameter budgets, with the best 10-qubit configuration (80 priority pairs, shallow depth) reaching a PR-AUC of about 0.9192 and the best 15-qubit shallow configuration (10 priority pairs) reaching about 0.9229. At 10 qubits, introducing correlation-guided entanglement improves recall and PR-AUC over a no-pair baseline, but increasing depth from one to three or five layers does not improve PR-AUC, while at 15 qubits, very high entanglement budgets increase precision but reduce recall and PR-AUC, and deeper 15-qubit circuits drive recall very high but cause precision to collapse, highlighting a precision–recall trade-off. The authors further note that computation time grows with both circuit depth and coupling budget.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-037, C-040]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Under a design where the quantum layer simply replaces a dense layer in a capacity-matched neural network with shared classical trunk, the authors report that classical baselines such as logistic regression and XGBoost achieve the highest precision, while the classical neural network attains the best recall among purely classical models. Against these baselines, the best-performing hybrid configuration improves PR-AUC by an absolute +0.0042 over logistic regression and increases recall by +0.0468 absolute over the classical neural network, with parameter counts between the classical and hybrid networks differing by less than 1%.
    [codes: C-002, C-011, C-017, C-024, C-025, C-032, C-033, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The study is explicitly limited to simulator-based experiments using idealized quantum circuits; the authors acknowledge that hardware noise and connectivity constraints could change the observed behavior and would substantially increase runtimes. They also note that the 15-qubit, 3-layer configuration had to be excluded because training repeatedly collapsed to a degenerate solution, indicating potential instability of deeper circuits, and they highlight that the anonymized PCA-like features of the fraud dataset restrict semantic interpretability of which financial attributes are being coupled by the entanglement scheme.
    [codes: C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose extending their correlation-guided entanglement design to real quantum hardware and systematically studying its robustness under noisy, hardware-constrained conditions as key directions for future work.
    [codes: C-044]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The core claimed contribution is a data-driven priority-entanglement scheme that uses train-only feature correlations to determine which feature pairs to entangle before a strongly entangling block, thereby injecting a correlation-guided inductive bias into a hybrid variational quantum circuit. Combined with data re-uploading to handle all 30 features on 10–15 qubits and a controlled layer-swap comparison design, the authors position this structured, correlation-aware entanglement as the main novelty underlying the reported recall and PR-AUC gains.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-007, C-011, C-012, C-019, C-020]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper emphasizes a controlled comparison by matching parameter budgets and using an identical classical feature-extraction trunk for both classical and hybrid models, with near-equal parameter counts and wall-clock time used as the relevant compute metric. The dataset is handled carefully for class imbalance by retaining all 492 frauds and downsampling legitimate transactions, applying class-weighted binary cross-entropy and a lowered decision threshold (default 0.3) to favor recall, and computing the Pearson correlation matrix on the training split only to avoid leakage before reordering features for entanglement mapping. Experimental rigor is further supported by extensive repeated randomized trials (100 runs for 10-qubit and 20 for 15-qubit configurations), explicit documentation of the Intel Xeon simulation hardware, and discussion of how runtime scales with depth and coupling, alongside an interpretation that shallow, structured circuits lie on an efficient frontier where increased depth or entanglement produces diminishing or negative returns.
    [codes: C-002, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors argue that excessive entanglement budgets tend to over-mix and degrade recall and PR-AUC, reinforcing their conclusion that moderate entanglement and shallow depth form an empirical sweet spot for this fraud detection task.
    [codes: C-006, C-039, C-040]

Both quantum and tensor models are optimized with stochastic gradient descent, and gradients for the quantum circuit are computed via the parameter‑shift rule.
    [codes: C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-008]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across the full backtest, the tensor network model achieves the best portfolio performance, delivering superior excess return and information ratio compared with all benchmarks, despite having the fewest parameters. The quantum neural network (QCL) is overall inferior to classical neural networks in risk‑adjusted excess return, though it attains excess returns competitive with them at the cost of higher tracking error. Performance is time‑varying: before 2016 QCL behaves similarly to linear regression, but after 2016 it outperforms the linear model, and in the latest market environment both the quantum and tensor models outperform classical neural networks, while neural networks perform particularly poorly in the last three years.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-011, C-012, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-045, C-047]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum and tensor approaches are explicitly benchmarked against linear regression and classical neural networks with comparable parameter counts. The tensor network outperforms all classical models, including linear and neural networks, on excess return and information ratio, suggesting a more effective architecture despite fewer parameters. The quantum neural network underperforms neural networks over the entire period in risk‑adjusted terms but remains competitive in excess return and eventually surpasses linear regression after 2016. The authors interpret the superior performance of quantum and tensor models over linear regression as indicating an ability to learn nonlinear relationships, while neural networks appear prone to overfitting and fail to adapt in the latest market regime.
    [codes: C-002, C-010, C-011, C-015, C-016, C-038, C-003, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-045, C-046, C-050]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The analysis is constrained to a small set of 10 features because the QCL architecture requires one qubit per feature and simulating more qubits becomes computationally intensive, limiting model complexity. To reduce computational burden further, models are re‑estimated only once per year in the rolling backtest rather than at every rebalance. The quantum experiments are conducted in a noiseless simulation, so no hardware noise or error‑correction issues are addressed, and the work is situated in the NISQ era where full‑scale error correction is not yet available. The authors also acknowledge that their hypothesis about quantum techniques better controlling overfitting is unconfirmed and requires further examination, and they note that it is unknown whether the observed superiority of tensor networks would persist with more features and parameters.
    [codes: C-030, C-034, C-039, C-007, C-049, C-053]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose several directions for future research: testing whether the tensor network’s apparent superiority persists when increasing the number of features and model parameters, and rigorously examining the conjectured overfitting control of quantum models. They also suggest extending the analysis to other geographic markets such as the U.S. or global equities, investigating applicability to other asset classes like bonds and currencies, and exploring quantum counterparts of recurrent architectures for time‑series financial modeling.
    [codes: C-049, C-053, C-054, C-055, C-056]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is framed as applying quantum circuit learning and quantum‑inspired tensor network machine learning to a real‑world financial problem—cross‑sectional stock return prediction with portfolio backtesting—under NISQ‑era constraints. The authors highlight that these quantum and tensor models, with carefully controlled parameter counts, can outperform standard linear regression and neural networks in certain regimes, suggesting potential advantages in capturing nonlinear feature interactions and possibly in mitigating overfitting, though the latter is presented as speculative.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-038, C-047, C-048, C-050, C-052]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses a clearly defined cross‑sectional formulation with linear regression and neural networks as benchmarks, employing ReLU activations and similar parameter scales across models for fair comparison. All models, including QCL and tensor networks, are trained via stochastic gradient descent minimizing mean squared error, with QCL gradients computed using the parameter‑shift rule; the authors note but do not use DMRG, favoring implementation simplicity. The dataset consists of monthly TOPIX500 constituents with ten ranked and normalized features and returns, and a rolling 3‑year training/1‑year test backtest from 2008–2021, forming equal‑weight long‑only top‑quintile portfolios evaluated against TOPIX500 using excess return, tracking error, and information ratio. They also emphasize that the tensor architecture (MPS) and model sizes are standardized for comparability, and that numerical experiments are done in a noiseless simulator.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors repeatedly interpret the superior performance of quantum and tensor models over linear regression as suggesting an ability to capture non‑linear relationships among features, and they link observed performance deterioration of neural networks in recent periods to overfitting and market instability. They also explicitly speculate that quantum techniques may have better control over overfitting, while stressing that this remains to be validated.
    [codes: C-006, C-013, C-044, C-048, C-050, C-051, C-052]

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum state preparation as a distribution-generation task, where measurement probabilities must match a desired target distribution for use in simulations and pricing problems. It focuses on modeling one-dimensional financial and statistical distributions, including NVDA return distributions and log-normal price distributions for European call option pricing, as well as extending to structured two-dimensional probability patterns such as digit images on an 8×8 grid.
    [codes: C-003, C-006, C-028, C-032, C-033, C-038]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a hybrid variational framework that integrates discrete-time split-step quantum walks with parameterized coin operations to implement an Adaptive Distribution Generator (ADG). Coin operators are realized as three-parameter unitary gates (U3-type) within DTQW/SSQW evolutions, with a classical optimizer iteratively tuning these coin parameters to minimize mismatch between simulated and target distributions, using measurement-based cost functions and gradient-descent updates. For 2D pattern generation, they introduce two entangled quantum walkers sharing a four-dimensional coin space, with evolution governed by entangled 2D walk and conditional translation operators that correlate motion along x and y, and they encode 2D images via amplitude/intensity mapping. All circuits are simulated using NVIDIA’s CUDA-Q/cuQuantum GPU-accelerated framework to improve scalability.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-009, C-012, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Benchmarking on six one-dimensional target distributions, including NVDA returns and various canonical statistical families, shows that the optimized quantum-walk-based ADG can closely match target distribution shapes, with a trade-off in which more coin parameters improve expressiveness and reduce final errors at higher computational cost. In an option-pricing example with a 5-qubit, 16-point price grid, the simulated European call prices track the Black–Scholes benchmark well for at- and in-the-money strikes but exhibit significantly larger errors for deep out-of-the-money options. For two-dimensional tasks, the method is reported to generate recognizable 8×8 digit patterns (0–9), with the authors attributing this capability to entanglement between coin registers enabling complex spatial interference.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-014, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-034, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: For the European call option experiment, the authors compare prices obtained from the QWs-based ADG against analytical Black–Scholes values, reporting that the quantum-walk-based prices closely track the benchmark around at- and in-the-money strikes but deviate more for deep out-of-the-money options. While they also state that GPU-accelerated CUDA-Q simulation reduces computational overhead and improves scalability relative to conventional methods, no explicit classical algorithmic baselines are quantitatively benchmarked beyond the analytical pricing formula.
    [codes: C-004, C-026, C-034]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors note that as the model scales to more sophisticated target distributions, prior quantum-walk approaches encounter performance bottlenecks, motivating their CUDA-Q implementation. They acknowledge a capacity limitation whereby heavy-tailed distributions, such as certain financial returns, may require a larger number of coins to capture subtle tail behavior, increasing computational time. In the option-pricing setup, they identify coarse price-grid discretization as a major source of error, particularly in distribution tails with sparse probability mass, and they also highlight that iterative parameter updates and finite sampling introduce variance that disproportionately affects payoffs dependent on low-probability events.
    [codes: C-010, C-029, C-031, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: To enhance precision, the authors propose using more position qubits for finer price-grid resolution and adopting advanced error-mitigation or denoising techniques. They also plan analytic work to systematically map how variations in the coin parameters (θ, φ, λ) relate to resulting statistical features of the generated distributions. Structural extensions under consideration include multi-coin architectures and continuous-variable quantum walks to enable richer and more finely discretized generative models, as well as deploying the ADG on near-term quantum hardware and developing noise-resilient variants to preserve distribution fidelity under realistic device noise.
    [codes: C-037, C-040, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to introduce a Quantum Walks–Based Adaptive Distribution Generator (QWs-based ADG) that uses variationally tuned split-step quantum walks to generate target probability distributions with high precision and efficiency, implemented within the CUDA-Q framework for GPU-accelerated scalability. A further contribution is the extension of this framework from one-dimensional financial and statistical distributions to two-dimensional generative tasks via entangled coin registers, demonstrated on 8×8 digit pattern generation.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-008, C-009, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-026, C-027]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study formulates state preparation as matching measurement probabilities to target distributions and leverages a clear hybrid loop in which measurement-derived simulated distributions feed a classical optimizer that updates coin parameters via gradient descent. The authors describe using CUDA-Q with cuQuantum for GPU-accelerated circuit simulation to address scaling bottlenecks in prior quantum-walk models, and they explicitly analyze error sources such as discretization and sampling/optimization noise, along with design trade-offs between the number of coins, expressiveness, and runtime. However, the reported evaluation includes visual comparison for 2D digit outputs and qualitative fidelity claims rather than standardized quantitative metrics for all tasks, and details such as stopping criteria or dataset preprocessing are only partially specified in the codes.
    [codes: C-006, C-008, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-019, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-035, C-036, C-038]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper provides background on earlier ancilla-based controlled-rotation schemes for state preparation and formal definitions of DTQW and SSQW evolution operators, parameterized coin operators, and 2D entangled walk shift operators, which primarily serve as theoretical context rather than distinct finance-oriented claims.
    [codes: C-007, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-021, C-022, C-023]

=== PAPER 4dbaf2b286bf (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets variational quantum classifiers for financial classification tasks and frames barren plateaux as a central obstacle to their scalability and effective optimization, especially for real-world classification on noisy, nonlinear financial market data. The concrete finance problem is modeling the evolution/direction of the BET index in relation to well-known global indices using real financial time-series data.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-004, C-005, C-009]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a Noise-Optimization variational quantum classifier (NO-VQC), which is a hardware-efficient VQC where each d-dimensional instance is encoded via AngleEmbedding using Ry rotations on d qubits, followed by layers of Rx, Ry, Rz on each qubit with linear CNOT entanglement and a single-qubit Pauli-Z expectation value as the classifier output. Training minimizes a squared-error loss, and a noisy optimization mechanism adaptively adds small uniform noise to the (standardized) training data when stagnation is detected or at random, thereby altering the loss landscape and potentially moving parameters out of barren plateau regions; experiments use a simple generic circuit as the baseline for illustrating these effects and fix noise hyperparameters such as the stagnation window, shift magnitude, probability, and number of noisy steps.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-023]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The study reports that the NO-VQC approach significantly improves predictive performance compared to the baseline VQC, with statistical tests indicating that the median accuracy improvements are significant overall and that in about 60% of separate experiments the noise mechanism yields significantly better results, while in the remaining 40% there is no significant difference. The authors also find that NO-VQC tends to reduce overfitting, showing smaller gaps between training and test accuracy than the baseline VQC, and that for certain layer configurations (e.g., 4, 5, and 2 layers for NO-VQC, and 3 layers for VQC) both quantum variants feature among the best-performing models. Gradient analyses suggest that with the noise mechanism the average gradient and its variance oscillate, enabling continued exploration and avoiding early stagnation, and that in one example larger-layer circuits do not exhibit clear barren plateaux while smaller-layer circuits tend to reach a plateau or minimum more quickly.
    [codes: C-006, C-026, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors compare NO-VQC and baseline VQC against a suite of classical machine learning models (SVM, decision trees, random forests, logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors) and claim that their quantum approach provides results comparable to those of established classical methods on the financial prediction task. They further observe that the classical baselines exhibit high overfitting, with pronounced gaps between training and test accuracy, whereas NO-VQC shows smaller overfitting, which is presented as a qualitative advantage of the noisy quantum classifier.
    [codes: C-007, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-032]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly acknowledges several limitations of the proposed noisy optimization mechanism: there is no guarantee that shifting the data by noise will lead to an improved solution, since excessively large noise may move the search into regions of the loss landscape that are not better and potentially worse than the ones escaped. The authors also note that even if the loss function stops improving because a minimum has been reached, this minimum may not correspond to a good classification outcome in terms of predictive performance. More generally, they state that they are not aware of any mechanism that can ensure a noise-induced shift will yield improvement, underscoring that the method remains a heuristic without formal guarantees.
    [codes: C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: As a direction for future work, the authors propose investigating the choice of appropriate noise distributions tailored to variational quantum classifiers or specific data distributions, implying that the current uniform noise choice is preliminary and might be improved or specialized.
    [codes: C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The claimed contribution is a novel noise-based optimization approach for variational quantum classifiers that seeks to mitigate barren plateaux during training by adaptively perturbing the training data with small uniform noise when optimization stagnates or randomly, thereby reshaping the loss landscape and enabling continued search. The work also highlights, in a financial application, that this mechanism can enhance VQC performance and reduce overfitting relative to a baseline VQC without such noise.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-015, C-017, C-019, C-026, C-033]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper uses real financial market data as its benchmark, specifically modeling the BET index relative to other indices, and motivates this as a challenging noisy, nonlinear domain. For experimental rigor, baseline VQC and NO-VQC are evaluated on identical train–test splits with the same randomly seeded initial parameters to control for initialization effects, and a GradientDescent optimizer is chosen partly because it is susceptible to barren plateaux and local optima, making it suitable to test the proposed mechanism. Noise hyperparameters such as stagnation window, shift magnitude, random application probability, and number of noisy steps are fixed and reported, and performance differences are evaluated using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test at a 0.05 significance level, providing a nonparametric statistical assessment of median accuracies across runs. The use of a simple, generic circuit as baseline is explicitly stated to clarify how the noise mechanism deforms the loss function, and gradient behavior over training is analyzed to support the mechanism’s effect on the optimization dynamics.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors conceptually distinguish three possible situations when resuming optimization on the original data after a noise-induced shift, but the individual scenarios are not detailed in the extracted codes and thus are not mapped to other dimensions.

=== PAPER 50989fdc9ad1 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the core obstacle for quantum algorithms in finance and statistics as the lack of efficient, updatable state-preparation routines for loading classical probability distributions into quantum states, particularly when worst‑case arbitrary states are prohibitively deep and ancilla‑intensive and when existing methods require updating many circuit parameters each time model parameters change (C-001, C-002, C-004). It formulates the problem as preparing quantum states that encode statistical distributions and mixtures, Odistr|0⟩ = ∑x p(x)|x⟩, with p(x) arising from parametric or maximum‑entropy models, and then using these states for downstream tasks like derivative pricing and risk analysis (C-012, C-035, C-038).
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-012, C-035, C-038]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors introduce a statistics‑informed parameterized quantum circuit (SI‑PQC) framework that links quantum state preparation to intrinsic statistical symmetries via the maximum entropy principle, using observables with conservative expectations as symmetry‑defining constraints (C-007, C-008, C-014, C-015). Within this framework, they decompose distributional information into fixed constraint functions fk (encoding prior model knowledge) and tunable parameters λk (encoding data uncertainty), and implement a maximum entropy distribution loader (MEDL) in three steps: unitary dilation of normalized constraint functions, linear combination of these via block encoding, and QSVT‑based imaginary‑time evolution to approximate the exponential form (C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020). The circuit architecture is a static state‑preparation structure with model parameters explicitly encoded as rotation angles, enabling reuse, deep compilation, and compatibility with a weighted distribution mixer (WDM) that reuses MEDL components and encodes parameter uncertainty in latent registers for mixture models, as well as with a variational learning protocol and QMCI/QAE for finance applications (C-009, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-029, C-030, C-035, C-037, C-038).
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-009, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-029, C-030, C-035, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that SI‑PQC, via MEDL, achieves universal expressiveness with an optimally dimensioned learning space and classical preprocessing complexity that is optimal in the number of model parameters M, since only O(M) rotation angles must be updated (C-011, C-019). For single distributions, the MEDL theorem gives single‑shot circuit depth O(n M df log(1/ε)) with success probability F²/4, improved to depth O(n M df log(1/ε)/F) with amplitude amplification, and analogous complexity bounds hold for mixtures under the WDM theorem with only logarithmic additional depth in the number of mixture components (C-021, C-022, C-026, C-028). SI‑PQC‑based learning is argued to reduce training complexity and improve generalization because it uses only Npara = M ≪ n independent gates and a repetition count Nrepeat independent of qubit number, leading to generalization error bounds driven by the small parameter count (C-033, C-034). In finance applications, the authors state that QMCI with SI‑PQC enables a quantum extension of incremental computing for pricing, yielding a favorable end‑to‑end resource expression, and that Greeks can be obtained directly via parameter‑shift rules on the SI‑PQC parameters (C-035, C-036, C-037). For risk analysis, they show numerically that slowly varying observables such as E[X] and E[ln X] serve as conservative constraints and that SI‑PQC can efficiently and accurately approximate empirical distributions to recover quantities like empirical VaR from simulated data (C-039, C-040).
    [codes: C-011, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-026, C-028, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Relative to classical or existing quantum‑assisted pipelines that rely on heavy preprocessing, the authors argue that a static SI‑PQC structure with only M tunable parameters avoids recomputing large preprocessed artifacts and thus preserves potential speed‑ups in time‑dependent models (C-004, C-005, C-009, C-019, C-023). For mixture models, they explicitly contrast WDM with straightforward QSP+LCU combinations that require Nθ repetitions of full circuits, claiming that WDM needs only logarithmic additional depth, leading to an exponential reduction in time and quantum resources for mixtures (C-006, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-010). In learning, they position SI‑PQC favorably against generic QML models whose generalization error scales with a larger parameter count, emphasizing that SI‑PQC uses only M independent gates (C-033, C-034). In pricing and VaR estimation, SI‑PQC‑based QMCI is presented as a quantum analogue of classical incremental computing and classical Monte Carlo, with the resource expression TTSSI−PQC intended to be lower end‑to‑end than approaches where state preparation dominates (C-035, C-036).
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-009, C-019, C-023, C-006, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-010, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that classical pre-processing approaches are fragile in time‑dependent settings because previously computed artifacts quickly become obsolete, erasing any prospective quantum speed‑ups; SI‑PQC is partly motivated as a remedy but they treat this as a limitation of many current methods (C-005). They also note that a simple combination of QSP routines with LCU for mixtures incurs prohibitive overhead, motivating but not fully eliminating mixture‑model complexity concerns (C-006). For their own proposal, they state that for small qubit numbers n, the asymptotic resource advantage of SI‑PQC can be diminished by larger constant prefactors, so practical gains may only materialize at moderate or large scales (C-041). They further mention that block‑encoding of certain linear functions can be viewed as a limitation of SI‑PQC, suggesting the need to hybridize with pre‑trained PQCs to address this gap (C-042).
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: As a way to mitigate current limitations in implementing linear functions within SI‑PQC, the authors suggest combining SI‑PQC with a pre‑trained PQC used specifically for block encoding, effectively proposing hybrid architectures as future work (C-042). They also state that SI‑PQC could be extended beyond the paper’s concrete tasks to loading and simulating time series and to designing quantum algorithms for non‑parametric and semi‑parametric statistical tests, indicating broader statistical and financial applications (C-043). Additionally, they point to a possible but unexplored connection between SI‑PQC and quantum state tomography or verification, explicitly leaving this line of inquiry open (C-044).
    [codes: C-042, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in introducing a statistics‑informed parameterized quantum circuit that embeds prior knowledge about data symmetries via observables with conservative expectations and the maximum entropy principle, yielding maximum‑entropy distributions as the ‘best unbiased guess’ when explicit formulas are unavailable (C-007, C-008, C-014, C-015, C-016). They further claim that this design leads to universal expressiveness with an optimally dimensioned learning space and a static circuit structure in which all model parameters appear only as rotation angles, enabling advanced compilation, reuse, and precise phase calculation (C-009, C-011, C-023). For mixtures, they present the WDM construction as novel in reusing MEDL components to encode parameter uncertainty in a latent space, achieving only logarithmic additional depth and, according to their analysis, exponential savings in time and quantum resources compared with naive QSP+LCU schemes (C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-010). Finally, they emphasize that SI‑PQC supports simultaneous learning of classical model parameters and quantum states, improving interpretability and potentially offering better generalization due to the small number of independent parameters (C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-034).
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-009, C-011, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-010, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the framework is grounded in a clear separation between fixed prior knowledge (encoded in constraint functions fk) and tunable data‑driven parameters λk, which dictates both circuit design and learning strategy and is explicitly aligned with the maximum entropy principle (C-014, C-015, C-016). The MEDL construction is specified as a three‑step, block‑encoding‑based process with formal theorems providing circuit depth and success probabilities, and the use of amplitude amplification and imaginary‑time evolution approximated via QSVT is analytically characterized (C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022). For learning, the authors employ a fidelity‑based loss that allows parameter extraction proportional to the number of free parameters, and they explicitly tie generalization bounds to the parameter count, emphasizing that SI‑PQC contains only M independent gates repeated O(log(1/εF)) times (C-029, C-030, C-033, C-034). In the financial experiments, they adopt a sliding‑window incremental scheme for online risk analysis and identify slowly varying observables such as E[X] and E[ln X] as conservative constraints for maximum‑entropy fitting, arguing that this yields accurate approximations of empirical distributions and VaR estimates, although detailed benchmarking against real financial data is not discussed in the codes provided (C-035, C-036, C-038, C-039, C-040).

Simulation of quantum computers on classical hardware is exponentially expensive in qubit number, and software workarounds such as swap operations or error correction introduce additional operations, noise, and qubit overhead. Many reported advantages are only theoretical or on very low‑complexity examples; speed‑ups often depend on problem‑specific parameters, and classical Monte Carlo’s massive parallelizability further raises the bar for quantum advantage. === PAPER 53a718c11ea8 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as anomaly detection on quantum data, specifically detecting point anomalies in quantum states themselves (pure and mixed) in a semi-supervised setting, which the authors term "quantum anomaly detection." They focus on classifying individual quantum states as normal or anomalous within this semi-supervised point-anomaly scenario and later generalize from pure to mixed quantum states, motivated by noisy processes and designed mixed-state outputs such as in NMR.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-006, C-024, C-025]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors construct quantum versions of kernel PCA and one-class SVM for anomaly detection on quantum data, building explicitly on classical algorithms as a foundation. For kernel PCA on pure states, they define a quantum centroid state, construct centered quantum data, and introduce a proximity measure f(ψ₀) implemented via inner-product estimation using a modified swap test, with an alternative protocol that prepares a superposition of centered data to improve scaling. For one-class SVM on pure states, they define a fidelity-based kernel matrix, reinterpret it as a density matrix to enable quantum simulation, use classical inversion as a baseline, and propose a quantum matrix inversion (HHL) route together with overlap-based proximity evaluation via a modified swap test. For mixed states, they extend kernel PCA by defining a mixed-state proximity measure that can be executed with logarithmic resources in the Hilbert-space dimension, and they extend one-class SVM by using a (super)fidelity-type kernel for mixed states whose proximity measures can also be computed with O(log d) resources.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-021, C-022, C-026, C-027, C-028]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The key theoretical result is that the proposed quantum kernel PCA and one-class SVM algorithms for anomaly detection on quantum states can be implemented with resources that scale logarithmically in the Hilbert-space dimension d, and, for pure states, also logarithmically in the number of training states M under certain constructions. Specifically, the initial kernel PCA proximity measure f(ψ₀) can be computed with resources O(poly(M log d)), and an alternative protocol reduces the dependence on M to O(log M); for mixed states, both kernel PCA and SVM proximity measures are claimed to be computable using O(log d) resources. The authors further provide sampling/measurement complexity estimates, stating that the number of measurements needed to estimate the anomaly score can scale as O(log(Md)) under a chosen tolerance, indicating favorable scaling in both system size and the number of training states in the idealized regimes.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-012, C-013, C-023, C-026, C-028]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical methods serve as both conceptual and computational baselines: the quantum algorithms are explicitly constructed from classical kernel PCA and one-class SVM formulations, and classical matrix inversion with cost O(M³) is identified as the standard way to obtain the SVM coefficients αᵢ needed for the anomaly score. The claimed quantum advantages are framed relative to these baselines, emphasizing logarithmic scaling in state dimension and, conditionally, in training-set size compared to classical approaches that would require resources polynomial in d and at least cubic in M.
    [codes: C-007, C-017]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several important limitations and technical conditions underlying their speedup claims. For the HHL-based one-class SVM, simulating the kernel matrix as a unitary requires K to be sufficiently low-rank and needs O(t²/ε) copies of K, imposing structural assumptions on the data. They also require a favorable condition number, expressed as 1/P_T ≲ O(log M), constraining the threshold parameter and effectively the spectrum of the kernel matrix. In the mixed-state setting, they explicitly note that achieving a "big quantum data" speedup in the number of training states demands additional requirements, including the ability to generate multiple copies of appropriate kernel density matrices, and they state that it is unclear how such kernel density matrices can be prepared with minimal assumptions. These caveats limit the generality and immediate practicality of the proposed speedups, especially for large and noisy mixed-state datasets.
    [codes: C-019, C-020, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper highlights two main directions for future work: extending quantum anomaly detection beyond point anomalies to other anomaly types in the quantum domain, which the authors explicitly defer to future studies, and addressing open challenges associated with achieving training-set speedups for mixed-state anomaly detection, particularly around preparing kernel density matrices under realistic assumptions.
    [codes: C-031, C-032]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors position their work as introducing quantum machine-learning algorithms specifically tailored for anomaly detection on quantum states, which they term "quantum anomaly detection," and as providing quantum kernel PCA and quantum one-class SVM constructions that operate directly on quantum data with logarithmic resource scaling in the dimension of the quantum states and, for pure states, in the number of training states. They further claim that these favorable scalings make the algorithms potentially suitable for big quantum data applications and that the extension from pure to mixed states, including appropriate fidelity-based kernels and overlap measures, broadens applicability to noisy or intrinsically mixed quantum processes.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is largely theoretical and algorithmic, focused on defining quantum analogues of classical kernel PCA and one-class SVM through constructions such as centroid states, centered quantum data, proximity measures, and overlap-estimation routines like modified swap tests, as well as quantum matrix inversion via HHL and density-matrix reinterpretation of kernel matrices. The paper carefully specifies resource scaling, measurement complexity, and structural assumptions (e.g., low rank and condition number constraints), but the codes do not indicate any empirical implementation details, datasets, or experimental validation, implying that reproducibility here primarily concerns reproducing the analytical derivations rather than benchmarking on concrete data.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None.

=== PAPER 5413b7728054 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum machine learning as a transformative approach to data analysis that can enhance classical supervised and unsupervised learning, with particular relevance for complex optimisation and high‑dimensional classification problems that challenge classical methods. It positions QML as important for sectors such as finance, alongside material science and healthcare, and motivates quantum computing via the slowdown of Moore’s law and the need to handle problems classical systems find intractable.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study focuses on quantum machine learning techniques that transform conventional algorithms into quantum algorithms by encoding data onto qubits, applying unitary operations, and measuring outcomes, leveraging superposition and entanglement for parallel state storage and computation. For supervised learning, the paper particularly highlights Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVMs) as quantum counterparts to classical SVMs, implemented as hybrid quantum‑classical solutions on NISQ devices, with an IBMQ/Qiskit experiment on a heart disease dataset. It also conceptually reviews Quantum Neural Networks, variational quantum classifiers, quantum kernel estimators, and other quantum classifiers and clustering methods drawn from prior literature.
    [codes: C-005, C-010, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-028, C-029, C-016, C-027]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that quantum‑enhanced models such as QSVMs and QNNs show strong performance on classification and regression tasks, and conclude that QML can enable rapid data processing with enhanced model accuracy in supervised learning. In their IBMQ experiment on the Kaggle heart disease dataset, the QSVM achieved a reported accuracy of 97.64% with an execution time of 14 seconds, compared to 94.3% accuracy and 33 seconds for the classical SVM. More generally, the paper emphasizes that quantum algorithms promise advantages in processing speed, memory efficiency, and the ability to address problems intractable for classical systems.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The core experimental comparison implements both QSVM and classical SVM on IBMQ, finding that the QSVM attains higher accuracy (97.64% vs. 94.3%) and lower execution time (14 s vs. 33 s) on the heart disease dataset. In its literature review, the paper cites prior work where quantum adiabatic classifiers outperformed AdaBoost, quantum dimensionality‑reduction methods and nearest‑neighbor algorithms achieved exponential or super‑exponential accelerations, and QSVMs can offer logarithmic time complexity with exponential improvements in training size and dimensionality. It also notes contrasting evidence from cited QSVM image and breast cancer studies where noise led to inferior quantum performance or accuracy, even when speedups (e.g., 234× faster QSVM vs. SVM) were reported.
    [codes: C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-040, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly acknowledges that current quantum computers are limited by qubit count and intrinsic noise, placing today’s devices in the NISQ regime and making it difficult to solve machine learning problems directly on such hardware. It stresses that designers must account for hardware limitations like noise, gate count, and error correction challenges, and notes from cited QSVM image‑classification work that noise can degrade performance on real quantum hardware. It also reiterates the classical curse of dimensionality as a challenge that motivates quantum approaches.

=== PAPER 55496bcdeaa7 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames an unconstrained black-box binary optimization problem, proposing to solve it with a variational quantum algorithm where binary decision variables are mapped to qubits and evaluated via an implicit loss function (C-001, C-008, C-013). Feature selection is chosen as the primary application: selecting a subset of features is treated as an NP-hard combinatorial optimization task whose quality is measured by the performance of a downstream model on a predefined metric, here log-loss (C-002, C-004, C-014, C-019).
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-008, C-013, C-014, C-019]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors introduce a variational quantum feature selection (VarQFS) method that recasts the black-box binary optimization as a ground-state search over an implicitly defined diagonal Hamiltonian, evaluated by sampling-based loss estimation (C-006, C-008, C-015). They use a Qiskit RealAmplitudes ansatz with linear entanglement and deliberately low depth (d = 0, 1, 2) to remain compatible with MPS simulation and noisy hardware (C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024). Optimization is carried out with an approximate quantum natural gradient optimizer (QN-SPSA), motivated by its connection to imaginary-time evolution and its promise for quantum problems, with overlaps and QFI estimated via compute–uncompute overlap circuits (C-009, C-010, C-011, C-022).
    [codes: C-006, C-008, C-015, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-022]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across experiments, the authors report that VarQFS achieves competitive and in some respects better performance than traditional feature selection methods, both on a reduced 20-feature benchmark and the full 59-feature dataset (C-003, C-028, C-034, C-036). On the 20-feature case, MPS-based training reaches a loss extremely close to the globally optimal training score obtained via exhaustive search (C-025, C-026, C-027). In the full-data setting, they observe that higher circuit depths tend to yield better best-sample test scores and that VarQFS can, for at least one seed in every setting, outperform classical baselines on roughly 90% of training instances (C-032, C-034, C-036). They also note that the ibmq montreal hardware run, despite noise and absence of error mitigation, manages to outperform traditional methods in some aspects (C-028, C-037).
    [codes: C-003, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-032, C-034, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum feature selection method is compared against classical baselines such as RFE and RFECV built on logistic regression, with the quality of subsets defined by the resulting model performance on log-loss (C-014, C-019, C-028). On the exhaustively solvable 20-feature problem, VarQFS finds feature subsets with slightly better test scores than RFE/RFECV, and on the full 59-feature dataset the best VarQFS configurations improve over classical baselines in terms of both train and test scores for some seeds and settings (C-025, C-028, C-034, C-036). The authors emphasize that classical methods are mostly greedy heuristics for this NP-hard problem, which leaves room for near-term quantum algorithms to be competitive (C-004, C-005).
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-014, C-019, C-025, C-028, C-034, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations. Methodologically, convergence of the variational algorithm relies on choosing an initial state with non-zero overlap with the ground state, which they implement via a nearly uniform state (C-012). In practice, hardware experiments use fewer SPSA/QFI resampling shots than simulations due to limited quantum resources, leading to less smooth convergence (C-029). The authors attribute observed outliers in hardware loss curves to both the stochastic nature of QN-SPSA and physical noise on the quantum backend, and they do not apply any error mitigation, which constrains achievable performance (C-030, C-037). For deeper circuits in the larger-scale simulations, they point out that QN-SPSA’s approximations are more likely to deviate from the true gradient and quantum Fisher information, hampering training at higher depth (C-033). They also report a strong dependence on random seeds in the full-data experiments, indicating significant variability in performance across runs (C-035).
    [codes: C-012, C-029, C-030, C-033, C-035, C-037]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors identify several avenues for future work: more systematic study and tuning of QN-SPSA hyperparameters to improve training stability and performance (C-038), deeper investigation of how entanglement structure in the ansatz affects results (C-039), and extensions of the method to enforce fixed-size feature subsets, e.g., requiring the final selection to contain exactly m features (C-040).
    [codes: C-038, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to introduce a variational quantum algorithm tailored for unconstrained black-box binary optimization, instantiated as a feature selection application where the objective is accessed only through sampled evaluations rather than an explicit Hamiltonian construction (C-001, C-002, C-006, C-008, C-015). It further emphasizes the use of a quantum natural gradient–based optimizer (QN-SPSA) motivated by its suitability for quantum problems and its connection to imaginary-time evolution, and demonstrates that this hybrid approach can be competitive with, and sometimes outperform, standard greedy classical feature selection heuristics on a real credit-risk dataset (C-005, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-016, C-028, C-036).
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-008, C-015, C-005, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-016, C-028, C-036]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: The experimental setup uses a publicly available German credit-risk dataset with 1,000 data points and 20 original attributes expanded via one-hot encoding, applying a 50/50 train–test split and checking that train and test subsets have comparable feature correlations to ensure representativeness (C-016, C-017, C-018). Baseline comparisons are clearly specified using logistic regression and log-loss, and the authors employ both MPS simulation with controlled entanglement and a real IBM superconducting processor (ibmq montreal) to assess performance across idealized and noisy settings (C-019, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024). Empirical loss is explicitly defined via measured shot frequencies, and finite-sample estimation is justified via Hoeffding’s inequality, indicating attention to statistical rigor in how the black-box objective is approximated (C-006, C-007, C-015).
    [codes: C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-006, C-007, C-015]

=== PAPER 57a58ac6ea72 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as establishing rigorous mathematical foundations for quantum linear regression by mapping classical regularized squared-loss regression into a quantum optimization problem via a variational Hamiltonian formulation, with an eye toward applications in financial forecasting such as Thai SET Index prediction using market features. The authors emphasize constructing a complete mapping from classical regression objectives, including L2-regularized loss, into quantum Hamiltonians whose expectation values represent the loss, thereby providing a proof-of-concept framework intended for financial modeling tasks. They further plan to tailor data preprocessing (e.g., truncating targets and scaling features) so that financial returns or derived targets respect the bounded quantum weight constraints.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-006, C-009, C-018, C-030, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-049]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is a variational, NISQ-compatible quantum linear regression algorithm that encodes classical regression weights as expectation values of Pauli-Z operators on parameterized quantum states and reformulates the squared loss as the expectation of a constructed Hamiltonian. The method specifies a parameterized quantum state ansatz, Pauli-Z measurement-based readout, explicit Hamiltonian constructions (including single- and two-feature simplifications) and matrix-building algorithms, and trains via a variational loop using parameter-shift gradient rules and a complete iterative algorithm. The framework is explicitly designed for shallow circuits on near-term hardware, includes efficient expectation computation procedures, and incorporates implementation details such as the intended software/hardware stack and measurement-shot complexity scaling with desired precision.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-010, C-013, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-047, C-050, C-051]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports theoretical results including a complete Hamiltonian representation of the squared loss, explicit forms for single- and two-feature Hamiltonians, and a closed-form relation between rotation parameters and Pauli-Z expectations yielding hard-bounded weights in [−1,1] that induce natural regularization. It provides a detailed characterization of quantum-induced and adaptive regularization behavior, including an implicit regularization term, varying strength across parameter space, and boundary behavior favoring certain weights, as well as a Riemannian metric on the parameter space and its degeneracies. The authors also prove convergence properties for quantum gradient descent (O(1/√K) to a stationary point) and derive robustness bounds showing maintained (but degraded) convergence under bounded noise, plus measurement-shot complexity scaling M = O(1/ε²) and conditions under which the quantum optimum exactly matches or best-approximates the classical optimum under weight constraints.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-009, C-011, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-023, C-024, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-049, C-055, C-059]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors explicitly compare their quantum formulation to classical L2-regularized linear regression, starting from the standard regularized squared-loss objective and its analytical solution and then establishing a mathematical framework that shows computational equivalence between the classical and quantum regression formulations. They prove that if the classical optimal weights lie within the quantum-induced bounds (‖w*classical‖∞ ≤ 1), the quantum solution exactly matches the classical optimum, while if the optimal classical weights exceed these bounds, the quantum solution is the best approximation within the constrained set. The paper also positions the method against HHL-based quantum linear system solvers and classical quantum-inspired methods via comparison tables, arguing that its variational, NISQ-oriented design and quantum-specific regularization differentiate it from those approaches.
    [codes: C-007, C-018, C-019, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-038, C-039, C-056, C-057, C-058]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations primarily related to hardware and geometric properties of the parameter space: finite measurement shots introduce statistical error in expectation value estimates, imperfect gate fidelities cause systematic bias, and limited coherence times lead to time-dependent degradation of measurement accuracy during training. The authors note that the induced Riemannian metric on the parameter space becomes degenerate at boundary parameter values corresponding to weights ±1, which may affect optimization behavior near those extremes. They further analyze that convergence under noise persists but with a degraded rate, thus recognizing that practical performance on real devices will be impacted by bounded noise and NISQ-era imperfections.
    [codes: C-041, C-052, C-053, C-054, C-055]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work centers on empirical validation and financial application: the authors propose implementing the quantum regression framework on Thai SET Index forecasting using Yahoo Finance data, with a detailed plan for financial feature engineering, data acquisition, and performance evaluation metrics. They outline preprocessing tailored to quantum constraints—such as target truncation and feature scaling—alongside a concrete implementation plan on quantum simulators and hardware to test the theoretical predictions. More broadly, they identify empirical studies on quantum platforms as the next step to substantiate the mathematical proof-of-concept in realistic financial modeling scenarios.
    [codes: C-008, C-043, C-046, C-048, C-060]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim to provide a comprehensive mathematical proof-of-concept and the first complete derivation of quantum Hamiltonians corresponding to regression loss functions with explicit matrix forms, yielding a full mapping from classical to quantum regression. They highlight innovations including a variational Hamiltonian formulation tailored to NISQ devices, geometric analysis of the induced Riemannian structure on quantum parameter spaces, rigorous convergence theory for quantum gradient descent in regression, and a theoretical framework for quantum-induced regularization that differs from classical regularizers. The work positions itself as filling a specific gap in the quantum machine learning literature by unifying Hamiltonian constructions, optimization analysis, and regularization theory within one quantum linear regression framework aimed at financial modeling.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-031, C-032, C-040, C-058, C-059]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper is theoretical rather than empirical, focusing on explicit derivations, algorithms, and complexity analyses rather than reporting numerical experiments. It specifies the classical baseline objective and closed-form solution for linear regression, then carefully constructs the quantum ansatz, readout, Hamiltonians, and matrix representations, including algorithmic procedures for Hamiltonian construction and efficient expectation computation. The training procedure is laid out via a full variational algorithm with parameter-shift gradient computation and a convergence analysis detailing rates and shot complexity, and the authors define intended evaluation metrics for future forecasting experiments. Data-related aspects such as feature engineering, target truncation, and feature scaling are presented as planned protocols for a future financial implementation, but no actual datasets or empirical results are yet provided.
    [codes: C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-040, C-044, C-045, C-048, C-050, C-051, C-059]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Most codes align with the core dimensions; remaining items primarily elaborate expected financial modeling benefits and the NISQ-oriented positioning and comparative analysis of the approach within the broader quantum ML landscape, including explicit comparisons to HHL-based and quantum-inspired methods, which reinforce, rather than extend beyond, the main narrative of theoretical advantage and practical orientation.

=== PAPER 58a29f9f57a7 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames financial fraud detection as a highly imbalanced, real‑time binary classification problem where legacy and existing classical fraud systems struggle with large high‑dimensional data, evolving fraud patterns, and produce many false positives and false negatives. It emphasizes that current systems cannot efficiently adapt to changing fraud tactics or handle the extreme fraud rarity (≈0.173% of transactions) present in real-world datasets. The authors position hybrid quantum–classical models as a way to improve recall and reduce false negatives under these constraints.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-032]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study uses a hybrid quantum–classical pipeline built around Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVM) with quantum kernels and Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC) optimized by COBYLA, combined with quantum feature selection. PCA is first applied for dimensionality reduction, then Quantum Feature Selection (QFS) is used to preserve nonlinear interactions, with QSVM operating on PCA-transformed data via a ZZFeatureMap feature map and VQC trained with a RealAmplitudes-style circuit optimized using COBYLA. A QUBO-based ensemble fusion mechanism, solved via simulated annealing, integrates predictions from quantum models (QSVM, VQC) and classical models (SVM, KNN) into a unified hybrid framework.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-010, C-012, C-020, C-021, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that their operational hybrid prototype improves recall and reduces false negatives compared to legacy systems, with all models showing very high accuracy under extreme class imbalance but more informative variation in Precision, Recall, F1, ROC‑AUC, and PR‑AUC. Individually, QSVM achieves Accuracy 0.998, Precision 0.25, Recall 0.72, F1 0.37, ROC‑AUC 0.91, PR‑AUC 0.32, while VQC obtains Accuracy 0.997, Precision 0.18, Recall 0.80, F1 0.29, ROC‑AUC 0.90, PR‑AUC 0.28. The QUBO-based hybrid ensemble yields the best overall performance with Accuracy 0.999, Precision 0.42, Recall 0.76, F1 0.54, ROC‑AUC 0.94, and PR‑AUC 0.47, and is interpreted as providing superior minority-class detection under severe imbalance.
    [codes: C-003, C-009, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical models such as SVM and KNN are trained in parallel as baselines and then incorporated into the QUBO-based hybrid ensemble, which the authors claim yields a favorable trade-off between model complexity, dataset fit, and detection accuracy relative to purely classical or purely quantum approaches. The paper further reports that coupling quantum feature selection with classical ensemble techniques improves fraud detection results, and that the QUBO ensemble combining quantum and classical learners outperforms individual quantum models on precision, F1, ROC‑AUC, and PR‑AUC; however, specific standalone classical baseline metrics are not detailed in the coded excerpts.
    [codes: C-006, C-013, C-014, C-037, C-038, C-046, C-047]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that existing legacy and classical fraud detection systems perform poorly under large, imbalanced, and evolving datasets, motivating but not eliminating similar challenges for their own approach. For their quantum models, they note that QSVM faces scalability constraints as qubit counts increase and that VQC performance is limited by optimizer convergence and circuit depth. [CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles the challenge of forecasting stock price trends in financial time series that are non‑stationary, exhibit long memory, and have low signal‑to‑noise ratios, which makes them difficult to predict and limits support for investment decisions. It specifically highlights the need for more effective models that can handle abrupt trend changes and provide long‑term multistep forecasts, an area the authors argue has been underexplored. The forecasting problem is formulated as multi‑step prediction of future closing prices based on historical prices and external factors, respecting causality by avoiding the use of future information in feature extraction.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-028]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a frequency‑domain enhanced bi‑directional recurrent quantum network (FDBRQ) that combines classical frequency‑domain processing, external feature attention, and a quantum neural network with a bi‑directional recurrent structure. The quantum component is organized into quantum circuit units (QCUs), each composed of a Quantum Encoder that converts classical embedding vectors into quantum data and a trainable Quantum Ansatz that processes these quantum signals using basic quantum gates; two such circuits propagate temporal features in forward and reverse time order to capture long‑term dependencies. The model explicitly leverages quantum computation’s parallelism together with neural network capabilities, using a 6‑qubit system due to practical constraints.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-040]

The authors note that incorporating external factors via attention significantly reduces prediction errors, and that in visual comparisons the FDBRQ forecasts appear closest to real values, with the model maintaining stable and best‑in‑class accuracy even in long‑term (20‑step) prediction tasks. They further observe that multistep prediction formulations help mitigate cumulative errors that typically plague rolling prediction approaches and that their method exhibits relatively stable results in medium‑term horizons.
    [codes: C-006, C-028, C-033, C-041, C-042, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-050, C-051]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The FDBRQ model is empirically compared against classical approaches, and the authors report that it outperforms these baselines on the four Chinese stock datasets, including under short‑, medium‑, and long‑term prediction horizons. Within the classical recurrent architectures, they observe that deep LSTM structures can outperform bi‑directional LSTMs in one‑step prediction, while for longer sequences bi‑directional LSTM performs better at capturing long‑term memory; nonetheless, their quantum‑enhanced FDBRQ is presented as having the best and most stable performance overall. They also note that classical LSTM methods with simple structures may suffer from overfitting on some datasets and that rolling prediction methods, often used with classical models, accumulate errors over time, in contrast to their multistep formulation.
    [codes: C-006, C-041, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050]

Central novel elements include the frequency‑domain embedding module that learns causal time–frequency features without future information leakage, the external feature attention enhancement that injects selected external factors into embeddings, and the bi‑directional quantum recurrent structure that marries quantum computational parallelism with neural network advantages to capture long‑term dependencies in financial time series.
