=== PAPER 59cca9744140 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles the challenge that efficient amplitude encoding of classical information is fundamental to many practical quantum algorithms, yet preparing arbitrary amplitude-encoded quantum states is known to be time‑consuming and difficult to deploy on current noisy devices. It specifically targets the open challenge of designing a unitary state preparation scheme that attains logarithmic circuit depth, which is regarded as the optimal scaling for unitary methods.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose an improved Matrix Product State (IMPS)–based amplitude preparation scheme that recursively applies Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to an MPS in canonical form, constructs fourth‑order two‑qubit unitaries to approximately disentangle the state to |0…0>, and then reverses this circuit for preparation, restricted to two‑level qubits and universal two‑qubit gates. Parallel disentangling is enabled by arbitrarily selecting qubit pairs and scheduling non‑interfering operations in parallel, yielding a Tree Tensor Network (TTN)–like structure and, for hardware‑constrained settings, a denser Hypercube Tensor Network (HTN) constructed via graph edge contractions that model realistic chip topologies. At the gate‑decomposition level, they introduce an equivalence class of two‑qubit unitaries and a modified cosine‑sine/KAK‑based decomposition so that any fourth‑order unitary from the SVD can be implemented with two CNOTs plus single‑qubit gates instead of three CNOTs.
    [codes: C-009, C-011, C-012, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The main claimed result is that the IMPS scheme achieves amplitude preparation with logarithmic circuit depth, reducing conventional MPS depth from O(n) to O(log n), and that it remains compatible with arbitrary hardware connectivities while exhibiting topological adaptability. At the gate level, they claim an approximately one‑third reduction in two‑qubit gate count by showing that the required fourth‑order unitaries can be decomposed into two CNOTs instead of three, and they argue that this directly addresses the two‑qubit gate bottleneck on NISQ hardware. Theoretically, they identify a broad class of states with bounded MPS rank (including many common functions and entangled states) for which preparation is efficient, and they formally state that MPS rank‑2 states can be prepared exactly; numerically, HTN‑based methods are reported to achieve higher fidelity than MPS, TTN, and HEN at comparable depths, fidelity is observed to improve with increasing U‑depth, random‑state fidelity decreases and stabilizes as qubit number grows, and on n×m grid chips the required depth scales as roughly (m+n)/2 (≈O(√N) when m≈n), with a 12‑qubit 3×4 example showing that the chip‑adapted method attains higher fidelity at U‑depths 5 and 10 than traditional MPS at depth 11.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-010, C-014, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-029, C-032, C-033, C-040, C-041, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-048, C-049]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper does not report direct comparisons against purely classical state‑preparation or classical simulation algorithms; instead, all comparisons are among different quantum circuit constructions (MPS, TTN, HEN, and HTN) at fixed circuit depth, using a hardware‑efficient network as an additional quantum baseline to make fidelity comparisons at equal depth more fair. Subadditivity and submultiplicativity results on MPS rank over a ring structure are used to analyze which function classes admit low‑rank representations, but this remains an internal tensor‑network characterization rather than a performance benchmark against classical methods.
    [codes: C-031, C-038]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that arbitrary amplitude‑encoded state preparation is intrinsically time‑consuming and challenging on current noisy devices, and that optimizing circuit depth for arbitrary hardware topologies remains a difficult open problem. They explicitly note that existing approaches such as reinforcement learning for topology optimization provide only promising preliminary results and lack formal mathematical guarantees, and they caution that their own work still requires extensive hardware experiments, as well as further optimization to mitigate noise and decoherence, to substantiate and robustly validate the proposed framework. They also highlight that truncation procedures differ between method families in their numerical study, which constitutes a caveat for the comparability of reported fidelities.
    [codes: C-002, C-039, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions include using algorithmic optimization methods—potentially including reinforcement learning—to find near‑optimal edge contraction orders for general chip graphs, thereby improving depth on arbitrary topologies, and conducting extensive experiments on real quantum hardware to substantiate the simulated results. The authors also propose further work on noise and decoherence mitigation to enhance the reliability and performance of their amplitude‑encoding framework.
    [codes: C-026, C-051, C-052, C-053]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The claimed contributions are: an improved MPS (IMPS) protocol for amplitude encoding that reduces circuit depth from O(n) to O(log n) via recursively SVD‑based, parallel disentangling and that is adaptable to arbitrary hardware topologies; a two‑qubit gate optimization using Cartan’s KAK/modified cosine‑sine decomposition that shows any required fourth‑order unitary can be realized with two rather than three CNOTs, leading to an approximate one‑third reduction in two‑qubit gate count; and the identification and analysis of a broad class of bounded‑MPS‑rank states and functions, including rank‑2 cases that can be prepared exactly, which together delineate when their scheme is provably efficient.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-012, C-014, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-029, C-030, C-032]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper grounds its construction in canonical MPS and TTN/HTN tensor‑network structures and defines an explicit infidelity metric to evaluate state‑preparation accuracy. Numerical experiments focus on analytically specified bounded‑rank functions and benchmark probability distributions, supplemented by random complex amplitudes averaged over multiple samples for reliability, and use a hardware‑efficient network as an additional quantum baseline at matched depth. The authors note that truncation and reset schemes differ between MPS/TTN and HTN/HEN methods, which they acknowledge as a caveat, and they provide a concrete 3×4 grid‑chip example to illustrate how custom contraction schemes can be instantiated to match realistic topologies, though all evaluations are performed in simulation rather than on physical hardware.
    [codes: C-015, C-022, C-023, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-042, C-044, C-045, C-047]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Additional technical details include the emphasis that two‑qubit gates are the primary bottleneck on NISQ hardware, motivating the two‑CNOT decomposition, and the observation that general continuous functions can often be well approximated by leading terms in Fourier or Taylor expansions, suggesting that many practically relevant amplitude functions may yield low‑rank MPS representations. They also illustrate representative low‑rank states such as cosine and linear functions, GHZ, and W states, and explain that non‑interfering operations on non‑adjacent edges in the chip graph can be executed in parallel to reduce depth.
    [codes: C-006, C-018, C-025, C-031, C-033, C-034, C-041, C-043, C-046]

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets intrusion detection for bank smart vaults, where heterogeneous, high-dimensional security data from IoT sensors, biometrics, and access logs must be monitored in real time for anomalous activity. The authors argue that traditional, mainly machine-learning-based IDS struggle to capture intricate nonlinear intrusion patterns in such data and that there remains a need for IDS capable of efficiently processing heterogeneous smart-vault data streams in real time.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-015, C-029, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The proposed QAID system uses a hybrid classical–quantum architecture in which classical preprocessing and SVM infrastructure are combined with quantum feature encoding and quantum kernel methods, specifically a QSVM classifier. Classical feature vectors are encoded into quantum states via rotation-gate-based feature maps U(x), and the quantum kernel is defined as the squared absolute value of the inner product between encoded quantum states; this custom quantum kernel is then plugged into an SVM training procedure that solves a quadratic optimization problem. Implementation is carried out in Python using NumPy/SciPy/scikit-learn on the classical side and Qiskit and PennyLane for the quantum components, with real-time integration via an API to the bank’s smart vault network.
    [codes: C-002, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the main test set, the QAID QSVM achieved an accuracy of 96.5%, precision of 95.2%, recall of 97.0%, and a high F1-score (97.5%) and ROC-AUC (0.98), with a mean classification time of 0.015 seconds per sample, which the authors describe as near real time. Additional simulations on a synthetic dataset of 1000 samples with 50 features yielded similarly strong F1-score (97.5%) and ROC-AUC (0.98), and the system is reported to perform well under simulated adversarial attacks. The authors claim that QSVM-based QAID enhances anomaly detection, precision, operational resilience against adversarial attacks, and effectively encodes intricate nonlinear associations in the security data, and that hybrid implementations and circuit optimizations support near-real-time operational use.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-016, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-045]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The QAID system is reported to consistently outperform conventional IDS techniques, with the quantum-kernel SVM beating a classical SVM baseline by approximately 4–6 percentage points on accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The authors motivate this performance gap by arguing that classical machine-learning-based IDS lack the ability to capture intricate, nonlinear intrusion patterns in high-dimensional smart-vault data, whereas the quantum kernel better encodes such nonlinear associations.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-019, C-029, C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that quantum feature encoding and kernel computation are computationally expensive, even though hybrid implementations and circuit optimizations are used to achieve near-real-time detection. The PQC layer uses adaptive ansatz selection and circuit configurations to manage circuit depth, with an expectation-based cost function and gradient-style updates; the classical optimizer (e.g., Adam + COBYLA) iteratively updates circuit parameters based on quantum measurement outcomes under a depolarizing-plus-readout noise model. The framework incorporates explicit error mitigation and resource-aware scheduling to optimize circuit depth and quantum resource usage under NISQ constraints, aiming to avoid unnecessary circuit complexity.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames a financial product recommendation and investor clustering problem as a Max-Cut optimization task on an investor similarity graph, targeting portfolio management and insurance recommendation use cases. It argues that classical clustering and factor-model approaches struggle with scalability and capturing complex, nonlinear relationships in financial data, and that investor clustering via Max-Cut can help address scalability and regulatory constraints in portfolio management workflows. Within this framing, investor nodes and their relationships are encoded into a graph whose partitioning under Max-Cut is intended to support more robust recommender decisions for financial institutions.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-036]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors employ the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for Max-Cut on a weighted investor similarity graph, highlighting its use of superposition and entanglement to explore many candidate cuts in parallel and claiming potential computational advantages. This QAOA component is embedded in a broader hybrid pipeline that includes feature selection via an ensemble of classical scoring methods, construction of a similarity graph, spectral graph compression based on normalized Laplacian eigenvectors, quantum optimization on the compressed graph, inverse mapping of labels back to the original graph, and Nyström-based projection for new investors. The spectral compression method projects the adjacency matrix into a low-dimensional Laplacian eigenvector space (B = UᵀAU), supports approximate reconstruction (Â = UBUᵀ), and uses inverse label propagation (ŷᵢ = sign((UℓB)ᵢ) for binary partitions) so that QAOA can operate on a reduced-size graph that fits NISQ-era qubit and connectivity constraints.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-010, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-031, C-032, C-040]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that spectral compression exhibits a strong logarithmic relationship between compression ratio and Max-Cut approximation quality (R² = 0.98), with 50% compression (k = 15 for n = 30) yielding about 89.4% cut approximation accuracy with 1.57% standard deviation across random graphs. They identify an "optimal" operating point around a compression fraction k/n ≈ 1/3 (about 67% compression) where they argue quantum advantage would be most favorable given resource constraints. Large-scale tests on 1000 stochastic block model graphs show that the community-coarsening framework maintains community structure with a mean Adjusted Rand Index of about 0.72 (±0.004), and outlier graphs with poor alignment are explained by sparse connectivity in overlap regions. In a real-world insurance recommendation case with 100 investors and 4 products, the trained model produces exactly matching labels for all training investors and yields a plausible label for a new investor, with P@1, R@1, and NDCG@1 all equal to 1 under the single-recommendation setting.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-039, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Relative to classical brute-force Max-Cut, the paper notes empirically observed exponential time complexity in the classical exhaustive search baseline, using it as a reference point when motivating the use of QAOA-based graph cuts. Traditional classical techniques such as statistical clustering and factor models are described as facing scalability limits and failing to capture complex, fat-tailed relationships in investor data, which is used to justify exploring hybrid quantum-classical graph cut approaches. The spectral compression experiments also compare compressed-graph Max-Cut solutions against full-graph exact Max-Cut and full-graph Louvain clustering, reporting high approximation accuracy and structural agreement, though these comparisons are primarily about quality rather than demonstrated runtime speedups.
    [codes: C-006, C-011, C-012, C-022, C-027, C-028, C-034]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that current quantum hardware has limited qubit counts, coherence times, and connectivity, which necessitates graph compression and hybrid quantum–classical implementations rather than fully quantum workflows. They emphasize that efficient graph compression is crucial for any realistic deployment, implying that without strong compression the approach would not scale to practical financial graphs under existing hardware constraints. For the insurance recommendation case, they highlight a constraint that only one product can be recommended per investor (K = 1), which simplifies evaluation metrics but also limits the expressiveness of the recommender setting. They also recognize that stability and regulatory concerns in finance demand the ability to ensure that introducing new investors does not retroactively change previous recommendations, which shapes their methodological design. Overall, the paper positions its findings as simulator-based and subject to hardware maturity caveats before any real QPU deployment.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-016, C-038, C-039, C-043]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work proposed by the authors includes integrating quantum-specific compression techniques, such as entanglement-guided sparsification, to further reduce resource overhead and better exploit quantum structure. They also plan to deploy the full pipeline on actual quantum processing units to benchmark real-world performance against simulator-based results. Additionally, they suggest extending the framework to dynamic graph settings to support real-time portfolio rebalancing and other time-evolving financial applications.
    [codes: C-044, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s key contribution is a hybrid framework that combines QAOA-based Max-Cut with spectral graph compression and community coarsening to enable investor clustering and financial product recommendation under NISQ hardware constraints. Methodologically, it introduces a Laplacian-based compression scheme with theoretical justification from spectral clustering, an end-to-end training pipeline that integrates feature-selection ensembles, compression, quantum optimization and Nyström extension for incremental investors, and a multi-scale validation protocol including synthetic Erdős–Rényi and SBM graphs plus a real-world insurance case.   DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work specifies a detailed end-to-end training and deployment pipeline, including an ensemble-based feature ranking scheme with normalized score aggregation, explicit spectral compression and reconstruction formulas, and an algorithmic workflow from feature selection to model updating. The authors employ a multi-scale validation protocol that tests compression accuracy on synthetic graphs, performs large-scale consistency checks on 1000 SBM graphs, and then applies the method to a real-world insurance dataset with clearly stated evaluation metrics (P@1, R@1, NDCG@1) tailored to a single-recommendation scenario. === PAPER 6190538f1800 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper is framed as a conceptual review of the core engineering and physical challenges that must be solved to make quantum computation practical, covering decoherence, state preparation, error correction, and gate implementability as obstacles to realizing promised applications such as cryptography, optimization, and financial modelling.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-016, C-053]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors do not implement a specific quantum algorithm; instead they describe the general quantum computing model based on qubits, superposition, and entanglement, and discuss unitary gate transformations as the mathematical mechanism for algorithms such as Shor’s factoring, without presenting a concrete algorithmic or hardware method.
    [codes: C-004, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-023, C-032, C-035, C-055]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: As a conceptual review, the paper does not report empirical or quantitative results; its main conclusion is an argued assessment that key technical problems in quantum gate design, state preparation, and error correction remain unsolved, largely because quantum computation is essentially an analog process that is difficult to control precisely.
    [codes: C-053, C-054, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors contrast quantum and classical computing by noting that classical logic cannot efficiently simulate quantum phenomena, which motivated Feynman’s proposal, and that Shor’s algorithm threatens RSA whose security relies on the hardness of factoring for classical algorithms; they also argue that, unlike in classical digital systems, small errors in inherently linear quantum processes cannot be eliminated via simple redundancy or standard error-correction strategies.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-010, C-019, C-029]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper is centered on limitations: (1) Decoherence and environmental sensitivity make qubit states fragile, with superpositions collapsing under interaction or measurement and coherence becoming harder to maintain as the number of qubits increases or systems are miniaturized, and with initial entanglement with the environment already present before computation begins. (2) Error correction is fundamentally constrained: decoherence cannot be handled via classical-style redundancy, existing codes typically assume only single-qubit errors and focus on bit- and phase-flip errors, small analog errors cannot be removed in a linear quantum process, the no-cloning theorem prevents copying unknown states for diagnosis, and errors are nonlocal, with stuck faults and other perturbations not straightforwardly reversible. (3) Gate implementation is limited by finite precision and classical control inaccuracies that are likely to introduce phase errors into required unitary transformations. (4) State preparation and algorithm design face scalability and physical constraints, as realistic state transitions in large systems using only local transformations are deemed unrealistic, quantum statistical constraints complicate algorithm design, and NMR-type experimental models are argued not to validate quantum algorithms. (5) At a field level, the authors emphasize that nobody yet knows how to build a useful fault-tolerant quantum computer and that technical solutions to fundamental tasks of gate design, state preparation, and error correction are still lacking.
    [codes: C-005, C-013, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-033, C-034, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-053, C-054]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors highlight several future directions: ongoing research into quantum error-correction techniques to improve computational reliability; a general call to explore alternative approaches and unconventional ideas for building fault-tolerant quantum machines; and expectations that, over the next five to ten years or more, quantum computing could progressively impact domains such as AI/ML, financial modelling, cybersecurity, logistics, manufacturing, chemical and drug discovery, and battery and semiconductor design, while organizations and data center administrators should start monitoring these disruptive trends in anticipation of eventual adoption.
    [codes: C-006, C-040, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions itself as a review that synthesizes and emphasizes current challenges and limitations in quantum computation, arguing that despite attractive mathematical ideas like using unitary transformations for problems such as factorization, the field still lacks practical, fault-tolerant solutions for quantum gate design, state preparation, and error correction, partly due to the essentially analog nature of quantum computation.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-039, C-053, C-054, C-055]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: There is no experimental or algorithmic implementation in this paper, so issues of datasets, benchmarks, or reproducible protocols do not arise; instead, the discussion is conceptual and argumentative, drawing on known principles (e.g., no-cloning, decoherence) and prior work to motivate claims about engineering feasibility and the absence of fault-tolerant constructions.
    [codes: C-001, C-032, C-035, C-039, C-053, C-054]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper also provides general explanatory material on qubits, superposition, and entanglement, emphasizing that measurements collapse superpositions and that entangled qubits exhibit nonlocal correlations; it stresses that quantum speedup is not simple parallelism over basis states but arises from entanglement and probability amplitudes, and notes external recognition of quantum information science via a Nobel Prize as a marker of the field’s maturation.
    [codes: C-004, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-041]

=== PAPER 6278f0d22ba5 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames stock price and stock market movement prediction as a difficult task due to high volatility, complex non-linear relationships, and high-dimensional financial data, for which existing classical ML models often achieve only moderate accuracy and struggle as variables increase. It formulates the need for a faster, non-linear prediction model that can better handle uncertainty and complexity, motivating exploration of quantum-classical hybrid approaches for stock price movement prediction and aiming for increased accuracy and near-quadratic computational speedup. Quantum computing is presented as promising because of its probabilistic nature, ability to process complex data and explore solution spaces in parallel, potentially improving prediction efficiency and precision in finance.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-024, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: As a review, the paper discusses several quantum and hybrid methods rather than implementing a specific algorithm: quantum feature maps to encode classical financial data via angle or amplitude encoding, variational quantum circuits (VQCs) as trainable parameterized circuits optimized by classical algorithms, and hybrid quantum-classical architectures where classical preprocessing and post-processing surround a quantum core. It also covers quantum support vector machines and quantum neural networks conceptually, plus quantum annealing for feature selection, and proposes an original multi-layer modular hybrid architecture with an input layer aggregating financial data, a classical ML layer for dimensionality reduction, a quantum layer for modeling and simulation, and an output layer implementing human-in-the-loop feedback.
    [codes: C-005, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-045, C-056, C-057, C-058, C-059, C-060]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Being a review, the paper mainly reports results from cited studies: it notes that incorporating external factors into classical ML models can improve prediction accuracy, including a hybrid Prediction Rule Ensembles–DNN model that achieved about a 5% accuracy increase, a Random Forest with modified investment strategy reaching roughly 91.27% accuracy, and an LSTM with technical indicators achieving 93% accuracy on select Vietnamese stocks. For quantum-related methods, it cites work showing QSVM outperforming classical SVM on some datasets, quantum annealing–based feature selection for stock indicators showing promising results, and a hybrid QLSTM exhibiting about a 9% prediction accuracy improvement over classical LSTM in a simulated noiseless environment. The authors also mention that quantum data embedding might improve classical ML models, framing these as promising rather than definitive results of their own experimentation.
    [codes: C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-034, C-041, C-042, C-045]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The review repeatedly contrasts classical and quantum/hybrid methods. It states that traditional statistical and ML approaches often fail to capture the complex non-linear and high-dimensional dynamics of financial markets, and that classical stock prediction models typically yield only moderate accuracy, with performance deteriorating or problem complexity exploding as more variables are added. Against this baseline, the authors cite classical hybrid improvements (PRE–DNN, Random Forest, LSTM with technical indicators) and then reference studies where QSVM outperforms classical SVM on some datasets and where a hybrid QLSTM beats a classical LSTM by about 9% accuracy in noiseless simulation, though this quantum advantage disappears on real hardware. Overall, quantum and hybrid methods are presented as potentially more expressive or efficient, but empirical advantages remain conditional and context-dependent.
    [codes: C-007, C-009, C-010, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-034, C-041, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper highlights several limitations of current quantum approaches for stock prediction. Hardware-wise, present-day quantum computers are described as being in their infancy, with restricted qubit counts and high error rates, and noisy simulators often outperform real devices because they use simplified noise models. Algorithmically, robust and efficient quantum algorithms for financial applications are still under development, quantum neural and neural-inspired approaches "lack coherence" and require further study, and preparing financial data for quantum algorithms demands specialized techniques. The authors further note that understanding and interpreting the results of quantum-based models is difficult, and that in one cited case the accuracy gains of a hybrid QLSTM seen in noiseless simulation vanished when run on actual quantum hardware. They also implicitly acknowledge that current hybrid quantum-classical work is fragmented and that their proposed multi-layer architecture remains under development rather than experimentally validated.
    [codes: C-044, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors outline multiple future research directions: developing more efficient and robust quantum algorithms tailored to financial applications, improving the scalability and accuracy of quantum computers, and exploring new hybrid architectures that more effectively combine quantum and classical components. They also call for methods to interpret and explain quantum model outputs, further exploration of quantum-neural approaches that currently lack coherence, and emphasize that increasing numbers of hybrid architectures are anticipated as the field matures. Additionally, they point to quantum Monte Carlo simulation as a key technique for achieving the sought near-quadratic speedup and present their own multi-layer hybrid architecture as groundwork for upcoming studies in stock price movement analysis and decision-making using quantum technology.
    [codes: C-013, C-027, C-044, C-052, C-053, C-054, C-055, C-056, C-062]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions itself as a comprehensive review of quantum-classical hybrid approaches for stock price movement prediction, synthesizing concepts such as quantum feature maps, VQCs, QSVMs, QNNs, and quantum annealing in a finance context. Beyond summarizing the literature, the authors propose a novel multi-layer, modular hybrid quantum-classical computer model for stock prediction—with dedicated input, classical ML, quantum, and human-in-the-loop output layers—and claim that this architecture is expected to significantly increase prediction accuracy relative to traditional methods while laying groundwork for future quantum-finance studies.

=== PAPER 629ad7ff1054 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as modeling financial market dynamics and volatility risk in a way that captures empirically observed deviations from Gaussian random walks, such as excess kurtosis, turbulence, volatility clustering and price jumps. It links price formation to unbalanced market orders decomposed into a binary market polarization component and multiple binary trading-volume-related volatility components, arguing that probabilistic descriptions of such dynamics should incorporate quantum interference terms reflecting cognitively motivated quantum-like decision behavior.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-006, C-009, C-010, C-012]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors introduce Quantum Artificial Neural Networks (QuANNs), specifically recurrent QuANNs arranged as a Quantum Neural Automaton where each market component is modeled by a three‑neuron quantum network that evolves via unitary, conditionally applied single‑neuron gates (phase transforms and rotations) on qubit‑encoded neuron states. The overall market state is represented as a normalized superposition over neural firing patterns, with quantum interference affecting amplitude updates; probabilities are not fixed ex ante but are updated round‑by‑round via a nonlinear deterministic (and, with noisy gates, stochastic) map induced by the quantum dynamics, and noisy unitary gates are further modeled via stochastic Hamiltonians leading to stochastic rotation angles.
    [codes: C-002, C-007, C-008, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-030, C-031, C-041, C-040]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Simulations of the QuANN-based market model reportedly generate financial turbulence markers, including volatility bursts, clustering volatility and price jumps, along with excess kurtosis in returns distributions over a wide parameter range; the degree of leptokurtosis and turbulence is especially sensitive to the baseline volatility parameter v0 and to the number of volatility components, with higher v0 values tending to suppress excess kurtosis and turbulence. The authors show that expected returns emerge as probability‑weighted averages over eigenvalues of a returns operator, that ensemble averages of projections match projection weights, and that quantum interference in amplitude updates yields nonlinear deterministic probability dynamics; they also claim that introducing noisy quantum gates induces a stochastic nonlinear probability map while having limited impact on the transition between leptokurtic and platykurtic regimes. More broadly, they argue that the same quantum computational structure simultaneously generates nonlinear deterministic dynamics and nonlinear stochastic processes, providing a synthesized description of financial dynamics.
    [codes: C-003, C-009, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-038, C-039, C-041, C-043]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper contrasts its quantum market model with the classical Gaussian random walk framework, emphasizing that the empirically relevant excess kurtosis and volatility‑related turbulence constitute statistically significant deviations from Gaussian behavior that motivate the quantum approach. However, it does not report any explicit quantitative benchmarking or computational performance comparison against specific classical econometric or machine‑learning models, instead positioning the quantum model conceptually as an alternative that can reproduce non‑Gaussian features.
    [codes: C-004, C-009, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that even when the simulated returns distribution approximates a Gaussian, this normality is not robust: the Gaussian fit depends on the particular sample path and cannot be assumed as a dynamically fixed probability law holding indefinitely. They further indicate that the model’s parameter regimes can eliminate excess kurtosis and turbulence markers (e.g., at higher v0), implying sensitivity and potential instability in reproducing heavy‑tailed behavior, and they explicitly describe the lack of a stable Gaussian law as a caveat rather than a firm prediction.
    [codes: C-035, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future extensions, the paper proposes allowing the rotation angle in the unitary neuron gates to change stochastically, effectively using stochastic Hamiltonians to model external noise and thereby inducing noisy unitary gates and a stochastic nonlinear map in the probability dynamics, as a way to better capture random external influences on market behavior.
    [codes: C-040, C-041]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is framed as introducing QuANNs—specifically recurrent QuANNs organized as a Quantum Neural Automaton—for financial market dynamics and volatility risk modeling, thereby embedding quantum interference and quantum adaptive computation directly into the probabilistic description of returns. The authors also claim novelty in showing how this quantum AI structure can bridge deterministic nonlinear dynamics and stochastic nonlinear processes in finance, providing a unifying framework that connects quantum cognition–motivated nonlinear probability updates with financial risk modeling.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-007, C-008, C-013, C-023, C-042, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper develops a detailed quantum neural formalism: neuron firing states are encoded as qubits in two‑dimensional Hilbert spaces, network states are normalized superpositions, and evolution is governed by conditional unitary link operators with single‑neuron phase and rotation gates, from which explicit transition tables for amplitudes are derived. The probabilistic interpretation is given via projection norms as decision weights and ensemble averages, and the model specifies how returns are represented as eigenvalues of a returns operator and how probabilities are updated round‑by‑round rather than imposed ex ante; at the same time, the work is entirely simulation‑based with synthetic dynamics and does not describe empirical datasets or code release, so reproducibility relies on the analytic update rules rather than shared implementations.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-030, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper situates its approach within a broader cross‑disciplinary context, arguing that evidence from quantum cognition—where human decision behavior in certain tasks is computationally isomorphic to quantum adaptive computation—motivates incorporating quantum interference terms into probabilistic models of market behavior. It interprets squared amplitudes in the quantum neural state as non‑additive decision weights and contends that quantum AI can conceptually bridge major lines of research in finance involving nonlinear stochastic dynamics, decision theory, and risk modeling.
    [codes: C-005, C-020, C-029, C-042, C-044]

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses the problem of estimating the fill probability (execution likelihood) of RFQ responses in institutional algorithmic trading of European corporate bonds, treating accurate fill probability estimation as a core and competitively important component of market-making strategies. It formulates the study as finding quantum data transformations that reduce prediction error for fill-probability models over confined intraday trading periods, using market-state representations built from RFQ and surrounding market information.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-009, C-012, C-013]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach uses a Projected Quantum Feature Map (PQFM) as the quantum transformation, implemented via gate-based circuits on IBM Heron/ibm_torino hardware and noiseless simulators, to generate enriched feature vectors from market-state inputs. Quantum-generated features are produced offline as a decoupled component, measured to yield classical quantities that can be stored and reused, and are integrated into downstream classical statistical learning models for fill probability estimation.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-010, C-016, C-018, C-023, C-024]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Using real production-scale intraday RFQ data, the authors report a relative out-of-sample performance gain of up to 34% in trade backtesting scores for models that use quantum hardware–transformed features compared with those that do not. These uplifts are observed when models are trained on datasets where the inputs have been transformed by quantum algorithms executed on IBM Heron/ibm_torino devices, with the headline result being an overall performance gain of up to 34% across models.
    [codes: C-003, C-005, C-032]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The study compares models with and without access to quantum hardware–transformed data, showing that classical statistical learning models augmented with quantum features can achieve higher out-of-sample test scores than their purely classical counterparts, with reported uplifts of up to 34%. This comparison is structured around identical downstream model classes, differing only in whether they consume the original classical feature set or the quantum-transformed features.
    [codes: C-005, C-032]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors emphasize that they do not infer any generalizable theory or causal economic mechanism from the observed performance gains, stressing that the analysis is empirical and dataset-specific without generalization guarantees. They acknowledge that inherent noise in current quantum hardware appears to contribute to the observed uplift, but the exact role of this intrinsic noise in driving performance gains is not understood, especially given observed noise-induced drifts across repeated hardware runs. Consequently, the specific quantum feature map cannot be used to claim a theoretical explanation of the effects, and attempts to reproduce the hardware benefits with artificially induced noise in simulations fail, underscoring that the results remain heuristic and not theoretically grounded.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-038]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper notes that clarifying the exact role of intrinsic quantum hardware noise in producing the observed performance gains requires further investigation, indicating that future work should focus on disentangling noise effects and developing a theoretical understanding of why certain noisy hardware executions appear empirically beneficial.
    [codes: C-033, C-034, C-035, C-039]

The system architecture deliberately decouples quantum feature generation (run offline as PQFM transformations on hardware or simulator) from the online real-time response system, with all quantum outputs reduced to classical feature vectors for storage and downstream use, reflecting a practically motivated hybrid design grounded in real trading data.

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum machine learning as a way to search for potential quantum advantage in realistic classification tasks from finance and vision, focusing on high-dimensional, often imbalanced industrial/financial data such as credit-scoring and MNIST images.   DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The core method is a hybrid quantum–classical network that 'squeezes' a variational quantum circuit between a classical front-end and back-end, allowing the classical network to reduce feature dimensionality before quantum encoding so that the number of qubits can be chosen independently of the number of input features and output classes. The authors deliberately adopt a straightforward design for the encoding/variational circuit and distinguish between two training/architecture variants (with vs. without data re-uploading) while using TensorFlow Quantum as the software stack to enable seamless joint training of classical and quantum components. Classical preprocessing networks map high-dimensional data (e.g., many finance features or 784 MNIST pixels) to a smaller set of parameters suitable for angle encoding on a limited number of qubits, and a classical output layer performs final classification.
    [codes: C-036, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-013, C-016, C-017, C-030, C-031, C-019]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across finance and MNIST experiments, the authors report that the hybrid network achieves an advantage over a purely classical neural network when considering several performance measures, including accuracy and AUC. On the balanced credit-scoring sample, the hybrid approach shows better performance than the classical benchmark, and data re-uploading is reported to be superior to repeating only the variational part of the circuit. On the unbalanced finance sample, differences between quantum variants that are not visible in accuracy emerge in AUC. For MNIST, the QNet is said to learn substantially faster than the classical NNet, and its confusion matrix indicates that it can separate all ten handwritten digits, though the classical model displays less overfitting. The authors also note a practical result that, using TensorFlow Quantum, relatively large circuits (e.g., 10 qubits with 10 layers) can still be simulated on a notebook.
    [codes: C-003, C-024, C-025, C-028, C-032, C-033, C-035, C-018]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The study explicitly benchmarks the hybrid QNet against a fully classical neural network constructed with a comparable number of trainable parameters, using both accuracy and AUC as evaluation metrics. On the balanced finance sample, the hybrid model outperforms this classical baseline, and in the unbalanced sample, the authors stress that while accuracy alone appears similar, AUC reveals differences between approaches. On MNIST, the hybrid network is reported to converge faster in training and to reach high training accuracy, but the classical network exhibits less overfitting when comparing train and test performance, suggesting that any hybrid advantage is nuanced and metric-dependent.
    [codes: C-015, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-028, C-032, C-035, C-027]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations. Conceptually, they stress that overfitting remains a concern in quantum machine learning just as in classical settings, and they observe overfitting empirically both on the finance data (when applying trained networks to unseen cases) and on MNIST through a train–test accuracy gap, with the classical benchmark showing less overfitting. They also highlight metric-related limitations: accuracy can be misleading for unbalanced datasets, since a naive classifier assigning all observations to the majority class can already reach high accuracy, making AUC necessary to meaningfully differentiate models. From a scalability perspective, they state that a brute-force QML treatment of MNIST with all 784 pixel features is hardly possible, necessitating dimensionality reduction. Finally, all experiments are performed on simulators in the NISQ era, implying that device noise and hardware constraints are not yet addressed in the reported results.

The authors specifically identify regularization as an open problem, stating that methods to regularize quantum networks to avoid overfitting must be studied. They also emphasize that future work should investigate the impact of realistic error rates on physical quantum devices, since all current experiments are simulator-based.

They stress the architectural feature that the classical front-end trainably reduces feature dimensionality so that the number of qubits is decoupled from the number of input features and classes, and they systematically compare two quantum variants (with and without data re-uploading) against a parameter-matched classical baseline to explore potential performance advantages of such hybrid designs.
    [codes: C-002, C-036, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-013, C-001]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is grounded in the NISQ context and uses TensorFlow Quantum after comparing alternative frameworks, with the explicit rationale that it provides seamless joint training of classical and quantum components and efficient simulation even for circuits with around 10 qubits and 10 layers. The authors design a classical encoding front-end that trainably scales down high-dimensional, potentially imbalanced industrial/finance data to match limited qubit resources, and they explicitly construct classical benchmarks with matched parameter counts for fair comparison. They discuss evaluation choices in detail, arguing that accuracy is misleading for unbalanced datasets and therefore augmenting it with AUC, and they carefully construct both balanced and unbalanced finance samples to study metric behavior under class imbalance. [CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as managing commercial bank liquidity under deposit outflows into a central bank digital currency, where CBDC-induced shifts threaten banks’ liquidity positions and regulatory ratios. This challenge is cast as a sequential decision-making problem in a multi-bank network, with each bank’s state including liquidity metrics (e.g., LCR, NSFR), CBDC flows, interbank exposures, and stress indicators, so that an agent can learn funding actions that minimise funding costs and avoid regulatory breaches.

  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a hybrid Quantum-Enhanced Soft Actor-Critic (QSAC) framework in which the critic network incorporates a 4‑qubit, 6‑layer hardware-efficient variational quantum circuit (VQC) motivated by the exponential scaling of the Hilbert space with qubit number. Trainability issues are tackled via identity block initialization, layer‑wise training, and use of local cost functions to mitigate barren plateaus; the quantum critic is embedded in a classical SAC backbone chosen for its stability and sample efficiency in continuous control, with classical preprocessing and readout layers surrounding the VQC. A multi‑bank simulation environment models five heterogeneous banks with interbank lending and contagion, and quantum noise is represented using an IBM Nairobi–calibrated NISQ noise model with Zero Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) as the primary error mitigation strategy.
    [codes: C-002, C-014, C-015, C-003, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-023, C-007, C-021, C-026, C-027]

In the multi‑bank CBDC stress simulation, QSAC reduces average funding costs by about 8.1% versus classical DRL baselines and achieves zero Liquidity Coverage Ratio breaches in out‑of‑sample tests, with statistically significant improvements over classical SAC and stochastic MPC, and modest performance gains from increasing VQC depth. Ablation studies suggest that the VQC layer contributes a genuine, though modest, performance enhancement over parameter‑matched classical networks, scenario‑specific gains persist across different stress scenarios, key features such as LCR and CBDC flow are most influential according to gradient-based attribution, and projected cost reductions scale with bank size to yield multi‑billion‑euro annual savings under the authors’ assumptions. Against stronger Model Predictive Control baselines, the advantage narrows to about 3.2%, though statistical tests still show QSAC performing significantly better than both classical SAC and SMPC on the simulated task. === PAPER 66f18ee7b813 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles the independent component analysis (ICA) blind source separation problem, aiming to recover latent sources and mixing coefficients from observed mixtures, and formulates this as efficient computation of an ICA contrast function on a quantum computer under an oracle/sample-access model. The authors particularly emphasize applications to separating transcriptomic signals and denoising financial time series for forecasting.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-013]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a gate-based quantum algorithm that adapts Kernel ICA (KICA): given oracle access to samples, they perform quantum preprocessing (mean and covariance estimation and whitening), block-encode centered Gram matrices, use phase estimation and amplitude estimation to obtain eigenvalues and overlaps, and then reconstruct a modified contrast matrix whose entries are absolute values to accommodate measurement constraints. This quantum-estimated contrast is then fed into a classical optimization loop on the Stiefel manifold using the Cayley transform to enforce orthogonality, yielding a hybrid quantum–classical ICA procedure.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper claims that its contrast-function estimation subroutine achieves an exponential reduction in complexity dependence on data scale N compared to classical ICA, with formal theorems bounding the relative error of the quantum-estimated contrast and showing improved guarantees in a near-independent regime. Whitening is shown to reduce ICA difficulty by reducing degrees of freedom, and the authors analytically argue that the adapted contrast landscape declines linearly toward the optimum, making optimization easier near independence. Numerical experiments on synthetic mixtures indicate the contrast minima remain reachable under measurement error, success rates depend mainly on mixing extent, state norms and query counts scale favorably with N and error parameters, and Amari error decreases as sample size grows. On real data, they report a clear correlation between transcriptomic components obtained by their method and those from stabilized ICA, and for Nikkei 225 forecasting they find that ICA preprocessing improves accuracy and that the QICA-SVR configuration they report achieves the best consistency in their setting.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-010, C-014, C-015, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors position their method against classical ICA by noting that any classical ICA algorithm must scale at least linearly in the sample size Ω(N), whereas their quantum contrast computation has polylogarithmic dependence on N under the stated assumptions. They also compare qualitatively to a stabilized-ICA implementation on transcriptomic data, reporting a clear correlation between independent components, and in financial forecasting they benchmark QICA-SVR against classical ICA-SVR and plain SVR, finding similar or slightly better consistency and noise reduction benefits. In the discussion they further argue that current quantum-inspired matrix eigendecomposition approaches have complexity O(1/ε⁶), which they claim falls short of the performance of their quantum approach.
    [codes: C-005, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-040]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly state that the quantum speedup they achieve is confined to the contrast-function computation subroutine and does not accelerate the classical optimization loop over the contrast landscape. In their technical analysis they also ignore a term in the preprocessing error that they argue contributes nothing to the Gram matrices, which constitutes a simplifying assumption about error propagation.
    [codes: C-018, C-036]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper highlights several future directions: exploring quantum acceleration for the optimization process itself to handle larger numbers of independent components; investigating alternative input models that might similarly reduce sampling complexity for contrast computation; and extending the proposed approach from linear to nonlinear ICA models.
    [codes: C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main claimed contribution is a gate-based quantum algorithm that efficiently computes a modified KICA contrast function using quantum linear-algebra primitives, yielding an ICA method that, under a quantum sample-access model, achieves exponentially reduced dependence on data scale compared to classical ICA. They also emphasize the design of an adapted contrast function built from absolute values to make it amenable to quantum measurement, together with a hybrid scheme that combines this quantum contrast estimation with Stiefel-manifold optimization, and demonstrate its applicability to both transcriptomic source separation and financial time series forecasting.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-040]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper bases its quantum design closely on the established Kernel ICA framework, including whitening preprocessing and determinant-based contrast, and carefully adapts it by modifying the contrast to use absolute-valued Gram-matrix entries to suit quantum measurements. The technical analysis explicitly tracks approximation and preprocessing errors in theorems and notes which error terms are neglected because they do not affect Gram matrices. Numerical tests on synthetic mixtures use Amari error and scaling studies (e.g., state norms, relative errors, query complexity) to support the theoretical guarantees, while real-data experiments include a transcriptomic dataset compared against stabilized ICA and a Nikkei 225 forecasting task where they quantify improvements via normalized mean squared error and consistency. However, all experiments are carried out via classical simulation of the quantum procedures, and code availability is not indicated in the coded excerpts.
    [codes: C-007, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors note empirically that the success rate of their procedure in simulations depends mainly on the extent of mixing, and they report that contrast function minimization remains effective under injected measurement errors, with query complexity observed to be significantly better than their conservative theoretical bounds.
    [codes: C-027, C-028, C-031]

=== PAPER 674c681a57d0 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The report frames the problem as the heavy computational burden of pricing financial derivatives and computing risk measures such as Value at Risk (VaR), which commonly rely on Monte Carlo simulation and PDE solvers, and surveys quantum computing techniques that might accelerate these tasks, with a particular focus on developments since a prior NEASQC deliverable. It also notes a separate line of work that seeks to build quantum-inspired models of financial markets rather than just speeding up classical methods.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors review several gate-based quantum approaches: (i) quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC), which uses an oracle U to load the path probability distribution and a unitary V to encode the payoff, together with amplitude estimation schemes; (ii) quantum algorithms for PDE-based pricing that map option pricing PDEs to imaginary-time evolution under a Hermitian Hamiltonian and then simulate this evolution variationally on NISQ hardware; and (iii) other approaches such as quantum finance modelling based on a Merton–Schrödinger equation, quantum deep hedging via quantum reinforcement learning layers, and martingale pricing via quantum linear programming and density-operator-based “quantum assets.” All of these are discussed under an explicit NISQ-computing focus because of limits in qubit counts, circuit depth, and noise.
    [codes: C-005, C-010, C-011, C-030, C-031, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the algorithmic side, the report emphasizes that quantum amplitude estimation (AE) can in principle reduce the number of oracle calls compared to standard Monte Carlo, while parallel AE variants typically offer better depth control for NISQ devices. However, empirical and theoretical analyses cited in the report show that even low-strength noise can prevent achieving the quadratic speedup, with error saturating beyond a certain number of Grover applications, and that linear AE schedules tend to perform best under realistic noise. The report also highlights that approximate state loading may yield lower overall error than exact loading on noisy hardware, that engineered likelihood functions combined with Bayesian inference improve performance over conventional likelihoods, and that a variational PDE solver for option pricing can be implemented with poly(d·log(1/ε)) few-qubit gates on small quantum computers.
    [codes: C-003, C-008, C-017, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-028, C-034, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The report repeatedly benchmarks quantum proposals against classical Monte Carlo and PDE methods: Monte Carlo is described as the de facto industry standard because it is easy to implement, general, and scales well with dimension, while PDE solvers can converge faster in low-dimensional cases. Quantum amplitude estimation is presented as promising a quadratic reduction in required samples/oracle calls versus classical Monte Carlo in ideal conditions, and some PDE-based quantum solvers are said to potentially offer exponential speedups in very specific cases, though the authors stress that most of the observed performance improvements in recent work are only up to constant factors rather than changes in asymptotic scaling. They also caution that when realistic noise and error correction are taken into account, the effective speedup over classical methods may disappear for all practical instance sizes.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-007, C-008, C-019, C-041, C-043]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors enumerate multiple limitations. Hardware-wise, current NISQ devices suffer from limited qubit counts, restricted circuit depths, and significant noise, which motivates focusing on shallow, NISQ-compatible algorithms and leads to observations such as noise being the main limiting factor in AE experiments and the saturation of error improvements beyond a small number of Grover iterations. Methodologically, unitary-synthesis-based initialization is only applicable when the payoff evolution can be represented as a unitary, and initialization procedures must preserve relative phases—something that variational methods risk violating by introducing arbitrary phases. Both parallel and sequential MLAE approaches exhibit fundamental issues: depth limits on NISQ hardware stop error reduction beyond a certain point; critical points can make MLAE estimators biased and prevent further error reduction even without noise. For PDE-based quantum pricing, extracting a single amplitude in high-dimensional grids becomes a readout bottleneck that can eliminate any theoretical quantum advantage. Quantum deep hedging is constrained by the need for at least one qubit per time step and additional challenges when modelling rough paths. Finally, in a longer-term, fault-tolerant regime, the authors argue that the overhead of error correction may render quadratic speedups ineffective by pushing the problem sizes at which any speedup appears into an impractically large regime.
    [codes: C-005, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-032, C-037, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Looking ahead, the report suggests that near-term practical benefits from quantum computing in pricing and VaR may come less from speedups and more from reductions in energy consumption, implying an agenda of studying energy–accuracy trade-offs for quantum versus classical methods. The authors also implicitly point to further research on NISQ-friendly techniques such as approximate state loading, improved amplitude estimation under noise, and more efficient variational PDE solvers, though they do not lay out a detailed roadmap.
    [codes: C-017, C-021, C-033, C-034, C-044]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The document positions itself as an updated state-of-the-art review of quantum techniques for derivatives pricing and VaR computation, specifically covering work published since an earlier NEASQC report D5.3, rather than as a paper introducing a single new algorithm. In its conclusions, it claims that there have been no major breakthroughs in the area over this period and that most recent contributions merely refine existing methods with constant-factor performance improvements, while also synthesizing a critical perspective on how noise and error-correction overhead threaten the practical realization of advertised speedups.
    [codes: C-006, C-011, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the review organizes QAMC work into three application blocks and dissects common subroutines such as initialization and amplitude estimation, giving particular attention to how different AE variants (parallel, sequential, generalized Grover, QSP-based) trade off depth, bias, and robustness to noise. It notes that approximate state loading can outperform exact loading on noisy devices, and that engineered likelihood functions combined with Bayesian inference offer better statistical behaviour than conventional likelihoods, indicating attention to estimator properties. The focus on NISQ constraints—circuit depth control, phase preservation in variational loading, and small-qubit variational PDE solvers—also reflects a concern for realistic implementability, although the report itself does not present new experimental datasets or reproducibility artefacts but rather synthesizes existing studies.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-017, C-019, C-021, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-034]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The review also observes an increasing interest in applying QAMC to path-dependent options and discusses a strategy based on computing an expectation at a suitably chosen future time to mitigate high-dimensional readout complexity in PDE-based pricing models. Additionally, it introduces a Random Quantum Amplitude Estimation (RandomQAE) method that estimates the signed square root of the amplitude to address critical-point-induced bias, and it briefly surveys conceptual quantum finance frameworks, including quantum assets defined via density operators, beyond purely algorithmic accelerations.
    [codes: C-012, C-027, C-033, C-039]

=== PAPER 67ed9d74dd96 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets data classification problems where quantum machine learning might accelerate data processing by leveraging quantum interference, with a specific focus on making amplitude-based data loading practical despite the exponential gate cost of exact loading and the prior restriction to real-valued vectors. It formulates the task as preparing a parametrized quantum state that approximates a given complex-valued target state for use in a compact-kernel classifier, including an application to credit card fraud detection framed as distinguishing normal from fraudulent transactions. The authors explicitly note that earlier approximate amplitude encoding methods cannot handle complex-valued data, narrowing their applicability to such classification settings.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-009, C-007, C-034]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose an approximate complex amplitude encoding (ACAE) scheme that extends prior approximate amplitude encoding to complex-valued vectors by optimizing a parametrized, hardware-efficient ansatz to prepare a model state that matches the target data state up to a global phase. They replace the earlier maximum mean discrepancy cost with a fidelity-based objective that is sensitive to complex amplitudes and estimate this fidelity and its gradients using classical shadows, while computing gradients via the parameter-shift rule. The method is integrated into a compact amplitude encoding framework and used to implement the compact Hadamard classifier with constant-depth ACAE-based preparation of the training state, and a restricted Ry/CNOT encoder for real-valued test data.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-006, C-009, C-010, C-012, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-023, C-024]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: For the Iris experiments, the ACAE training-data encoder reaches a fidelity of 0.994 and the test-data encoders achieve fidelities above 0.999, leading to perfect classification on the easier setosa–versicolor task and some errors on the more challenging versicolor–virginica pair. The authors report that misclassifications in the harder Iris task disappear when exact data (i.e., without approximate encoding) are used, indicating that encoding accuracy affects classification, and they also observe that reducing fidelity from ~0.99 to ~0.7 still keeps accuracy above 80%. In the credit card fraud detection experiments, using four features and small training subsets, all 8 selected test transactions are correctly classified and, in an additional simulation on 48 randomly chosen instances, 42 are correctly classified.
    [codes: C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-033, C-041, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper does not present explicit quantitative comparisons with classical classifiers; instead, it notes qualitatively that classical data loading into quantum states would require exponentially many gates and that the CHC can be implemented in a more compact quantum circuit than other quantum classifiers. The effect of encoding errors is indirectly compared against an 'exact data' (non-approximate encoding) quantum baseline in the Iris experiments, where misclassifications are resolved when exact data are used.
    [codes: C-002, C-021, C-022, C-033]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that prior approximate amplitude encoding could not handle complex-valued data and that MMD-based costs are unsuitable for general complex amplitudes because probabilities depend only on squared magnitudes, motivating their change of objective. They highlight that straightforward fidelity estimation via tomography is exponentially costly in observables, and that classical shadow methods require sampling from n-qubit Clifford unitaries with O(n^2 / log n) entangling gates, which may be challenging to implement in practice. The training procedure entails an O(2^n) classical summation in the fidelity calculation, so runtime scales exponentially with qubit count, and they observe from simulations that the depth of the variational circuit needed to reach high fidelities grows superlinearly with the number of qubits, raising scalability concerns. The authors further note that reaching high fidelity for large systems may suffer from barren plateaus because gradients of global fidelity-based costs can decay exponentially with system size, that 23 qubits would be needed to cover all data in the full fraud dataset, and that the random Clifford measurement required for classical shadows is itself a practical obstacle.
    [codes: C-003, C-011, C-013, C-015, C-018, C-022, C-040, C-042, C-043, C-045]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: To mitigate training issues such as barren plateaus, the authors point to localized fidelity measurement schemes as a promising direction. They also suggest that improved constructions of Clifford circuits with depth upper bounded by roughly 2n plus logarithmic terms could make the classical-shadow-based fidelity estimation more practical on quantum hardware.
    [codes: C-044, C-046]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main claimed contribution is an extension of approximate amplitude encoding to handle complex-valued data via a fidelity-based cost, enabling approximate loading of complex data into shallow circuits, supported by classical-shadow-based fidelity and gradient estimation. Building on this, the paper claims an implementation of the compact Hadamard classifier that avoids the prior critical assumption of exact, exponentially costly state preparation by using ACAE to generate the required quantum state with constant-depth circuits, and demonstrates this approach on both a standard Iris dataset and a credit card fraud detection task.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-012, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-023]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the authors use a hardware-efficient ansatz and parameter-shift rule for training, with explicit circuit-width reporting (five qubits for the Iris and small fraud instances) and clear specification of training/test splits and tiny training sets (e.g., four samples per class for both Iris and fraud). The Iris experiments involve carefully defined splits and report both fidelities and classification outcomes, including an analysis of misclassifications and their relation to feature overlap and encoding accuracy. For fraud detection, they restrict attention to four PCA-based features (V1–V4), use highly subsampled training data, and then perform both targeted tests and an additional random-instance evaluation; they also carry out a scalability simulation varying qubit counts and depth requirements. All results are obtained on simulators, and no real quantum hardware or noise models are discussed in these codes.
    [codes: C-016, C-017, C-019, C-021, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all verified codes fit within the primary reporting dimensions.
    [codes: —]
