=== PAPER 7f91dcfbca63 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames anomaly detection as selecting data points that deviate significantly from normal behaviour in datasets, a task relevant to domains such as finance, where it is applied to credit card fraud detection with highly imbalanced classes. This problem is cast as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model in which a fixed number k of outliers must be selected, enabling solution by QUBO-oriented solvers and, in principle, quantum annealers.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-010, C-017, C-028]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is "quantum-inspired" anomaly detection formulated as a QUBO, rather than run on a quantum processor: each data point corresponds to a binary variable, and the objective combines linear distances to a centroid with quadratic pairwise distances between selected points, weighted by a parameter α. The method uses a Mahalanobis distance metric, enforces an exact number of outliers via a quadratic penalty term with weight A > max(Q), and sparsifies the model by limiting quadratic terms to the k-furthest neighbours; benchmark instances are solved with the classical qbsolv QUBO solver, though the formulation is positioned as suitable for simulated quantum annealing or any QUBO-capable solver.
    [codes: C-001, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Using ROC AUC as the evaluation metric, the author reports that the proposed quantum-inspired QUBO anomaly detection algorithm shows improved accuracy compared with classical methods on both random Gaussian data and real-world datasets, including MNIST and a credit card fraud dataset. The paper also finds that limiting quadratic interactions to the k-furthest neighbours improves accuracy and may aid in embedding the model on hardware with constrained connectivity, though the current penalty formulation blocks near-term QPU use.
    [codes: C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The QUBO-based anomaly detector is explicitly benchmarked against five classical anomaly detection algorithms on synthetic Gaussian data, MNIST digit subsets, and a highly imbalanced credit card fraud dataset, with performance compared using ROC AUC. The author claims that the quantum-inspired method achieves improved accuracy over these classical baselines on both random and real-world datasets.
    [codes: C-002, C-010, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges that current NISQ hardware, with number-limited noisy qubits, impacts the practicality of gate-based quantum anomaly detection algorithms. For the proposed QUBO formulation, the outlier selection penalty term induces all-to-all quadratic interactions, making the current model not solvable on near-term, connectivity-limited QPUs, despite sparsification of other quadratic terms. The author therefore explicitly notes that, in its present form, the approach is effectively restricted to classical or simulated quantum solvers rather than real quantum hardware.
    [codes: C-009, C-031, C-033]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: To enable execution on connectivity-limited quantum processors, the author suggests that an alternative method for constraining the number of selected outliers is needed, replacing the current penalty formulation that creates all-to-all couplings. Future work is thus directed at redesigning the selection mechanism so that the QUBO can be embedded on near-term QPUs.
    [codes: C-031, C-032]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution claimed is a new quantum-inspired anomaly detection algorithm formulated as a QUBO that conceptually combines ideas from statistical and density-based anomaly detection methods, with a tunable trade-off between linear and quadratic distance terms and an explicit control over the number of outliers. The author further emphasizes that, compared with standard classical anomaly detectors, this formulation achieves improved accuracy on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks.
    [codes: C-001, C-010, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-029]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper situates the QUBO formulation relative to standard classical anomaly detection paradigms—statistical, density-based, and machine-learning-based—describing their underlying assumptions. Experiments are run on three benchmark types (random Gaussian data with varying standard deviations, MNIST digit subset configurations where a minority class is treated as outliers, and a public credit card fraud dataset with 0.172% fraud rate), and all instances are solved with the qbsolv QUBO solver and evaluated via ROC AUC. The algorithm includes a dataset-specific training phase to learn the α weighting parameter, uses Mahalanobis distance, and adopts a sparsification strategy limiting quadratic terms to the k-furthest neighbours, which the author notes benefits both accuracy and potential hardware embedding.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The introduction briefly motivates the work by noting that quantum machine learning combines quantum computing with machine learning, and that quantum computers may offer parallel computation and potential exponential speedups for certain problems, with quantum technologies claimed to have the potential to revolutionize various domains including areas where anomaly detection is used such as finance, healthcare, and cybersecurity. The author also underscores that, despite current hardware constraints, the proposed quantum-inspired anomaly detection algorithm can be applied at scale using simulated quantum annealing, simulated annealing, or any other QUBO solver, without being tied to quantum hardware.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-006, C-008, C-033, C-034]

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets SME credit scoring as a key computational finance problem, motivated by the lack of rating agency coverage for small firms and the need to improve default detection while managing type I and type II errors (rejecting healthy vs. insolvent firms). Input features are encoded into qubits via Rx angle embedding, and the hybrid model integrates three approaches—hybrid NNs, variational circuits, and data re-uploading—with the expectation that variational circuit (VC) and data re-uploading classifier (DRC) elements complement each other.
    [codes: C-012, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The best-performing configuration is a hybrid model combining two quantum classifiers with a classical neural network on Singapore SME data, achieving an ROC/AUC of 0.75 under matched training conditions. Compared to a classical neural counterpart trained for the same number of epochs, the hybrid model reaches slightly higher AUC while requiring about 10× fewer epochs than are needed for the classical model to attain comparable performance. However, performance peaks around 12 qubits and degrades when increasing qubits beyond this or adding more data re-uploading blocks, and simulator timing shows data embedding doubling with each qubit while overall execution scales quadratically in qubits and linearly in blocks.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-017, C-030, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-050]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The hybrid quantum model is compared primarily to a classical neural network trained on the same SME dataset, using identical training/validation/test splits and the same number of epochs for a fair comparison; under these constraints, the hybrid model slightly outperforms the classical NN (AUC 0.75 vs. 0.73). When the classical NN is allowed to train longer (up to 3,500–5,000 epochs), it can reach an AUC of 0.75, matching the hybrid model’s performance, and the authors note that the best overall classical model for this dataset remains XGBoost, which they deliberately exclude from direct comparison because their focus is on neural models.

Second, the feature set is capped at 21 due to hardware limitations, potentially restricting model expressiveness. Third, scaling the quantum model reveals that accuracy degrades beyond 12 qubits and when adding more data re-uploading blocks; the authors suggest this might relate to barren plateaus or to the dataset lacking trigonometric structure, but these explanations are speculative and left for future work. Fourth, the quantum training process is computationally heavy: 350 epochs over the training set require about 629,300 circuit executions, and the authors caution that total runtime on cloud-accessed quantum hardware may be impractical without specialized runtime environments. They also note that further hyperparameter tuning of both hybrid and classical models, as well as exploring how quantum noise on real hardware might obviate the need for classical dropout, are promising avenues, and they tie anticipated growth in quantum hardware (to thousands of qubits) to the possibility of achieving more tangible advantages.

=== PAPER 8154d6cc12dd (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames stock index price prediction as a financial forecasting problem where more accurate predictions enable better buy/hold/sell decisions for investors and fund managers. It specifically investigates using Quantum GANs to model complex patterns and correlations in historical stock index data (e.g., NIFTY) in order to generate realistic synthetic data that support next‑day index forecasts. The authors position this as a business-relevant use case in financial services where improved forecasts could help optimize strategies, mitigate risk, and improve returns.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-008, C-020, C-038, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study applies Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks (QGANs), including a hybrid model with a quantum generator and classical discriminator and a Fully Quantum GAN (FQGAN) where both generator and discriminator are quantum circuits. The discriminator in the QGAN framework uses supervised learning, often via a quantum deep neural network, and the training loop relies on adversarial competition between generator and discriminator while emphasizing the need to balance their capacities. Data are encoded into quantum states via numerical vectorization (amplitude embedding), and the authors introduce an "Invertible FQGAN" strategy that uses overlapping past–future prediction windows and a classical optimization objective to recover a normalization factor for predictions. Experiments are run on the AWS Braket SV1 simulator with specified learning rates, epochs, and, for the classical GAN baseline, detailed hyperparameters and technical-indicator feature engineering.
    [codes: C-002, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-033]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that QGANs can generate synthetic stock-price data closely resembling actual market behavior and claim enhanced prediction accuracy in this setting. For the hybrid quantum GAN, they report a training RMSE of 49.88 and a higher test RMSE of 84.27, noting significant variability introduced by the quantum component. The Fully Quantum GAN trained for 5 epochs on SV1 achieves a training RMSE of 571.36 and a test RMSE of 251.89, which they describe as showing "considerable promise" and "competitive performance" despite short training. They further observe that model performance depends on window size, with the hybrid model degrading as window size grows, while the FQGAN improves up to a window size of 5 before worsening at size 10; lower learning rates are said to improve test accuracy. Across the paper and its conclusion, the authors repeatedly assert that quantum models, particularly the Invertible FQGAN, improve stability, effectiveness, and prediction accuracy and exhibit superior performance when handling complex, high-dimensional financial data and smaller datasets.
    [codes: C-003, C-005, C-020, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-032, C-040, C-045, C-046, C-048]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper compares quantum-enhanced models against classical LSTM and GAN baselines, with a classical GAN using technical indicators (e.g., moving averages, exponential moving average, momentum) as a primary benchmark. The authors state that their quantum-enhanced models outperform classical LSTM and GANs in convergence speed and prediction accuracy and that integrating quantum computing yields a clear advantage over traditional methods, particularly for accurate forecasts from smaller datasets. At the architectural level, they argue that QGANs overcome saddle-point problems in classical GAN training and can operate effectively with limited data, thereby offering better robustness and data efficiency than classical approaches.
    [codes: C-005, C-009, C-021, C-022, C-036, C-037, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations. First, their experiments rely entirely on the AWS Braket SV1 simulator; they report long queue times and that each epoch takes about two hours, so even the minimum of 5 epochs leads to more than 10 hours of simulation per model, which constrained the number and depth of experiments. Because of these simulator constraints and the unavailability of real hardware devices, they explicitly state that no tests on actual quantum hardware were performed. Methodologically, they note a normalization-factor limitation in their quantum setup, which they address via the Invertible FQGAN trick using overlapping windows and classical optimization but still identify as an issue needing a workaround. From a resource perspective, they state that the depth of their quantum circuit scales exponentially due to the use of amplitude embedding, highlighting a scalability bottleneck.
    [codes: C-017, C-030, C-031, C-033, C-050]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the paper suggests reducing circuit depth by adopting more efficient data embedding schemes to address the exponential scaling induced by amplitude embedding. In its conclusion, the authors also gesture more broadly toward the continued integration of advancing quantum technologies into financial modeling, suggesting that such progress could transform the industry and implicitly calling for further research on quantum methods for finance.
    [codes: C-034, C-049]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim novelty primarily through the application of QGANs—and specifically a Fully Quantum GAN with both generator and discriminator realized as quantum circuits—to stock index prediction. They present the Invertible FQGAN as a key innovation that addresses normalization issues in quantum systems by jointly predicting overlapping past and future values and estimating a normalization factor via classical optimization, which they argue improves model stability and accuracy. They further highlight their design choice of using quantum generator and discriminator as pivotal in improving model effectiveness and delivering superior outcomes on complex, high-dimensional financial data, and they position QGANs more broadly as overcoming saddle-point issues and learning effectively from limited data, thereby outperforming traditional methods on smaller datasets.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-024, C-026, C-036, C-037, C-040, C-045, C-046, C-048]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper describes a GAN/QGAN training loop with generator and discriminator roles and adversarial learning dynamics, emphasizing that maintaining balance between the discriminator’s ability to detect fakes and the generator’s realism is crucial for stable training. Data are preprocessed via numerical vectorization/tensor conversion for quantum compatibility, with the classical GAN baseline enriched using common technical indicators such as 7‑day and 21‑day moving averages, exponential moving average, and momentum, and trained using Adam with specified learning rate, batch size, and epochs—indicating some transparency about classical hyperparameters. On the quantum side, experiments are run on the AWS Braket SV1 simulator with documented epoch counts and learning rates, and a one-step-ahead forecasting setup with defined past-window sizes is reported. However, the reliance on a simulator with very long epoch times, absence of real-hardware evaluations, and the admitted exponential circuit-depth growth from amplitude embedding suggest practical reproducibility and scalability constraints that may limit experimental breadth and realism.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-013, C-015, C-016, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-027, C-031, C-033]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper situates its work within a broader narrative that quantum computing, via properties like superposition, entanglement, and parallelism, may improve the speed, accuracy, and efficiency of solving complex financial optimization and forecasting problems, including discerning hidden patterns that might elude classical models, overcoming saddle-point issues in GANs, and enabling quantum-powered, forward-looking analysis for securities departments and fund managers. These claims are framed as potential or promised benefits for financial institutions rather than rigorously demonstrated outcomes within this single study.

=== PAPER 8248c1859e99 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets the "input problem" in quantum algorithms, emphasizing that the cost of loading classical data into quantum states is a major obstacle to achieving quantum advantage, because exact amplitude loading of arbitrary vectors can require circuits with depth exponential in the number of qubits. Within this broader issue, financial time-series data (priced in currency units) are one of four application domains used to study how severely this input bottleneck manifests in practice.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-023]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors introduce AMLET (Automatic Multi-layer Loader Exploiting TNs), a tensor-network-based circuit compilation method for amplitude encoding that can be tailored to arbitrary circuit depths and does not require variational optimization. AMLET constructs state-preparation circuits via careful fusing, splitting, and reordering of tensor indices, delaying SVD truncations so that approximations are introduced later in the process; both AMLET and a baseline layer-by-layer MPS-based algorithm provide monotonic depth–accuracy trade-offs without parameter optimization, thereby avoiding barren plateau issues. Under bounded depth or bounded number of layers, the classical cost of constructing the circuits scales as O(M) in the vector length for both the layer-by-layer approach and AMLET.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across finance, images, fluid mechanics, and protein structure datasets, the authors claim this is the broadest numerical analysis to date of classical-data loading into quantum computers, finding that required circuit depths are often several orders of magnitude smaller than those implied by a general exponential-scaling loading algorithm. For finance, circuit depth increases only moderately with qubit count and exhibits relatively small variance across instances, while images are empirically the easiest dataset to load, proteins show smoothly increasing depth suggesting even very large proteins might be loadable with depth below 200, and turbulent fluid data is the hardest, with some anomalous depth jumps attributed to error cancellation. In all tested settings, AMLET yields shorter depths than the layer-by-layer method for the same total error, with 16‑qubit improvements between about 8% and 25%, and in absolute terms the general amplitude-encoding algorithm would require at least 2^15 layers for 12 qubits and 2,715 layers for 16 qubits, far exceeding depths observed with AMLET, even though depths remain substantial in a subset of difficult cases.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-040]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The main classical comparison is conceptual: the authors contrast AMLET-loaded circuits with those generated by a general amplitude-encoding algorithm, noting that for 12 and 16 qubits such a general state-preparation circuit would need at least 2^15 and 2,715 layers respectively, whereas their compiled circuits are often several orders of magnitude shallower. They also benchmark AMLET against a classical layer-by-layer MPS-based loader, finding that AMLET consistently achieves shorter depth (by roughly 8–25% at 16 qubits) for the same total approximation error, which they attribute to requiring far fewer SVD truncations.
    [codes: C-008, C-010, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The evidence presented is limited to numerical experiments on simulators rather than implementations on physical quantum hardware, so hardware-specific issues such as noise and connectivity are not empirically addressed. The authors also acknowledge that, although depth reductions are significant relative to general loading schemes and the MPS baseline, some datasets—particularly turbulent fluid data—still require substantial circuit depths in a subset of cases, indicating that the input bottleneck is mitigated but not eliminated.
    [codes: C-039, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose extending AMLET beyond standard amplitude encoding to more complex data encodings as a future research direction. They also suggest developing modified versions of AMLET that respect fixed circuit patterns or specific hardware topologies, which would make the approach more applicable to realistic quantum devices.
    [codes: C-037, C-038]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims two main contributions: introducing AMLET, a tensor-network-based automatic multi-layer state loader with tunable depth and no variational optimization, and conducting what they describe as the broadest numerical analysis so far of classical-data loading into quantum computers using real-world datasets from finance, images, fluid mechanics, and proteins. They emphasize that AMLET’s design—especially delayed truncations and fewer SVD truncations—enables consistently shorter-depth circuits than an existing layer-by-layer method and far shallower circuits than the standard exponentially-scaling loading algorithm.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-012, C-018, C-032, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study relies on numerical experiments across four real-world domains, each with domain-specific quality metrics: a one-currency-unit error threshold for finance, an image error threshold of ε < 10^-3, two error conditions including momentum conservation for fluid data, and RMSD-based criteria for protein coordinates (the latter implied by quantitative extraction though not explicit in the codes). Both AMLET and the layer-by-layer approach provide monotonic accuracy–depth trade-offs without optimization, side-stepping issues like barren plateaus and enhancing determinism and reproducibility of the compiled circuits; the classical construction cost is analyzed and shown to scale linearly in vector length for bounded depth, but implementation complexity is nontrivial due to the need for careful index fusing, splitting, and reordering.
    [codes: C-006, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The observed anomalous non-monotonic depth behavior in turbulent fluid data, where some 12-qubit circuits are deeper than corresponding 14-qubit circuits, is specifically attributed to error cancellation effects in the chosen moment metrics, highlighting sensitivity of depth estimates to dataset-specific error structures.
    [codes: C-029]

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets credit card fraud detection as an anomaly-detection problem and develops quantum protocols for identifying fraudulent transactions within highly imbalanced credit card data. They primarily employ IQP-style circuits with threefold data re-uploading as the quantum feature map, scaling each input feature by a prefactor η=0.1 before encoding, and briefly note an alternative projective kernel based on local Pauli observables.
    [codes: C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Using average precision as the main metric, the authors report that quantum fraud detection can challenge and in some regimes surpass classical protocols as the number of features/qubits increases, particularly when using IQP kernels with re-uploading. In supervised settings, quantum kernels show a clear performance separation from classical RBF kernels at N=20 features and appear less prone to overfitting as dimensionality increases. In unsupervised anomaly detection, IQP-based quantum kernels achieve up to AP≈0.7 at N=20 qubits, corresponding to a reported 15% gain over the classical baseline, and re-uploading is specifically associated with better average precision among quantum variants.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-022, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The study establishes classical baselines using both supervised (logistic regression and SVC) and unsupervised (one-class SVM) methods evaluated with average precision, observing that supervised classical performance peaks around 5–10 features and degrades with more features while the OC-SVM’s AP gradually increases then saturates around 0.55 at ~15 features. Against these baselines, quantum kernels—especially IQP circuits with re-uploading—are reported to offer slightly higher supervised performance than logistic regression/SVC in the 5–10 feature regime and a clear advantage at 20 features, and in the unsupervised setting to outperform OC-SVM with an AP increase of about 15% at 20 qubits.
    [codes: C-003, C-009, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-022, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that quantum-kernel fraud detection is currently better suited to checking highly prioritised transactions rather than en masse screening, due to computational and latency constraints. Training cost is highlighted as large because Gram-matrix construction scales quadratically with the number of samples, and inference requires O(N_d N_s) kernel evaluations, which can be prohibitive at scale unless per-sample testing can be reduced to sub-millisecond times for real-time use. They also note that achieving a strong, practically relevant quantum advantage will likely require going beyond the 20-qubit regime studied here, towards 50–100 qubits and deeper quantum kernels, implying that the present results are at a relatively small scale.
    [codes: C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions include developing tailored strategies for constructing Gram matrices using randomized or sparse approaches instead of brute-force full evaluation, in order to reduce quadratic scaling in sample size. The authors also emphasize the need to optimize the number of measurement shots so that kernel estimates are near-deterministic while keeping Nshots as small as possible, potentially exploiting structure in the kernel.
    [codes: C-038, C-039]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions its main contribution as developing and empirically studying quantum kernel-based protocols for anomaly (fraud) detection on credit card data, with a focus on unsupervised quantum machine learning. It further claims that IQP-based quantum kernels with data re-uploading can challenge and surpass well-tuned classical baselines in terms of average precision as feature and qubit counts increase, providing an early indication of potential quantum advantage in this fraud-detection setting.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-022, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses a heavily subsampled and artificially balanced version of a public credit card fraud dataset (500 samples with 25 frauds), applies standard scaling followed by PCA to retain only the first N principal components, and consistently evaluates performance via the threshold-free average precision metric, explicitly preferring AP over F1 for imbalanced anomaly detection. Classical baselines are trained with hyperparameters tuned by random search using cross-validation AP, and the same PCA+scaling pipeline feeds both classical and quantum models, with quantum encoding implemented via a feature map that scales each feature by η=0.1 before loading into the circuit.
    [codes: C-002, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-018, C-023, C-024]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors connect model performance improvements to business value by noting that even a few-percent increase in average precision for fraud detection can translate into multi-million savings for financial institutions. They also discuss hardware-specific timing estimates, suggesting that superconducting circuits may enable microsecond-scale circuit evaluations, trapped ions offer slower but high-fidelity operations at roughly 100 µs per sequence (about 10 kHz), and photonic systems could in principle achieve the fastest training times, though such photonic platforms are not yet fully mature for deterministic gates.
    [codes: C-030, C-035, C-036, C-037]

=== PAPER 858a41cdb5b2 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as designing quantum algorithms that can efficiently handle and manipulate arrays (including matrix-like data structures) by directly embedding their entries into quantum amplitudes, and providing an end-to-end pipeline from data loading through arithmetic manipulation to information extraction that can support such array-based tasks. The authors argue that direct amplitude embedding simplifies subsequent algebraic operations on the stored information compared with register-based encodings.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-007, C-008, C-009]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The proposed method is a direct amplitude-embedding framework where array entries f(i,j) are stored as amplitudes c_ij of a two-register 'quantum matrix' state, with indices i and j representing rows and columns respectively, and arithmetic is performed directly on these amplitudes without square-root encodings or register-based value representations. The pipeline is modularized into separate stages for data loading (including pointwise loading under an efficient-oracle assumption and specialized constant-array loading), an arithmetic toolkit on arrays (reversal, permutations, pairwise sums, reductions, scalar and array multiplication, scalar products), and information extraction via a Quantum Coin amplitude-estimation scheme enhanced by an iterative Grover-style zoom-in procedure and amplitude shifts over confidence intervals. Specific gate-level mechanisms include masking and controlled-X for row reversal, pivot-based recursive multi-controlled-X permutations and cyclic permutations with added controls, Hadamard-based pairwise addition and Walsh–Hadamard reductions, controlled rotations for multiplication by constants within [0,1], array multiplication with products encoded in specific ancilla branches, and composition of array products with reductions to obtain scalar products.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-005, C-007, C-008, C-010, C-013, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that state-of-the-art generic n‑qubit state preparation requires a number of CNOT gates scaling as 2^{n+1}, motivating their search for more efficient loading in structured cases such as constant arrays. For constant arrays, they state that their loading procedure uses, in the worst case, n_I X-gates, two Y-rotations, and a single multi-controlled NOT, and from this they infer that, in principle, exponentially fewer operations are needed on a quantum computer to load a constant array than in the generic case. Within the arithmetic layer, they quantify that whole-matrix reversal can be more efficient than row- or column-only reversal, that reductions place row sums into the first column, and that array multiplication encodes the product of two arrays in the joint |0⟩ ancilla branch, which can then be combined with reductions to yield scalar products. For readout, they show that their Quantum Coin method with amplitude shift and iterative Grover amplification increases the measurement probability of the target basis state according to the standard amplification relation, effectively boosting the success probability within a specified confidence interval.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-020, C-027, C-031, C-032, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper primarily contrasts quantum vs. quantum approaches to state preparation, noting that existing generic loading techniques require exponentially many CNOTs in the number of qubits, whereas their constant-array loading uses only a number of gates scaling with the number of row qubits and a single multi-controlled NOT. On this basis, they claim that, in principle, exponentially fewer operations are needed to load constant arrays on a quantum computer, though the detailed comparison to classical loading costs is not elaborated beyond this asymptotic statement.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations and conditional assumptions. They state that pointwise loading of generic arrays is 'generically not efficient', underscoring that their loading advantages are restricted to structured cases such as constant arrays and that the overall efficiency of their array multiplication procedure is tied to the efficiency of the underlying loading process. They explicitly assume the existence of a suitable efficient oracle for data loading, without which the end-to-end scheme would not be efficient. They also note that multiplication by a constant via controlled rotations is initially restricted to numbers between 0 and 1. At the operation level, they point out that swaps of two entries in an array are demanding operations, reflecting a cost overhead for fine-grained permutations. For their approximation of linear shifts via step functions, they caution that the method becomes inefficient if the required precision scales as 1/N in the number of discretisation points, indicating unfavorable scaling for high-accuracy piecewise approximations.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-021, C-029, C-030, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The provided codes do not report explicit statements about future research directions or proposed extensions beyond the presented framework and examples.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions its novelty in offering a general-purpose framework for quantum algorithms that operate on arrays via direct embedding into amplitudes, thereby avoiding square roots and register encodings and, according to the authors, enabling simpler handling and combination of stored information. They highlight the modularization of the quantum algorithm pipeline into data loading, arithmetic manipulations, and read-out, and the construction of an efficient toolkit of quantum arithmetic operations on arrays, including explicit examples on manipulating generic oracles such as constant shifts and step-function approximations to linear shifts. They further claim that for constant arrays this framework can, in principle, achieve an exponential reduction in the number of operations required for loading compared with generic state-preparation methods.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-009, C-010, C-017, C-037, C-039]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the authors emphasize a modular pipeline that treats data loading, arithmetic operations, and read-out as separable components, allowing each to be analyzed in terms of gate counts and efficiency. For resource estimates, they adopt the customary use of CNOT counts as a primary complexity indicator for state preparation and articulate explicit gate-level procedures (e.g., masking with controlled-X for row reversal, recursive pivot-based permutations, Hadamard-based reductions, controlled rotations for scalar multiplication, and Quantum Coin Grover iterations for readout). However, the codes do not indicate the use of real financial datasets, benchmark instances, or reproducible code artefacts; rather, the work is presented at the level of abstract array manipulation and oracle examples, with performance characterized via analytical gate counts and scaling arguments.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Some codes provide additional detail on the behavior of specific example constructions: for example, the constant-shift oracle example stores the difference array f − s, and the step-function shift is described as the most rudimentary approximation to a linear function. === PAPER 85fbbb9f2a42 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames its work around the open question of whether quantum machine learning offers a clear advantage over classical machine learning, noting that such advantages have not yet been extensively or clearly demonstrated, especially on noisy, few-qubit NISQ hardware and with large, imbalanced datasets relevant for business contexts such as credit risk and fraud detection. It formulates the problem as developing QML workflows that circumvent qubit-number constraints while handling big, imbalanced financial datasets by focusing on input preprocessing and dimensionality reduction choices for binary classification tasks. The authors explicitly target realistic business-like settings where datasets may be imbalanced and have either small or large numbers of features.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-008, C-009, C-010]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study employs two NISQ-oriented quantum machine learning methods: a quantum support vector classifier (QSVC) based on a quantum feature map, and a variational quantum algorithm (VQA) / variational quantum classifier. Classical data are first reduced in dimension and then encoded on only two qubits using either a Qiskit ZZFeatureMap for QSVC or angle encoding in PennyLane for the VQA, explicitly to demonstrate usability under the small-qubit constraint typical of business-relevant NISQ devices. Quantum encoding is a central design choice, and the experiments are run purely on noiseless simulators (Qiskit Aer and PennyLane) to allow fast iteration, with noise explicitly subtracted from simulations.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-017, C-018, C-015, C-016]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The core empirical finding is that incorporating Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) in the preprocessing stage improves the performance of quantum classifiers, particularly VQA, and in some cases enables them to outperform baseline classical classifiers on the evaluated metrics. On the UCI credit card default dataset, LDA emerges as the best dimensionality reduction method for both QSVC and VQA, with the VQA+LDA configuration achieving very high balanced accuracy, while some other quantum configurations such as QSVC with SKPP fail to separate classes at all. On the fraud detection dataset, LDA again provides the best preprocessing for both QSVC and VQA, and the quantum algorithms offer a small performance advantage over an LDA-based classical approach; moreover, four quantum configurations reportedly exceed the best baseline precision metric.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-007, C-022, C-023, C-021, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors benchmark their quantum models against several classical classifiers (including logistic regression, KNN, decision trees, Naive Bayes, and SVM) and report that, on the UCI credit card default dataset, these classical baselines struggle to separate the minority class, with the best reported precision and F1-scores remaining relatively low. In this regime, VQA with LDA is claimed to outperform the classical baselines in balanced accuracy and overall performance metrics. For the fraud detection dataset, classical baselines perform comparatively well, yet the quantum algorithms with LDA preprocessing are said to provide a small advantage over the classical LDA-based approach, and specifically, four quantum algorithms surpass the best classical precision value. The authors further propose a broadened notion of quantum advantage that need not require beating all classical models outright, but may instead be interpreted as extracting information differently or more effectively from the data.
    [codes: C-003, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-030]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly acknowledges several methodological limitations that temper its quantum-advantage claims. First, all experiments are run on simulators with noise subtracted, so hardware noise and realistic NISQ error characteristics are not evaluated. Second, the classical machine learning baselines are not specifically tuned to the datasets; default parameters are used throughout, and logistic regression fails to converge on the fraud dataset under these defaults, which may understate classical performance. Third, on the quantum side, the parameters of the quantum feature map are fixed (e.g., number of repetitions and feature dimension) and not tuned, and the exploration of different ansatz structures for VQA is left for future work, meaning the reported quantum results may not reflect optimally configured circuits. These caveats collectively limit the strength and generality of the reported quantum-classical performance comparisons.
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors highlight multiple avenues for future research. They propose a deeper investigation into why LDA appears to outperform PCA in their supervised quantum classification setting, with the aim of understanding how LDA may provide a better data representation for qubit encoding. They also plan to study the role of PCA in unsupervised tasks, where its strengths may differ. On the quantum side, exploring alternative ansatz designs for the VQA is flagged as an interesting direction to assess the sensitivity of results to circuit structure. Finally, they call for extending their benchmarking approach to additional datasets with higher feature counts and to other domains, in order to build a more general and robust benchmark of QML preprocessing strategies.
    [codes: C-031, C-032, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions its main contribution as a "preprocessing perspective" on quantum machine learning, arguing that appropriate classical dimensionality reduction—specifically LDA—can unlock performance advantages for NISQ-era quantum classifiers under severe qubit constraints. It claims novelty in demonstrating, across two business-relevant financial datasets with class imbalance and differing feature dimensionality, that LDA-based preprocessing both improves classical encoding into two-qubit quantum circuits and can enable QSVC and VQA models to match or outperform classical baselines on certain metrics, thereby reframing quantum advantage as partly a question of how classical data are represented before quantum encoding.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-022, C-027, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study focuses on binary classification using two financial datasets chosen to emulate realistic business scenarios with imbalanced labels and varying feature dimensionality, including the UCI Default of Credit Card Clients (22% defaulters) and a high-dimensional fraud-detection dataset with 114 features and class imbalance. === PAPER 86891f250a78 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames its objective as surveying supervised and unsupervised quantum machine learning techniques that have actually been executed on quantum hardware, with a specific emphasis on real‑world applications in high‑energy physics, finance, and healthcare rather than toy problems. It focuses on how data (classical vs quantum) are defined and encoded into quantum feature spaces, highlighting efficient data loading and representation as central challenges for making these applications practical.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-010, C-013, C-019, C-020]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The survey centers on two main QML frameworks—quantum kernel methods and variational quantum algorithms—detailing their conceptual distinction and implementation via parameterized quantum circuits and kernel similarity measures. It systematically reviews encoding strategies (basis, amplitude, angle, data re‑uploading, Hamiltonian encodings), circuit structures (feature map vs model circuit separation in VQCs, Swap‑test classifier), and optimization and gradient techniques (SPSA, quantum gradient methods, parameter‑shift, quantum natural gradient and QN‑SPSA, shot‑frugal optimizers, local cost functions) as the key levers for making these methods workable on near‑term devices.
    [codes: C-003, C-007, C-008, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-057, C-061, C-070]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across domains, the authors report that amplitude encoding can in principle offer exponential memory savings and that randomized measurement strategies can improve the scaling of quantum kernel estimation. They highlight observed robustness and faster convergence of certain optimizers (SPSA under noise and quantum natural gradient methods, including QN‑SPSA) and cite results such as exponential speedup claims for qPCA, high‑fidelity quantum GAN state replication, and tensor‑network approaches whose qubit requirements scale only logarithmically or are input‑size independent. Application‑wise, they note that high‑energy‑physics studies largely pursue gains in small‑data regimes, finance feature‑selection with QN‑SPSA converged on 20‑qubit hardware, quantum‑data‑driven models appear more promising than those on classical data, and some healthcare image‑classification experiments on real hardware achieve accuracies comparable to classical baselines, though vulnerabilities and hardware‑induced performance gaps are also observed.
    [codes: C-023, C-031, C-036, C-039, C-041, C-042, C-044, C-047, C-048, C-051, C-052, C-054, C-066]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The survey repeatedly benchmarks QML performance against classical ML, using classical models as baselines and noting that in many cases current quantum methods only match but do not exceed classical performance. In high‑energy physics and healthcare, the authors report comparable AUC‑ROC or accuracy to standard classical classifiers, with specific examples where more expressive encodings yield no improvement on real hardware relative to simpler encodings or classical baselines. They also emphasize that there may exist efficient classical algorithms that achieve performance comparable to quantum approaches, underscoring that convincing empirical evidence of a clear quantum advantage over classical learning remains limited so far.
    [codes: C-002, C-048, C-052, C-062, C-063]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors catalogue extensive limitations: hardware constraints such as limited qubit connectivity, noise, short coherence times, and state‑preparation and measurement errors, which in turn cause long running times and instability between simulator and hardware performance. They emphasize data‑related bottlenecks including the difficulty of efficiently encoding classical data (data‑loading problem), amplitude encoding’s potentially exponential gate cost, quadratic scaling and noise in quantum kernel estimation, and the lack of efficient, standardized data loaders or QRAM. On the algorithmic side, they highlight barren plateaus in variational training, the need for careful ansatz design, inefficiency of backpropagation for PQCs, and scaling issues for methods like qPCA on larger datasets. They also note that more complex encodings can amplify hardware noise without improving performance, that QGANs risk mode collapse, that quantum hardware’s noise and coherence constraints limit attainable circuit depth, and that full quantum error correction introduces overhead that can erode speedups. Further, they stress security and privacy gaps—including vulnerability of QML classifiers to adversarial examples, lack of built‑in privacy mechanisms, and insufficient exploration of differential privacy—as well as meta‑level limitations such as the lack of standardized benchmarks and quantum datasets, limited empirical evidence of quantum advantage, possible parity with unknown classical algorithms, and poor transparency around hyperparameter choices, all of which hinder interpretability, reproducibility, and progress.
    [codes: C-006, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-020, C-024, C-029, C-030, C-035, C-041, C-043, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-053, C-055, C-056, C-058, C-060, C-062, C-063, C-068, C-071, C-072, C-075]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors call for developing and testing quantum gradient and hybrid optimization methods (e.g., quantum gradient techniques, QN‑SPSA), designing shot‑frugal optimizers and local cost functions to mitigate barren plateaus and measurement overheads, and advancing quantum autoencoder‑based error mitigation or correction. They argue that standardized benchmarks and easily preparable quantum datasets are needed to assess QML fairly, alongside systematic methods for choosing optimal encodings and ansätze that scale. They also highlight research gaps in privacy‑preserving QML (including differential privacy), in explainable quantum ML (XQML), and in distributed or ensemble‑style schemes such as quantum federated learning and quantum boosting to better utilize limited near‑term hardware. QRAM and improved quantum data preparation are identified as longer‑term directions for addressing data‑loading and storage challenges.
    [codes: C-037, C-057, C-059, C-061, C-064, C-065, C-067, C-069, C-070, C-073, C-074, C-076]

Their contribution lies in organizing these hardware‑level studies by application domain, explicating core frameworks (quantum kernels vs variational algorithms), encodings, and optimization strategies, and drawing cross‑cutting conclusions about limitations, open questions on quantum advantage, and needed benchmarks and transparency practices.

The authors also note that many studies rely on small datasets or limited‑data regimes, and that gaps in standardized benchmarks and quantum datasets currently impede rigorous, fair evaluation of QML against classical baselines.

=== PAPER 872cedb13e27 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets the challenge of efficiently loading classical probability distributions into quantum states for financial applications, noting that exact state preparation scales as O(2^n) and undermines quantum advantage for large n (data-loading bottleneck) and that existing qGANs are unstable and not robust on NISQ devices (noise and expressivity limits) (C-001, C-008, C-010). It specifically frames qGANs as approximate probability loaders for tasks such as derivative pricing and risk assessment, where distributions like 2D Gaussians and log-normals need to be embedded into quantum states for downstream algorithms including Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) (C-009, C-020, C-026, C-027, C-060).
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-010, C-009, C-020, C-026, C-027, C-060]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a noise-resilient hybrid qGAN architecture that extends the Zoufal et al. framework by combining advanced loss functions (WGAN-GP and MMD) with expressive variational ansätze—EfficientSU2 and a 6-qubit QCNN—and explicit NISQ noise modeling via depolarizing channels on CX gates (C-028, C-029, C-033, C-034, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-043). Training uses a differentiable PyTorch–Qiskit workflow with parameter-shift gradients, ADAM optimization, and a WGAN-GP objective plus gradient penalty to stabilize learning, while target distributions are discretized to 8×8 grids for loading (C-003, C-031, C-032, C-035, C-036, C-041, C-050, C-029). For the financial-pricing demonstration, this qGAN-based loader prepares log-normal distributions that feed into Quantum Amplitude Estimation on up to 10–20 qubits on IBM superconducting hardware (C-006, C-025, C-050, C-059, C-060, C-061).
    [codes: C-028, C-029, C-033, C-034, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-043, C-003, C-031, C-032, C-035, C-036, C-041, C-050, C-006, C-025, C-059, C-060, C-061]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across 2D Gaussian and log-normal benchmarks, the EfficientSU2–WGAN-GP (R8) variant achieves sub-0.01 Wasserstein distances, with a reported mean WS ≈ 0.0027 ± 0.0004 and fidelity > 0.9, and is visually almost indistinguishable from the target PMFs, with t-SNE analysis suggesting that the generators learn the underlying distribution manifold rather than memorizing samples (C-014, C-030, C-052, C-054, C-055, C-064). Noise sweeps under depolarizing noise up to p = 0.02 show approximately linear degradation and then saturation, with the best model maintaining WS ≈ 0.0046 ± 0.0004 and high relative entropy, while hardware experiments on IBM’s 20‑qubit devices indicate that EfficientSU2–WGAN-GP achieves lower VaR estimation error than QCNN, evidencing relative robustness under realistic noise (C-056, C-057, C-058, C-059, C-065). In the financial application, QAE with qGAN-loaded log-normal distributions attains European call pricing errors below 1%, with hardware estimates around 5.47 ± 0.07 and claims of 100× reduction in required shots for a given precision in simulation (C-006, C-060, C-061, C-062).
    [codes: C-014, C-030, C-052, C-054, C-055, C-064, C-056, C-057, C-058, C-059, C-065, C-006, C-060, C-061, C-062]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The proposed hybrid qGAN variants are benchmarked against both a baseline RY–CZ qGAN and classical WGAN-GP and MMD-GAN models, with the EfficientSU2–WGAN-GP circuit reporting substantially lower Wasserstein distances and statistically significant improvements (Wilcoxon p < 0.01) over the RY–CZ baseline on the 2D Gaussian task (C-046, C-052, C-053). The authors also report that their architecture achieves lower VaR estimation error under noise on IBM hardware compared to QCNN-based quantum models, and they highlight a 25% hardware error reduction in QAE-based pricing relative to a baseline qGAN loader and 100× fewer shots than a classical Monte Carlo-based estimate at matched precision in simulation (C-058, C-059, C-061, C-062).
    [codes: C-046, C-052, C-053, C-058, C-059, C-061, C-062]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges that all experiments are restricted to n ≤ 20 qubits, and that scaling to higher-dimensional financial problems will require more advanced noise mitigation and error-correction strategies (C-067). It also notes practical constraints from cloud hardware access, with queue delays of approximately five hours per model on IBM systems, which impede large-scale benchmarking despite partial mitigation via Qiskit Runtime parallelism (C-068). The authors explicitly frame these points in a limitations section as ongoing practical and theoretical constraints on the current approach (C-066).
    [codes: C-066, C-067, C-068]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future research directions include deploying qGANs in cross-institutional, privacy-preserving financial analytics settings—suggesting federated or distributed learning across institutions (C-069). The authors also propose coupling their loaders with fault-tolerant or error-corrected QAE for scalable risk computation, scaling to higher-dimensional (3D+) financial manifolds via tensor-network-based ansätze for portfolio-level data, and exploring hybrids between qGANs and quantum diffusion models to enhance diversity and gradient stability (C-070, C-071, C-072).
    [codes: C-069, C-070, C-071, C-072]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim to advance quantum generative modeling by introducing a noise-resilient, hybrid qGAN framework that simultaneously addresses efficient approximate data loading and stability under realistic NISQ noise for financial distributions (C-002, C-028, C-029, C-063). Their main contribution is the integration of WGAN-GP and quantum-kernel MMD losses with expressive, noise-aware ansätze (EfficientSU2 and QCNN) and a differentiable PyTorch–Qiskit workflow, yielding a best-performing EfficientSU2–WGAN-GP (R8) model that they describe as achieving state-of-the-art performance on the studied 2D Gaussian and log-normal benchmarks (C-003, C-024, C-025, C-031, C-033, C-064).
    [codes: C-002, C-028, C-029, C-063, C-003, C-024, C-025, C-031, C-033, C-064]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work emphasizes NISQ realism via explicit depolarizing noise models on CX gates, parameter-shift gradients, and noise sweeps from 0–5% to quantify robustness, together with checkpointing to manage long training runs (C-013, C-034, C-035, C-042, C-043, C-056). Experimental design includes four hybrid variants, classical and qGAN baselines, detailed hyperparameters, and a plateau-based convergence criterion; performance is assessed with multiple metrics (Wasserstein distance, KL/relative entropy, KS tests, fidelity) and accompanied by PMF heatmaps, t-SNE visualizations, and noise–fidelity curves, with some results backed by Wilcoxon significance tests (p < 0.01) (C-041, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-053, C-055, C-056). The implementation is described as using PyTorch–Qiskit integration and IBM’s 20‑qubit hardware without GPU acceleration, and the authors position their approach as building systematically on prior qGAN and noise-mitigation literature (C-004, C-021, C-023, C-047, C-059).
    [codes: C-013, C-034, C-035, C-042, C-043, C-056, C-041, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-053, C-055, C-004, C-021, C-023, C-047, C-059]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper also provides background context on GAN training pathologies (mode collapse, vanishing gradients) and how WGAN-GP and MMD-GAN address them, including references to empirical improvements on classical image benchmarks, as well as prior findings on zero-noise extrapolation and readout calibration in quantum hardware (C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-032). These elements serve mainly as theoretical and literature context rather than core parts of the new experimental contribution.
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-032]

=== PAPER 88e005f67ca2 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses cross-sectional equity return prediction in noisy, non-stationary financial markets, motivated by the view that many classical forecasting models struggle with noisy inputs, regime shifts, and limited generalization capacity. The task is instantiated using the JPX Tokyo Stock Exchange Kaggle competition, predicting a two-day holding return target for a universe restricted to more liquid stocks and evaluated via long-short portfolio performance. The authors frame quantum machine learning as a potentially promising pathway to enhance stock market prediction under these challenging data conditions.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-010, C-012, C-013]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The core method is a hybrid Quantum Temporal Convolutional Neural Network (QTCNN) that combines a classical temporal encoder with parameter-efficient quantum convolution circuits, where the encoder extracts multi-scale patterns from sequences of technical indicators and passes compressed representations to the quantum part. Classical feature vectors are standardized cross-sectionally by day, then encoded into quantum states using angle embedding on multiple qubits; the quantum circuit applies hierarchical convolution–pooling with parameter sharing and leverages superposition and entanglement, and predictions are obtained by measuring Pauli observables. The study also implements several quantum or hybrid baselines, including a pure quantum neural network (QNN) classifier, a PQC-enhanced gradient boosting model (PQC+LGBM), a quantum LSTM (QLSTM), and a quantum adaptive self-attention (QASA) architecture to contextualize QTCNN’s design.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-014, C-015, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-027, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: In out-of-sample tests on the JPX dataset, the proposed QTCNN achieves an annualized Sharpe ratio of about 0.538±0.042, which the authors note as the highest among all models evaluated. They report that quantum-based architectures occupy the top three performance ranks, while a classical LSTM baseline attains the lowest Sharpe ratio (≈0.044±0.029). Ablation and scaling analyses indicate that adding the quantum circuit to the temporal encoder yields a statistically significant Sharpe improvement, that entanglement via CNOT gates materially contributes to performance, and that QTCNN’s Sharpe rises with the number of qubits up to around 10 before slightly declining at 12 qubits. Additional analyses show that QTCNN maintains superior gradient variance scaling relative to other quantum models, and that it remains above the best classical Sharpe ratio up to a simulated depolarizing error rate of roughly 0.01, with amplitude damping noise degrading performance less than depolarizing noise.
    [codes: C-006, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-046, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors benchmark QTCNN and other quantum architectures against a suite of classical baselines including Transformer and LSTM-based time-series models, as well as a temporal-convolution-plus-MLP architecture (TConv-MLP). QTCNN is reported to outperform all classical baselines in terms of out-of-sample Sharpe ratio, with the headline claim that its Sharpe of 0.538 represents roughly a 72% improvement over the best-performing classical baseline. Ablation results using TConv-MLP as a classical-only counterpart suggest that the quantum circuit on top of a temporal encoder delivers an additional statistically significant performance gain over the purely classical temporal model.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-025, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly cautions that its experiments are conducted entirely in a classical simulation regime and therefore do not constitute evidence of a computational quantum speedup, noting that they do not claim any such speedup under their current setup. The qubit scalability and noise-resilience findings are obtained under idealized or simplified noise models on simulators rather than on real NISQ hardware, implying that hardware-specific issues such as decoherence, gate infidelity, and readout noise are not fully captured. More broadly, although not made explicit in the codes, the reliance on a relatively short 22-day out-of-sample evaluation window and stride-subsampled data suggests limited statistical power for assessing long-horizon portfolio performance, and this should be treated as an implicit caveat about the robustness and generalizability of the reported Sharpe ratios.
    [codes: C-040, C-041, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Not addressed in this paper.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main claimed contribution is the design of a Quantum Temporal Convolutional Neural Network that fuses a classical temporal encoder—capturing multi-scale sequential patterns—with a parameter-efficient quantum convolutional circuit employing hierarchical convolution–pooling and parameter sharing, specifically tailored for cross-sectional equity return prediction. The authors further claim novelty in empirically analyzing quantum enhancement mechanisms such as Hilbert space expressibility, entanglement-enabled feature interactions, and quantum interference acting as an implicit feature selection process, and in providing a comparative benchmark where quantum-based architectures dominate performance rankings on the JPX financial forecasting task.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-033, C-035, C-038, C-043, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses the JPX Kaggle dataset with a clearly defined two-day holding-period return target based on raw closes while deriving features from adjusted close prices, and restricts the universe to officially flagged liquid stocks (Universe0) to avoid illiquid securities. Features are winsorized and then standardized cross-sectionally each day using L-score normalization, with fixed-length sequences (default length 20) formed for time-series models, and a weakly supervised labeling scheme where only the top and bottom p-ranked stocks by cross-sectional target are used as positive and negative classes. To manage computational cost and preserve market-regime diversity, the authors use stride-based subsampling of trading days combined with year-wise stratified sampling, and evaluate models via a long–short portfolio protocol using out-of-sample annualized Sharpe ratio as the primary metric, supported by paired bootstrap tests of performance differences. These design choices suggest attention to financial realism in data preprocessing and to statistical rigor in evaluating model differences, even though experiments are conducted on a reduced subset of days and in simulation.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-031, C-039]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors provide a conceptual discussion of possible quantum enhancement mechanisms: they emphasize Hilbert space expressibility as a means of representing complex financial patterns, entanglement via CNOT gates as a way to model interactions between different financial features, and quantum interference as an implicit feature selection effect that may help control overfitting in noisy market data.
    [codes: C-043, C-044, C-045]
[SILO OVERLAY]
  SILO_RELEVANCE: This paper is highly relevant to quantum_ml_finance because it is a direct application of a hybrid quantum-classical model to cross-sectional equity return prediction, with evaluation tied to portfolio Sharpe ratio rather than generic classification accuracy. It also provides concrete evidence on when quantum components, entanglement, qubit scaling, and noise robustness may matter for financial prediction tasks.
    [silo_relevance_score: high]

    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-022, C-020, C-014  dim_source: dimension_2]

    [codes: C-007, C-031, C-006, C-032  dim_source: dimension_3]

=== PAPER 88e7d870aeb0 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets automated trading and risk management in complex, highly variable financial markets, where traditional models struggle with nonlinearity, regime shifts, and tail risks (C-004, C-005, C-007). The authors frame the problem as learning profitable, risk-aware trading policies within a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) to better handle market uncertainty (C-010).
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-007, C-010]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study proposes a Quantum Attention Deep Q-Network (QADQN), a quantum-inspired reinforcement learning framework that integrates a multi-head quantum attention mechanism into a deep Q-learning architecture for financial decision-making (C-001, C-002, C-008). The method is motivated by quantum portfolio encoding, QUBO-based allocation, and Hamiltonian mappings (C-011, C-012, C-013), but these quantum formalisms are used only to guide feature mapping, with the attention blocks implemented as 4-qubit simulated circuits in a hybrid LSTM/MLP–plus–quantum attention stack (C-017, C-021).
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-017, C-021]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The QADQN framework reportedly achieves superior risk-adjusted performance, with higher Sharpe ratios (0.82 and 0.77), elevated Sortino ratios above 1.1, and constrained maximum drawdown of 19.24% across overlapping and non-overlapping test periods (C-003, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027). It delivers cumulative returns of 78.91% and 71.26% in these respective periods, while exhibiting selective trading behavior that identifies favorable entry and exit points and avoids unnecessary trades, and training completes within about six GPU-hours (C-024, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-033).
    [codes: C-003, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-033]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Compared with classical baselines, the QADQN agent is reported to consistently outperform both a Buy & Hold strategy and a DDPG reinforcement learning agent in terms of cumulative returns and risk-adjusted metrics over both overlapping and non-overlapping evaluation periods (C-023, C-024, C-025, C-030). The authors interpret these results as indicating that QADQN can better identify profitable trading opportunities and generalize to both familiar and unseen market conditions than the classical benchmarks (C-023, C-025, C-030).
    [codes: C-023, C-024, C-025, C-030]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors emphasize that all quantum-inspired components are executed via classical simulation, explicitly stating that they do not claim any quantum speedup or hardware-level advantage and that the quantum formalisms (portfolio encoding, QUBO, Hamiltonians) are only motivational rather than actually solved quantum processes (C-015, C-016, C-017). They acknowledge that the experiments are limited to a single S&P 500 asset with overlapping train-test windows and omit real-world trading frictions in parts of the setup, which restricts generality (C-018, C-038). They further note that current NISQ hardware constraints such as decoherence, noise, and limited qubit connectivity are not modeled, so results likely overestimate what current devices could deliver, and that their 4‑qubit attention design may not scale well since larger qubit counts would require deeper, noisier, and more expensive circuits (C-036, C-037).
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-036, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors propose broader validation via multi-asset portfolios and cross-market indices such as NASDAQ, FTSE 100, and Nikkei 225 to strengthen evidence of generalizability (C-034, C-040). They also suggest stress-testing the approach under extreme market events like the COVID-19 crash, and ultimately deploying QADQN in simulated real-time trading platforms and controlled live environments (C-035, C-039).
    [codes: C-034, C-035, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in introducing the Quantum Attention Deep Q-Network (QADQN), a quantum-inspired reinforcement learning framework that integrates a multi-head quantum attention mechanism into deep Q-learning for financial trading and risk management, intended to reduce overhead and enhance interpretability relative to standard transformer attention (C-001, C-002, C-008). It also highlights the use of quantum-motivated portfolio encoding and QUBO/Hamiltonian formulations to inform feature mapping, and the combination of POMDP modeling, Dual Thrust–style replay buffer initialization, and imitation-based learning to improve trading policy learning (C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014).
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the authors position their work as addressing shortcomings of GARCH, GBM, and standard deep learning models, which they describe as insufficient for nonlinear dependencies, regime shifts, and fat-tail risks, and as computationally demanding and sensitive to data irregularities (C-005, C-006, C-007). The experimental setup is specified with training on S&P 500 data from 2016-01-15 to 2020-01-15 using a 24-day rolling window, with both overlapping and non-overlapping evaluation periods, and transaction costs of 0.2% per trade with no leverage (C-019, C-020, C-022). They document that each quantum attention module uses four qubits, analyze that training complexity remains polynomial with a manageable quadratic factor from quantum attention, and report that training on four years of data completes within six GPU-hours, suggesting practical feasibility under their simulator-based setup (C-021, C-032, C-033).
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper notes qualitatively that the learned QADQN policy behaves in a risk-sensitive manner, implementing timely exits and dynamic position adjustments during downturns, which the authors link to its ability to mitigate downside volatility while maximizing returns (C-026, C-031).
    [codes: C-026, C-031]
