=== PAPER 8a2ce0575ff1 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies sector rotation in the Taiwan stock market, framing it as a sequential decision problem where an RL agent allocates capital across multiple industry sectors to maximize long-term investment returns. Sector rotation is described as reallocating capital between sectors across economic phases to generate alpha and manage risk, and is cast into an MDP where at each time step the agent observes an engineered financial state vector and selects sector allocations. The work specifically focuses on training an RL agent for this task within a hybrid quantum-classical framework.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors employ a hybrid quantum-classical reinforcement learning framework based on PPO, where the policy and value networks can be instantiated with quantum-enhanced backbones including a QNN, a QRWKV model, and a QASA Transformer variant. The QNN uses angle embedding to map classical features into low-dimensional quantum states processed by a variational quantum circuit; QRWKV replaces part of RWKV’s channel-mixing layer with a variational quantum circuit; and QASA replaces classical dot-product attention with a quantum attention mechanism implemented via a variational quantum circuit. All quantum models are relatively small NISQ-style circuits, e.g., the QNN is configured with 4 qubits and 2 quantum circuit layers, and are integrated into the PPO agent as function approximators.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-013, C-022, C-027, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-047]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the quantum-enhanced models (QNN, QRWKV, QASA) consistently achieve the highest cumulative training rewards within the PPO framework, with QASA attaining the highest final reward among all models. However, across backtests on the Taiwan market, these quantum models underperform classical LSTM and Transformer backbones on real-world investment metrics including cumulative return, annualized return, Sharpe ratio, and drawdown, with QASA showing the most pronounced mismatch by pairing the highest reward with the lowest cumulative and risk-adjusted returns. The authors also observe that classical models learn more stable allocation policies that are better aligned with long-term investment outcomes, and interpret the overall pattern as a significant gap between training rewards and realized investment performance.
    [codes: C-004, C-014, C-041, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-056, C-060]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Within a shared PPO framework with unified feature engineering and shared hyperparameters, the study systematically compares classical LSTM and Transformer backbones against quantum-enhanced QNN, QRWKV, and QASA networks. While quantum models often obtain higher training rewards, the LSTM and Transformer baselines deliver higher cumulative and annualized returns, better Sharpe ratios, and comparable or slightly better drawdown statistics, indicating that classical architectures are more aligned with long-term financial objectives in this setting. The authors highlight that classical models appear to learn more stable and generalizable policies, whereas quantum models tend to fit the proxy reward signal more aggressively but translate that less effectively into portfolio performance.
    [codes: C-002, C-013, C-017, C-027, C-029, C-030, C-046, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-056]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper identifies several limitations. First, at the finance/RL level, the authors stress that reward design is a persistent challenge in RL for financial decision-making and that their proxy reward—based on correctly predicting next-step top-N sector leadership—does not directly optimize long-term objectives such as cumulative return or Sharpe ratio, potentially incentivizing overfitting to short-term volatility rather than risk-adjusted returns. They explicitly interpret the observed reward–performance gap as an instance of this known issue. Second, on the quantum side, they note that practical QRL is constrained by NISQ hardware limitations, including significant noise, shallow circuit depth, and barren plateau phenomena, and further emphasize the expressiveness and optimization instability of quantum circuits under such constraints. They also mention broader training challenges for quantum models, such as susceptibility to noise and decoherence and the lack of standardized quantum-compatible financial environments. Empirically, they argue that the quantum models’ high expressiveness may make them more prone to overfitting the proxy reward and learning strategies that exploit reward-specific patterns that do not generalize to real-world portfolio behavior, especially when risk and volatility are considered. For QASA in particular, they suggest that its quantum attention mechanism may overemphasize spurious correlations or suffer from optimization instability, contributing to its poor out-of-sample performance.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-012, C-020, C-024, C-039, C-053, C-054, C-055, C-060, C-007]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose several directions for future research. They plan to refine reward shaping and regularization within the PPO framework to better align the learning signal with long-term investment goals, aiming to bridge the observed discrepancy between training rewards and actual performance. They argue that realizing practical benefits from quantum-enhanced models will require more robust encoding schemes, regularization methods, and reward designs tailored to financial objectives. They also explicitly call for future studies to investigate whether, under reward signals that more faithfully reflect long-term risk-adjusted returns, quantum models can not only match but potentially exceed classical baselines.
    [codes: C-018, C-058, C-059]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s contributions are framed as threefold: (1) introducing a reproducible QRL benchmark for sector rotation using real Taiwan stock market data; (2) providing a systematic comparison of classical and quantum-enhanced policy networks within a unified PPO-based hybrid framework; and (3) analyzing the discrepancy between training reward and investment performance, offering actionable recommendations for reward shaping and regularization. The authors also position their work as filling a gap in the literature by delivering empirical QRL evidence on a real-world financial task and by surfacing practical challenges of deploying quantum reinforcement learning in finance.
    [codes: C-001, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-023, C-024, C-008]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study employs a flexible PPO agent with interchangeable classical (LSTM, Transformer) and quantum-enhanced backbones, trained under shared hyperparameters to ensure a fair comparison. The authors construct a unified automated feature engineering pipeline that extracts technical indicators from sector-level price and volume data into a common feature matrix, and define a clear MDP setup with state, action (top-10 sector selection), and proxy reward specification. They train and evaluate on a large real-market dataset covering 2,646 listed companies grouped into 47 sectors over 2007–2025, using a fixed training–backtesting temporal split and a rolling-window simulation to approximate real-time decision-making and out-of-sample generalization. Performance is assessed with standard financial metrics (cumulative/annualized return, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown), and the authors emphasize that their PPO-based framework and dataset choices are intended to yield a reproducible benchmark for future QRL studies in finance.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-013, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-022, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-034, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-048, C-008]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors situate their work in broader literatures, noting that RL has been applied to tasks such as portfolio rebalancing, asset allocation, algorithmic trading, and hedging strategies, and that quantum machine learning has been proposed for applications including portfolio optimization, option pricing, credit risk modeling, and market simulation. They further emphasize that the reward–performance gap observed in their experiments is not unique to quantum models but reflects a known challenge in deep RL for finance more generally, reinforcing the cross-cutting importance of careful reward design.
    [codes: C-019, C-021, C-057, C-060, C-010]

=== PAPER 8d08019fb608 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper is framed as an extensive survey of how quantum machine learning (QML) can be applied to core quantitative finance problems, including portfolio optimization, market prediction and trading, option pricing, risk measurement (VaR/CVaR), credit risk, and fraud detection as anomaly detection. It motivates these applications by arguing that quantum properties such as superposition and entanglement could improve on traditional financial modelling and ML methods. The authors also carefully define central financial tasks and metrics (e.g., portfolio optimization, Sharpe ratio, VaR/CVaR, credit rating categories, and the treatment of fraud detection as a special case of anomaly detection) to ground the surveyed QML work in standard finance problem formulations.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-005, C-006, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: As a survey, the paper covers several families of quantum and quantum‑hybrid methods rather than implementing one specific algorithm. It explains basic gate‑model concepts (qubits, superposition, unitary gates) and positions QML within the NISQ era, emphasizing hybrid quantum–classical algorithms where parametrized quantum circuits (QNNs) are trained via classical optimizers. The authors describe key building blocks such as QAOA for combinatorial optimization, QAE for amplitude estimation, HHL for linear systems, and quantum PCA for eigenvalue problems, and then map these to finance use cases (e.g., QAOA and VQE for portfolio optimization, QAE and qGAN-based loading for derivative pricing, quantum kernels and QSVMs for classification and anomaly detection, and quantum GANs and kernel methods for fraud and credit risk). They also highlight architectures such as feature‑map plus variational layers in QNNs and multiple quantum kernel learning schemes used in risk and fraud contexts.
    [codes: C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-049, C-050, C-053, C-061, C-062, C-063, C-064, C-070, C-074, C-075, C-083]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors compile reported results across several financial subdomains. For portfolio optimization, cited work using quantum annealers and variational algorithms reports that optimized reverse annealing can be more than 100× faster than forward annealing, that gate‑model rebalancing on small portfolios is feasible on NISQ devices and can find portfolios within 5% of optimal adjusted returns, and that VQE can yield solutions close to exact ones under suitable hyperparameters. In market prediction and trading, they report studies where quantum deep hedging policies based on QNNs significantly outperform Black–Scholes hedges, quantum‑assisted feature selection improves predictive accuracy with lower dimensionality, quantum Elman networks achieve similar prediction quality with much smaller hidden/context layers, and hybrid deep QNNs demonstrate high forecasting accuracy across regression and extrapolation tasks, including for churn prediction and stock prediction. For pricing, the survey cites evidence that qPCA reduces noisy factors in interest‑rate models, qGAN‑based loading is gate‑efficient, QAE-based methods achieve quadratic or near-quadratic speedups for option pricing, shallow circuits can accurately price European and Asian options, unary encodings may be advantageous on near‑term devices, and several quantum approaches (including on IBM Q hardware) demonstrate quadratic or exponential speedups in steps or dimensionality for Monte Carlo and PDE‑based pricing. In risk management and fraud/credit analytics, the authors report that QAE-based methods offer near‑quadratic speedups for VaR and CVaR estimation, quantum feature selection on real credit risk data can match or surpass state‑of‑the‑art classical methods, quantum kernels can improve average precision as system size grows, QSVMs can deliver lower false positives and higher precision in fraud detection, QBoost offers interpretability benefits over classical boosting, quantum GNNs achieve AUC around 0.85 in graph‑based fraud detection, and quantum GAN and kernel setups show competitive or superior performance on anomaly detection benchmarks.
    [codes: C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053, C-054, C-055, C-056, C-057, C-058, C-059, C-061, C-062, C-063, C-064, C-065, C-066, C-067, C-068, C-069, C-070, C-071, C-072, C-076, C-079, C-081, C-084, C-085]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Across the surveyed studies, quantum methods are usually benchmarked against classical baselines. For optimization, the authors describe QA and VQE approaches that come close to or match the performance of existing classical solvers on problems of comparable size, and note that VQE can approximate exact solutions under good hyperparameter choices. In trading and hedging, QNN-based deep hedging strategies reportedly significantly outperform the Black–Scholes hedge, and quantum‑assisted feature selection and QENN architectures match or exceed classical models with fewer parameters. In risk and fraud analysis, QAE‑based VaR/CVaR estimation is claimed to surpass classical Monte Carlo in efficiency, quantum feature selection for credit risk can compete with or surpass state‑of‑the‑art classical methods, quantum kernels can outperform standard approaches in average precision as problem size grows, and QSVMs are reported to have lower false positives and higher precision than both classical and other quantum baselines. Some comparisons are negative or neutral: QSVMs in certain stock prediction experiments do not show clear advantages over classical SVMs, and in a blockchain phishing study no performance improvement is observed when increasing the number of qubits, which tempers expectations of uniform quantum superiority.
    [codes: C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053, C-054, C-055, C-056, C-057, C-059, C-060, C-063, C-066, C-067, C-068, C-069, C-071, C-072, C-076, C-079, C-081, C-084, C-085]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly acknowledges that current quantum hardware and algorithms face substantial limitations that constrain practical impact. At a general level, the authors stress that existing NISQ devices and simulators are still far from demonstrating robust quantum advantage, being restricted by limited qubit counts, noise, and decoherence. They note that scalability, hardware limits, and algorithmic complexity remain overarching challenges. In specific applications, they report that current hardware issues hindered QAOA-based FX reserves management to the point that only a few demonstrations succeeded even for a five-variable problem, and that available QPUs were not sufficiently stable or error‑tolerant for fraud detection at realistic scales. They also highlight more nuanced limitations in QML experiments: QSVMs show no clear performance advantage over classical SVMs in some stock prediction tasks, increased qubit counts did not yield better performance in a blockchain phishing detection setting, and certain speedup claims are theoretical or emulator-based rather than demonstrated on large‑scale, noisy hardware. The discussion of Black–Scholes assumptions and the curse of dimensionality in classical models further contextualizes where quantum methods are intended to help, while implicitly acknowledging that both classical and quantum approaches can be limited by modelling assumptions and high dimensional data.
    [codes: C-014, C-020, C-036, C-037, C-060, C-077, C-078, C-080, C-086]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors argue that overcoming hardware scalability, noise, and algorithmic complexity will be crucial to realize the potential of QML in finance, explicitly calling for continued research on more scalable algorithms and more capable devices. They also point to specific methodological avenues, such as further exploring unary encodings for option pricing which may offer practical advantages on near‑term hardware, and investigating how quantum noise and other QML properties might be harnessed to improve fairness in financial decision systems. The conclusion frames the field as a bidirectional exchange where financial problems can inspire new quantum methods, implicitly encouraging future research at this interdisciplinary interface.
    [codes: C-065, C-082, C-087, C-088]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions itself as an extensive, structured overview of quantum machine learning applications in quantitative finance, spanning portfolio optimization, trading, pricing, risk management, and fraud/anomaly detection. Its contribution lies in synthesizing technical background in finance and ML (e.g., definitions of portfolio optimization, VaR/CVaR, fraud as anomaly detection, feature selection/extraction, and ML evaluation metrics) with the building blocks of quantum and hybrid QML algorithms, then mapping these systematically onto financial use cases. The authors also emphasize the emerging, NISQ‑era perspective on QML and highlight a two‑way relationship where quantitative finance not only benefits from but also inspires the development of quantum methods, which they present as a distinctive framing of the field’s current state.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-031, C-038, C-043, C-088]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the survey dedicates space to explaining standard ML workflows and concepts (training pipeline, curse of dimensionality, feature selection and extraction, supervised/unsupervised/RL paradigms, neural network structures, and evaluation metrics like ROC/AUC), providing readers with the conceptual tools to assess QML studies. In the quantum risk and credit‑risk sections, the authors note papers that explicitly examine scalability and expected runtime, describe precise classifier and metric choices (e.g., logistic regression with log‑loss, average precision, false positives, interpretability), and report experiments on real‑world datasets, including credit risk and fraud detection data. They also mention works that test quantum kernels both in simulation and on real hardware, and a QML fairness verification framework that explores the impact of quantum noise, which signals attention to robustness and ethical aspects beyond raw accuracy. However, because this is a survey, it generally relays other authors’ methodological setups rather than enforcing a unified experimental protocol, and many reported results are drawn from small‑scale or idealized simulations, as suggested by repeated emphasis on NISQ limitations and hardware instability.
    [codes: C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-073, C-075, C-082, C-083]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Several codes provide core technical or definitional background but are not central to the survey’s comparative or evaluative claims. These include detailed formulations of mean–variance portfolio optimization and constrained/binary variants, the identification of algorithmic trading as quantitative, ML‑driven automation, and specific formal results about quantum subroutines (e.g., QAE, HHL, quantum PCA) that underlie many of the reviewed applications. They contribute to the paper’s pedagogical role rather than to specific findings or limitations.

=== PAPER 8d9fbaf6510b (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames a forecasting problem where, given a univariate time series up to time n, the task is to estimate the next value X_{n+1} using a quantum-walk-based modelling framework. The estimation target is explicitly the one-step-ahead value, and the authors illustrate this with small-n cases (n = 0, 1, 2).
    [codes: C-022, C-026, C-027, C-028]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors construct a time-series model based on a quantum walk driven by quantum Bernoulli noise, whose coin space H is infinite dimensional and whose state space is ℓ2(ℤ, H) with normalized state vectors. The time evolution of the walk is governed by a specified evolution equation, and the position distribution is defined as a countable probability distribution on ℤ; on top of this, a time-dependent evaluation function is introduced to connect the quantum-walk dynamics to forecasting. The resulting procedure is a quantum-inspired estimation algorithm where model parameters are obtained by minimizing this evaluation function and then using the corresponding quantum expectation of position as the forecast, averaging expectations when the minimizer is not unique.
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-025]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper states that it illustrates the basic properties of the proposed time-series model and provides several worked examples. For n = 0, 1, and 2, the authors derive explicit evaluation functions for the estimation procedure and analyze the minimizers: in one case the evaluation function V(θ) attains a unique minimum, leading to a specific estimated value (reported as X̂ = 0); in another case, the minimum is attained at two parameter values, and the estimated value coincides with the observed X2. These example-based outcomes are summarized in a table of estimated values.
    [codes: C-003, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors note that classical time-series models such as ARMA and GARCH play an important role in economics and finance, thereby situating their approach in relation to established methods. They also cite Konno’s prior quantum-walk-based time-series model and its interesting properties as a conceptual reference point for their work, but no direct empirical performance comparison with classical models is reported.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-010]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: Not explicitly addressed in the available coded excerpts. The paper mentions non-classical properties of quantum walks as motivation but does not, in the coded material, articulate concrete limitations of the proposed model, its scalability, or its applicability to real financial data.
    [codes: C-006]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Not addressed in this paper.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: Building on Konno’s earlier time-series model constructed from quantum walks, the paper claims to introduce a new time-series modelling framework based on a quantum walk driven by quantum Bernoulli noise and to illustrate its basic properties through analytical examples. The infinite-dimensional coin space and the specific evaluation-function-based estimation algorithm are presented as distinctive elements of this construction.
    [codes: C-003, C-009, C-010, C-015, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-025]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: The study is analytical and example-based rather than empirical: it focuses on defining the QBN-based quantum walk, its state space ℓ2(ℤ, H), time evolution, and probability distribution, and on deriving closed-form evaluation functions for small-n examples. The estimation algorithm is described stepwise but is only demonstrated on toy cases with very short sequences (n = 0, 1, 2), and no real financial dataset, numerical benchmarking, or quantitative error metrics are reported in the coded material.
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-034]

QSM uses superposition to encode up/down and magnitude information for single-asset price movements, while EAM uses an entanglement-inspired joint state space over four outcomes (up/up, up/down, down/up, down/down) and a correlation formula derived from these probabilities; in practice, all probabilities are estimated from historical sign frequencies and simulated classically.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-008, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-019, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-037, C-039, C-040]

For the EAM, they provide joint probabilities for the four up/down combinations between AAPL and MSFT, from which they compute a positive correlation of about 0.37, interpreted as the stocks tending to move in the same direction. In the discussion, they claim that the enhanced QSM and EAM yield more accurate and insightful predictions by capturing complex interdependencies.

They also claim zero data exposure due to off-chain storage and zk-SNARK-protected on-chain hashes, and report application-specific results such as 96% accuracy for credit scoring and a 98% detection rate for DeFi fraud, alongside a qubit-scaling advantage of O(log2 d), exemplified by using 5 qubits for 23-dimensional FICO data.

=== PAPER 910eaf0e9de4 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as enabling collaborative training of quantum machine learning models on sensitive data without centralizing that data, noting that strong quantum models can efficiently tackle challenging, high-dimensional tasks but that centralized QML creates acute privacy and compliance risks (e.g., leakage, adversarial access, and violations of GDPR/HIPAA). It motivates a federated quantum learning setting where multiple clients in privacy-critical domains, including financial forecasting and quantum finance, jointly train models while keeping their local datasets confidential.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-003, C-026, C-050, C-053]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is a hybrid quantum–classical privacy-preserving quantum federated learning (PQFL) framework in which each client trains a parameterized quantum circuit (e.g., QSVM-, VQC-, QCNN-style models) locally, encodes classical data into quantum states via a feature encoding circuit, computes gradients using the parameter-shift rule, and updates parameters with a classical optimizer such as SGD or Adam before sending encrypted updates. Quantum Homomorphic Encryption is used so the server can aggregate encrypted model updates without decryption, leveraging QHE linearity for secure summation, while Quantum Differential Privacy adds calibrated quantum or depolarizing/Pauli noise to model updates with noise parameters tied to a privacy budget; the overall workflow integrates local quantum training, encryption, and QDP into a unified protocol evaluated in hybrid quantum–classical simulation environments.
    [codes: C-006, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-051, C-052]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the authors report that centralized QML achieves about 91.4% accuracy, PQFL without QDP achieves a slightly reduced 90.1%, and PQFL with QDP further drops to 88.7%, which they characterize as a tolerable trade-off for added privacy at ε=1.2. They state that QHE and QDP together improve safety against eavesdropping and inference attacks and claim that PQFL maintains system scalability while introducing moderate additional communication overhead (e.g., 920–960 KB per round) and only marginal reductions in qubit utilization (from roughly 75% down to 70–72%), concluding that PQFL provides a well-balanced trade-off between accuracy, privacy, and overhead and is viable for privacy-sensitive applications such as quantum finance.
    [codes: C-015, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-005, C-050]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper positions its work against both centralized QML and classical secure federated learning, noting that conventional encryption and secure computation techniques from classical FL cannot be directly used in the quantum realm and that prior QML results suggest potential advantages in pattern recognition and optimization on high-dimensional data. However, the reported quantitative comparisons focus on centralized quantum baselines rather than classical ML baselines, and classical techniques are mainly discussed as conceptual precursors rather than direct performance comparators.
    [codes: C-011, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-041]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors highlight that existing secure FL methods and privacy-enhancing tools designed for classical settings cannot be straightforwardly applied in quantum systems, necessitating new mechanisms for quantum data and models. They also identify limitations in prior quantum FL and related privacy approaches that motivate their design: earlier quantum FL schemes lacked formal privacy guarantees; encrypting quantum models (e.g., in CryptoQFL) can enable secure aggregation but suffers from high computation time; quantum secure aggregation (QSA) struggled to scale to many clients and ensure fault tolerance; and hybrid transfer learning approaches required pretraining classical models and did not employ native quantum privacy techniques, leaving privacy gaps. Additionally, they note that QHE alone does not address inference attacks on decrypted models, hence the need for QDP to mitigate post-decryption risks.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-034]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Not addressed in this paper.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The central claimed contribution is the PQFL framework, which explicitly addresses gaps in prior quantum federated learning by integrating Quantum Homomorphic Encryption for secure aggregation and Quantum Differential Privacy for formal, noise-based protection against inference attacks, thereby targeting privacy, fault tolerance, and communication challenges in distributed quantum model training. The authors present PQFL as a practical and scalable approach for privacy-preserving quantum learning in sensitive domains, aligning with broader trends toward confidentiality in machine learning for sectors such as healthcare, technology, and finance.
    [codes: C-012, C-013, C-024, C-031, C-034, C-039, C-040, C-048, C-050, C-053]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is implemented and evaluated in hybrid quantum–classical simulation environments rather than on physical quantum hardware, with local client-side training of parameterized quantum circuits, gradient estimation via the parameter-shift rule, and classical optimizers for parameter updates. The experimental analysis reports accuracy, communication overhead, qubit utilization, and privacy budget ε, and interprets the overhead from encryption and QDP noise as moderate with marginal hardware cost; however, datasets are described in generic terms (e.g., healthcare, genomics, finance) rather than through concrete, domain-specific benchmarks, and no task-specific financial dataset or real-world deployment details are provided.
    [codes: C-014, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-039, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper reiterates that PQFL enables multiple clients to jointly train quantum models while maintaining data confidentiality and keeping local datasets within client boundaries, and that QHE-based encryption means no decryption is needed during communication, which is presented as strengthening resistance to eavesdropping and inference attacks in line with a broader move toward confidentiality across sectors. These points emphasize the cross-sectoral applicability (including finance) and security orientation of the framework beyond purely algorithmic contributions.
    [codes: C-003, C-009, C-018, C-021, C-026, C-031, C-040, C-051, C-052, C-053]

=== PAPER 9170a0c2d3a2 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames its main finance problem as a small-scale Markowitz-style portfolio optimization, where the goal is to maximize expected return while minimizing risk, and formulates this as a QUBO/Ising Hamiltonian whose ground state corresponds to the optimal discrete asset allocation vector solved via VQE on quantum hardware.
    [codes: C-022, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study focuses on variational quantum algorithms, specifically VQE for portfolio optimization and VQC for Iris classification, implemented on real IBM quantum devices using TwoLocal and RealAmplitudes ansatz families with different entanglement structures (full, linear, circular, pairwise), ZZ feature maps for VQC, and COBYLA as the optimizer selected after comparative testing. The authors also develop a heuristic metric combining transpiled circuit depth, quantum volume, and qubit-usage ratios to guide topology- and hardware-aware ansatz selection.
    [codes: C-006, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-029, C-031, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the authors find that hardware topology significantly affects VQE and VQC performance, with more complex ansatz connectivity yielding greater expressiveness but also causing transpilation-induced SWAP overhead that increases depth and error, so a balance between expressiveness and resource cost is needed. Across IBM devices, higher quantum volume is associated with better convergence and more stable results for both VQE and VQC, whereas low-volume hardware performs better with simpler, shallower ansatz. On IBM Cairo, VQC often exhibits barren plateaus that severely degrade classification quality, but carefully choosing local qubit clusters and qubit arrangements can sometimes allow training to escape these plateaus, and the proposed heuristic score generally predicts favorable hardware–ansatz combinations such as ibm guadalupe.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-007, C-008, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-046, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The VQE-based portfolio optimization is formulated so that the ground state of the Ising Hamiltonian corresponds to the classical optimal allocation, and the authors state that variational quantum algorithms have the potential to surpass traditional classical algorithms on various problems; however, in this work they primarily compare convergence behavior to the classical optimum rather than claiming any realized speedup or advantage over classical solvers.
    [codes: C-001, C-024, C-028]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that the noise and structural limitations of current quantum hardware, including device-specific topology and single-gate error rates, constrain the performance of VQAs and can induce phenomena like barren plateaus that hinder training. They also highlight that transpilation overhead from non-native connectivity, via inserted SWAP gates, increases circuit depth and error accumulation, making complex entanglement patterns challenging on today’s devices.
    [codes: C-002, C-010, C-011, C-014, C-015, C-037, C-039, C-045, C-048, C-050]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors suggest systematically exploring different qubit arrangements and selections as a mitigation strategy for vanishing gradients and barren plateaus in quantum machine learning algorithms such as VQC, implying that topology-aware qubit mapping could be further optimized.
    [codes: C-049]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to contribute an empirical analysis of how quantum hardware properties—particularly topology, quantum volume, and noise—affect the performance of VQE and VQC, and to derive from these experiments a heuristic metric function that aids in selecting an appropriate ansatz structure for a given quantum device, emphasizing the need for topology-aware ansatz design to balance expressiveness and transpilation cost.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-034, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-045]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses two benchmark tasks—VQE portfolio optimization with real market data and VQC on the Iris dataset—and evaluates multiple ansatz families and entanglement structures on real IBM hardware with a fixed medium transpilation optimization level. The optimizer (COBYLA) and learning rate are chosen based on observed convergence performance, and the heuristic metric is empirically calibrated using statistics such as mean transpiled circuit depth, quantum volume, and qubit-count ratios; the analysis of IBM Cairo further examines multiple local qubit selections to study topology and noise effects on training dynamics.
    [codes: C-006, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-036, C-037, C-040, C-041, C-044, C-046, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper also provides broader conceptual context, noting that highly entangled ansatz can offer higher expressive power for problem solving, that barren plateaus in VQA training can be exacerbated by noise, circuit complexity, and qubit connectivity, and that even gradient-free optimizers can suffer exponential suppression of convergence in such landscapes.
    [codes: C-012, C-014, C-015]

=== PAPER 9405b3330b09 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum computing as an emerging technology expected to disrupt business sectors, with finance anticipated as one of the earliest beneficiaries, particularly for cases where classical methods struggle, such as NP-hard finance problems like portfolio optimization. Within this broad context, the concrete problem tackled is a continuous-variable prediction task in asset pricing, instantiated as prediction of property prices using the Boston Housing dataset. The task is cast as a supervised regression problem amenable to quantum machine learning via hybrid quantum neural networks.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-021, C-022, C-026, C-027, C-033]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use hybrid quantum-classical neural networks where quantum neural networks are implemented as variational quantum circuits that process continuous degrees of freedom, embedded in a three-stage QNN pipeline consisting of feature encoding, parametrized quantum processing, and measurement with possible post-processing. Classical feature vectors are mapped to quantum states via unitary feature encoding (with three reviewed options: qubit/basis, angle, and amplitude encoding) followed by a parametrized ansatz circuit whose parameters are trained using gradient-descent–style numerical optimization, and outputs are obtained as expectation values of observables that serve as model predictions. For the main qubit-based hybrid model, they select angle encoding (AngleEmbedding) and a StronglyEntanglingLayers ansatz within PennyLane, placing the quantum layer between classical input and output layers; they also implement a photonic continuous-variable QNN using Strawberry Fields with DisplacementEmbedding, CVNeuralNetLayers including a Kerr nonlinearity, and integrate this into a hybrid neural architecture. Training is done with MSE loss on standardized and PCA-reduced features, and the hybrid approach is explicitly argued to be suitable for the NISQ era because it reduces qubit count and circuit depth demands.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-016, C-019, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the qubit-based task, the first hybrid quantum neural network model is reported to perform slightly better than a similarly structured classical neural network, with the authors noting that the QNN seems to generalize slightly better and produces predicted property prices whose variability more closely matches the targets. However, this hybrid model requires about three times longer training time compared to the classical NN. In contrast, the photonic continuous-variable QNN, constrained to very few input features, is described as essentially failing to learn anything meaningful.
    [codes: C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-040, C-046]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The study includes a classical neural network baseline with architecture and hyperparameters kept as similar as possible to the hybrid QNN to enable a fair comparison. Under these matched settings, the hybrid QNN is said to achieve slightly better performance and generalization than the classical NN, but at the cost of roughly triple the training time. The classical model is explicitly characterized as having generalized less well than the hybrid QNN on the property price prediction task.
    [codes: C-034, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: Several limitations are acknowledged at both the methodological and experimental levels. At the encoding level, qubit/basis encoding is described as mathematically simple but potentially limiting the expressive power of the model, while amplitude encoding is recognized as information-efficient yet practically difficult due to the lack of efficient state preparation methods; these tradeoffs motivate their choice of angle encoding. On the optimization side, the authors highlight the barren plateau problem for parametrized quantum circuits, where the variance of gradients vanishes exponentially with qubit number and depth, leading to extremely flat loss landscapes and making training difficult. For the photonic continuous-variable model, substantial computational constraints of the Strawberry Fields Fock backend are reported: simulations with six features ran out of memory, with five features they timed out after more than ten hours of training, and even the three-feature configuration that completed is described as having "not learnt anything at all." More broadly, they note that the NISQ context and current simulators constrain the size and complexity of circuits they can explore.
    [codes: C-012, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-046]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future research, the authors propose extending these experiments to large-scale quantum computers and actual QPUs when available, suggesting that more complex QNN architectures could then be explored. They also point to experimenting with different feature encodings and alternative ansatz designs as potential ways to improve performance. On the photonic side, they recommend investigating different continuous-variable QNN ansatzes and approaches and explicitly suggest leveraging higher-end photonic quantum hardware such as Xanadu’s Borealis to overcome current simulation limits.
    [codes: C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is positioned as presenting a quantum machine learning approach to continuous-variable prediction in a finance-relevant asset pricing use case via hybrid quantum neural networks, including both a qubit-based hybrid model and a photonic continuous-variable hybrid model. Within the broader claim that quantum computing may benefit finance, the work demonstrates a concrete hybrid QNN architecture for property price prediction and reports preliminary comparative behavior against a classical neural network.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-021, C-022, C-035, C-036, C-041, C-043]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper gives a reasonably explicit description of the QNN pipeline and encoding choices, including a review of encoding schemes (qubit, angle, amplitude) and quantitative circuit descriptors like expressability via KL divergence and entangling capability via the Meyer–Wallach measure, although it is not fully clear to what extent these metrics are empirically instantiated versus conceptual. Data handling is described: the Boston Housing dataset with 13 original features and 506 samples is standardized (mean and variance removed) and reduced via PCA to nine components explaining at least 95% variance, forming the inputs to the qubit-based hybrid and classical models; for the photonic model, feature count is further constrained by simulation limits. The software stack is clearly enumerated—PennyLane for differentiable hybrid programming, Strawberry Fields for continuous-variable photonic simulation, and TensorFlow Quantum/Keras for QNN design—supporting potential reproducibility, though no explicit code repository is cited. Experimental design includes matching most architecture and training parameters between the hybrid and classical neural networks to enable a fair comparison, and using mean squared error as an appropriate loss for the regression task, but reported results remain mostly qualitative (e.g., "slightly better" performance) without numerical metrics.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-019, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all codes were assigned to other dimensions.
    [codes: —]

=== PAPER 946a6e1b2725 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames a broad computational problem: classical machine learning is increasingly constrained by scalability and algorithmic efficiency limits, motivating exploration of quantum artificial intelligence (QAI) to overcome these bottlenecks and enhance learning performance in complex, high-dimensional problem spaces, including but not limited to finance. It positions quantum computing as a potential paradigm shift that leverages superposition, entanglement, and large quantum state spaces to address these issues.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-015, C-016, C-035]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: As a conceptual review, the paper surveys multiple quantum approaches for AI rather than implementing a specific method. It describes quantum support vector machines based on quantum-enhanced kernel estimation and quantum kernel methods for computing inner products in Hilbert space, quantum neural networks that integrate quantum circuits with classical training, and variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) as a key near-term framework using a hybrid quantum–classical optimization loop. It also covers quantum PCA for dimensionality reduction and emphasizes hybrid quantum–classical architectures as the preferred design in the NISQ era.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-019, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper does not present empirical or quantitative results; instead, it conceptually argues that QAI approaches could accelerate optimization, improve generalization in high-dimensional spaces, and provide potential speedups in tasks such as dimensionality reduction and classification. Reported performance advantages are framed as prospective or theoretical rather than as experimentally validated findings of this study.
    [codes: C-011, C-016, C-026, C-028, C-030, C-036, C-047]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Comparisons to classical methods are high-level and conceptual: the authors contrast classical ML’s scalability and efficiency limitations with quantum computing’s exponential state space and non-classical correlations, suggesting that QAI may overcome classical bottlenecks and provide better classification boundaries or speedups in tasks like PCA. Hybrid quantum–classical approaches are presented as a pragmatic way to combine strengths of both paradigms, but no empirical benchmarking against specific classical baselines is reported.
    [codes: C-002, C-008, C-011, C-015, C-016, C-025, C-026, C-030, C-031, C-043, C-048]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges extensive limitations across hardware, algorithms, and evaluation. On hardware, current NISQ devices suffer from limited qubit counts, noise, decoherence, short coherence times, and high gate error rates, making deep circuits impractical. On the algorithmic side, QAI faces issues of algorithmic stability, notably barren plateaus in variational quantum algorithms that hinder training, as well as challenges around data encoding/quantum feature mapping and readout. The authors stress that classical ML scalability constraints motivate QAI but also highlight that QAI itself is nascent, lacks standardized benchmarks for quantum advantage, generalizability, and robustness to noise, and must contend with broader ethical concerns around bias, fairness, security, and accountability. More generally, they describe implementation barriers such as circuit depth, hardware limitations, and data encoding as key obstacles to practical QML deployment.

=== PAPER 953d9d489a99 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as intelligent time-series prediction on nonlinear and often unpredictable financial (and related) data, motivated by the growing magnitude and heterogeneity of emerging data systems and the computational expense of conventional machine and deep learning methods. Time-series forecasting is positioned as critical for financial services and other domains, and the work explores whether a hybrid quantum–classical approach can better represent complex temporal patterns. The problem is formulated as a supervised forecasting task where financial time-series are encoded into quantum states and processed within a hybrid model.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-009, C-013, C-014, C-017, C-037]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach uses a Qiskit-based variational quantum circuit with parameterized rotation gates, entanglement layers, and a quantum feature map that encodes normalized, windowed time-series via angle encoding into a higher-dimensional Hilbert space. Expectation values from circuit measurements are turned into classical feature vectors, and the circuit parameters are trained via the parameter-shift rule within a joint loop where a Python-side optimizer (Adam/SGD) updates both quantum and classical parameters under a hybrid loss that balances quantum and classical contributions. Implementation relies on Python 3.10 with Pandas, Qiskit, NumPy, and the Qiskit Aer simulator, with provisions to substitute a cloud backend and to support batching, mini-batching, and parallel runs for hyperparameter search.
    [codes: C-002, C-012, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-036, C-039, C-044, C-047]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that their hybrid model achieves a prediction accuracy of 93.7%, an MSE of 0.014, and a correlation coefficient of 0.92 on evaluated datasets, with training loss generally converging after about 35 iterations. They claim reduced training time (~22%) and execution latency (~18%) relative to classical baselines, and scalability tests over multi-qubit simulations suggest accuracy is maintained as runtime grows with circuit depth across varying data sizes. Ablation analyses attribute most of the accuracy gains to the quantum feature mapping and show that removing quantum encoding extends convergence and reduces accuracy toward the baseline.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-006, C-019, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-048]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The hybrid quantum–classical model is directly compared to conventional neural network baselines, including LSTM, GRU, and a shallow feedforward network that share the same preprocessing. The authors report that the hybrid model attains higher prediction accuracy (93.7% versus 89.3% for the main classical baseline), along with approximately 22% lower training time and 18% lower execution latency. They also note that in ablation tests, removing quantum encoding degrades performance to around the classical baseline and increases the number of epochs to converge, suggesting the quantum components contribute to the observed gains.
    [codes: C-004, C-019, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-046, C-048]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that their study depends primarily on quantum circuit simulators, which limits claims about real hardware performance and necessitates future validation on physical devices with appropriate noise handling. They further note that their approach will require higher noise tolerance to be practical on real quantum backends and imply that current results may not fully reflect hardware-induced variability.
    [codes: C-050]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions include validating the framework on real quantum hardware backends instead of simulators, exploring transfer learning to adapt the hybrid model across multiple domains, and optimizing data encoding schemes to further enhance predictive performance. The authors also suggest that their Python-based design can facilitate such extensions by allowing easy modification of backends and encoding components.
    [codes: C-031, C-051]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims as its core contribution a Python-interfaced hybrid quantum–classical model that integrates quantum circuit simulation with classical optimization within a single workflow for smart time-series prediction, emphasizing Python's role as a bridge between quantum programming and machine learning systems. They highlight improved prediction accuracy, reduced training time, and enhanced model stability over classical neural networks, and present the architecture as a modular, reproducible framework that showcases how hybrid QML can leverage quantum feature maps to reveal patterns that classical networks might miss.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-011, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-028, C-052]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses both synthetic and real-time (including financial) time-series, with cleaning, normalization, windowing, and z-score scaling, followed by a 70%-15%-15% train/validation/test split to structure evaluation. Metrics include MSE, correlation coefficient, runtime, RAM usage, training time, and execution latency, and convergence behavior is reported via loss curves that stabilize after about 35 iterations. The workflow incorporates batching/mini-batching for large datasets, parallel runs for hyperparameter search, and explicit logging, error handling, and checkpointing to support rollback and reproducibility; error bars are reported to capture variability across seeds and small hardware-noise tests, and the implementation is described as modular and reproducible, built on standard Python tooling (Pandas, NumPy, Qiskit).

They also emphasize Python and Qiskit as enabling experimentation by flexibly linking quantum programs with machine learning systems.

It argues that classical models such as Black–Scholes and Markowitz rely on simplifying assumptions (efficient markets, normal returns) that often fail in practice, motivating the use of quantum computing’s parallelism and superposition to accelerate and improve market forecasting, portfolio optimization, risk analysis, and fraud detection.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles financial fraud detection, motivated by the large financial and reputational risks and high false-positive rates faced by institutions, and formulates it as a binary classification task over financial transactions to distinguish suspicious from non-suspicious activity. It positions this as a testbed to comparatively assess classical and quantum-hybrid machine learning models for fraud detection in an AML context.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-015]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study evaluates three quantum-hybrid approaches: a Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) that uses a quantum circuit to compute a kernel matrix, a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) built from a quantum feature map plus a trainable parametrised quantum circuit optimized classically, and a Hybrid Quantum Neural Network (HQNN) that embeds a variational quantum circuit as a hidden layer within a classical deep neural network. All quantum components are implemented via PennyLane in a way that is compatible with execution on real quantum hardware, even though only simulators are used in the experiments.
    [codes: C-004, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-036]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The main empirical finding is that classical tree-based models, especially Random Forest, achieve the strongest performance, reaching about 97.3% accuracy and an F-measure around 86.9%, and are reported as the best overall method on the fraud detection task. Among the quantum models, QSVM is the most promising, delivering relatively high precision (~77%) and a low false-positive rate (~1.36%), but with reduced recall and substantial computational overhead, while the other quantum-hybrid models perform markedly worse. Overall, the authors conclude that classical ensemble methods remain the preferred option for reliable fraud detection in this setting.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-037, C-041, C-045]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper performs a direct comparison between four classical baselines—Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost—and the three quantum-hybrid models, finding that classical tree ensembles, especially Random Forest, significantly outperform all quantum counterparts on accuracy, F-measure, and recall, while maintaining competitive false-positive rates. The discussion attributes this advantage partly to the richness of the engineered behavioural features, which classical ensemble models can exploit effectively, and it emphasizes a deployment philosophy in which robust classical models serve as the backbone, with quantum components treated as optional enhancements.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-022, C-006, C-037, C-038, C-029, C-045]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations: the experiments use only simulated quantum backends and do not run on real quantum hardware, although the implementation is hardware-compatible. They explicitly state that current quantum models underperform, citing algorithmic immaturity, difficulties in training variational circuits, and substantial computational overhead. They further note that the synthetic IBM AML dataset, even with complex behavioural features, may lack the specific structure needed to reveal any quantum advantage. More broadly, they conclude that quantum AI is not yet mature enough to outperform traditional algorithms in this practical, high-stakes fraud detection domain.
    [codes: C-035, C-039, C-040, C-046]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions include designing more tailored variational ansätze and adaptive feature maps to improve quantum model expressiveness without incurring training instabilities, exploring hybrid temporal architectures that combine temporal feature extraction (e.g., LSTMs) with variational quantum circuits, and using quantum autoencoders or metaheuristic feature selection to compress or select informative features. The authors also position the FD4QC architecture as a roadmap for gradually integrating more capable quantum components into financial security systems as the technology matures.
    [codes: C-042, C-043, C-044, C-047]

The FD4QC architecture is designed as an API-driven, classical-first system with automatic rerouting to classical surrogates if quantum backends fail and explicit flags indicating whether predictions come from classical or quantum engines, supporting operational robustness and auditability. === PAPER 99d3efa89dee (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies quantum generative models for learning low-dimensional probability distributions, including financial stock-return data, framing generative modeling as approximating an unknown target distribution Q by a parametric model P(θ) and optimizing the Kullback–Leibler divergence between them. The work is motivated by an industrial consortium that wants to understand the potential value of quantum generative models in practical sectors and by perceived limitations of classical GANs for complex distributions.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-009, C-017, C-013]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study benchmarks two main quantum training paradigms—Quantum Circuit Born Machines (QCBM), which learn a unitary U(θ) to encode the target distribution and are trained by directly minimizing KL divergence, and Quantum GANs (QGAN), which use a quantum generator and a classical discriminator. It compares continuous circuit architectures that output expectation values and require external noise with discrete architectures that encode the distribution in measurement probabilities, including a specialized copula variant that enforces uniform marginals. The authors explore different data normalizations (min–max and probability integral transform), with PIT naturally aligned to the copula architecture, and implement QCBMs with CMA-ES and QGANs with gradient-descent-based optimizers.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-029, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across over 1200 numerical experiments, the authors report that quantum models generally achieve comparable or better KL divergence with similar or fewer parameters than classical baselines, with extreme cases showing two orders of magnitude parameter reduction and a concrete example where a QGAN discrete copula model with PIT achieves KL 0.029 using 54 parameters versus a classical GAN’s 0.089 with 9475 parameters. They find that increasing the number of parameters systematically reduces KL divergence, that discrete copula architectures paired with PIT consistently deliver the best performance (especially in 2D) and efficient one-shot sampling, and that QGANs tend to perform slightly better than QCBMs though architectural choices and normalization have a larger impact. The authors also observe that discrete models are faster to train and sample but use more qubits, while continuous models are smaller but would take substantially longer to run on hardware.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-028, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper directly compares quantum generative models against classical GANs using KL divergence and parameter counts, noting that quantum models require similar or fewer parameters across all datasets and, in extreme cases, two orders of magnitude fewer. For the X and O synthetic datasets in both 2D and 3D, all quantum models outperform classical models with similar parameter budgets, with the discrete copula architecture in particular consistently outperforming classical counterparts. A highlighted example shows a classical GAN with min–max normalization using 9475 parameters to reach KL 0.089, whereas a QGAN with discrete copula architecture and PIT reaches KL 0.029 with only 54 parameters.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors emphasize that the stability of QGAN training is highly architecture-dependent, indicating that not all quantum configurations train reliably. They also acknowledge that the generalization capability of their generative models—how well they produce data not present in the training set—remains an open question beyond the scope of their experiments. Additionally, they note that the impact of decoherence and noise on quantum generative modeling has not been explored and must be addressed in future work, underscoring that their results are based on idealized simulations rather than noisy hardware.
    [codes: C-041, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future research directions identified by the authors include exploring the interplay between learning dynamics and generalization in higher-dimensional data settings, extending beyond the low-dimensional benchmarks used here. They also call for systematic investigation of decoherence and other noise effects on quantum generative models, implying the need for experiments on real quantum hardware or realistic noise simulations.
    [codes: C-043, C-045]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions itself as a systematic performance characterization of quantum generative models, comparing a broad range of architectures (continuous vs discrete vs discrete copula), training paradigms (QCBM vs QGAN), and preprocessing schemes (min–max vs PIT) to guide practitioners in model selection. A distinctive contribution is the introduction and empirical evaluation of a discrete copula circuit architecture tailored to PIT-transformed data, which the authors find empirically outperforms all other methods tested and exhibits improved training stability with PIT.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-007, C-011, C-012, C-016, C-038, C-039, C-042]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study is based on more than 1200 numerical experiments comparing scaling behavior by varying parameter counts and consistently evaluating performance via KL divergence between training and generated distributions. It systematically varies circuit architectures, data transformations, and training methods, using state-of-the-art optimizers (CMA-ES for QCBMs and gradient descent for QGANs) and explicitly examining trends such as decreasing KL with increasing parameters and the differential impact of PIT versus min–max normalization. The authors also articulate resource trade-offs—more qubits but faster sampling for discrete architectures versus fewer qubits but slower sampling for continuous ones—and report that their discrete designs allow single-shot sampling, which is noted as measurement-efficient and potentially relevant for hardware implementations.
    [codes: C-003, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-028, C-030, C-031, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper includes conceptual clarifications such as viewing quantum states as natural probabilistic generators due to their inherent randomness, and offers background definitions of GAN adversarial training and the role of copulas and PIT in simplifying dependence structures. It also specifies that the continuous quantum architecture requires an external source of entropy, analogous to classical generative models, and underscores that the copula circuit design enforces uniform marginals via its initialization and gate structure.
    [codes: C-010, C-018, C-023, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-029]

=== PAPER 99e391ee5e85 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets clustering of financial assets based on their correlation structure, arguing that relationships among assets are central to portfolio optimization and algorithmic trading and are naturally represented as signed, weighted graphs where both positive and negative correlations must be preserved. The clustering problem is formulated as an NP-hard signed-graph coalition structure generation task that maximizes intra-cluster edge weights, encouraging co-movement within clusters and discouraging negatively correlated pairs, and is cast into a QUBO form suitable for quantum processing.
    [codes: C-005, C-013, C-017, C-018, C-021, C-023]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose GCS-Q, a Graph-based Coalition Structure Generation algorithm that directly operates on signed, weighted correlation graphs and performs iterative partitioning via minimum cuts, using a stopping rule that dynamically infers the number of clusters. Each minimum-cut subproblem is formulated as a QUBO and solved on near-term quantum devices—primarily a D-Wave quantum annealer—with the option to use variational gate-model approaches like QAOA in hybrid workflows, enabling exploration of exponentially large solution spaces for NP-hard signed-graph clustering.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-011, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the authors report that GCS-Q consistently achieves higher clustering quality than classical baselines on both synthetic and real financial correlation graphs, measured by Adjusted Rand Index and a structural-balance penalty metric, while also determining the number of clusters automatically. On synthetic structurally balanced graphs and on real hourly Yahoo Finance data, GCS-Q attains the lowest penalty values, which the authors interpret as uncovering market structures that support diversification and mean-reversion strategies, and they further claim this constitutes the first demonstration of a quantum advantage in solution quality for practical asset clustering using real hardware. They also report that clustering 170 assets with k=10 on current hardware takes over 10 minutes, despite individual QUBO solve times being capped at one second.
    [codes: C-003, C-029, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-041]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper contrasts GCS-Q with classical clustering methods such as k-Means/k-Medoids, hierarchical clustering, PAM, and signed-graph spectral methods like SPONGE/SPONGEsym, arguing that these approaches suffer from limitations including lossy transformations of correlations into non-negative distances, manual hyperparameter tuning (especially the need to pre-specify k), and performance degradation when graphs are dense, have continuous weights, or exhibit heterogeneous cluster sizes. In experiments, PAM performs worst on synthetic data due to the correlation-to-distance transformation, and SPONGE-based methods degrade under continuous weights and stochastic cluster sizes, while GCS-Q outperforms all baselines in ARI and penalty measures even though the classical baselines are given k using the eigengap heuristic; the authors also note that prior quantum clustering work formulated a maximum clique QUBO that exceeded current annealer capacities, which GCS-Q avoids.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-012, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-036, C-042]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations: synthetic experiments are noise-free, focusing on ideal structurally balanced graphs and thus not fully capturing real-market noise; current quantum hardware and its connectivity restrict GCS-Q to roughly 175 nodes, constraining scalability; access via shared cloud infrastructure introduces latency and queue delays, leading to practical runtimes of over 10 minutes for clustering 170 assets despite per-QUBO solve times being capped at one second. They also implicitly note that their classical complexity remains O(n2^n) when executed without quantum hardware, underscoring the underlying computational difficulty.
    [codes: C-023, C-026, C-030, C-039, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work includes applying the learned clusters to downstream financial tasks such as asset allocation and empirically evaluating performance with portfolio metrics like Sharpe Ratio and returns. The authors also propose technical extensions: deploying GCS-Q on improved D-Wave hardware with Zephyr topology and better connectivity, exploring custom embeddings, leveraging gate-model quantum solvers with more qubit-efficient strategies, and benchmarking GCS-Q’s QUBO formulations against strong classical optimizers such as Gurobi.
    [codes: C-044, C-045]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty on several fronts: it introduces a data-driven GCS-Q algorithm that directly clusters signed, weighted correlation graphs without heuristic correlation-to-distance transformations, automatically infers the number of clusters, and is robust to realistic conditions like continuous edge weights and heterogeneous cluster sizes that prior work treated under more idealized assumptions. Most prominently, the authors assert that this is the first demonstration, to their knowledge, of a quantum advantage in solution quality for a practical financial task—asset clustering—validated with real quantum hardware on both synthetic and real financial datasets.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-010, C-012, C-020, C-024, C-025, C-038, C-042]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study builds signed, weighted undirected graphs from asset Pearson correlations, explicitly preserving both positive and negative relationships, and optimizes an intra-cluster weight objective that aligns with financial interpretations of co-movement and anti-correlation. Synthetic data are carefully constructed to mimic financial correlation structure with continuous signed weights and heterogeneous cluster sizes via Dirichlet allocation, while withholding noise to isolate algorithmic behavior, and real data are sourced from Yahoo Finance hourly prices with rolling log returns over a specified period. Evaluation uses ARI on synthetic data and a structural-balance penalty metric on real data, with classical baselines SPONGE, SPONGEsym, and PAM configured using the eigengap heuristic for k, and the implementation is made available as open-source code, supporting reproducibility.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Additional contextual notes include the reiteration that optimally clustering signed graphs with edge weights in [−1, +1] is NP-hard and that, when executed purely classically, GCS-Q has complexity O(n2^n), with the exponential factor arising from solving minimum cuts and the linear factor from dynamically determining the number of clusters. The authors also argue that GCS-Q’s better alignment with signed-graph structure and avoidance of idealized assumptions (such as uniform clusters and ternary edge weights) position it as particularly suitable for real-world financial correlation networks and support broader claims about the practical utility of near-term quantum computing for graph-based unsupervised learning in finance.
    [codes: C-004, C-012, C-023, C-039, C-042]
[SILO OVERLAY]
  SILO_RELEVANCE: This paper is highly relevant to quantum_ml_finance because it frames a real financial learning task as a quantum-amenable graph clustering problem and evaluates it on both synthetic and market data. Its main value for this silo is the direct mapping from financial correlation structure to QUBO/annealing workflows, plus evidence that quantum methods can outperform classical baselines on a practical asset-clustering task.
    [silo_relevance_score: high]
  KEY_POINT 1: Directly models financial relationships as a signed graph for quantum processing
    [codes: C-001, C-015, C-016, C-021  dim_source: dimension_2]
  KEY_POINT 2: Uses a quantum-native optimization path that avoids lossy correlation-to-distance preprocessing
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-012, C-022  dim_source: dimension_4]
  KEY_POINT 3: Reports improved clustering quality on financial data with automatic cluster-count selection
    [codes: C-003, C-020, C-029, C-034, C-036  dim_source: dimension_3]
