=== PAPER 9aa8ee9654b4 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as enabling privacy-preserving quantum machine learning that is robust against attacks such as membership inference by making the learning process differentially private, i.e., limiting the influence of any single training example. It focuses on demonstrating that a variational quantum classifier can be trained under differential privacy while maintaining useful accuracy, positioning this as a foundational step for secure QML applications that handle sensitive user data.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-006, C-010]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a hybrid quantum–classical model based on variational quantum circuits (VQCs), where classical differential privacy mechanisms are applied to the optimization process. Input data are encoded into quantum states via single‑qubit rotations Ry(arctan(xi)) and Rz(arctan(xi²)), and gradients of the quantum model are computed using the parameter‑shift rule before being modified by a differentially private gradient update that clips gradient norms and adds noise. Training uses the RMSProp optimizer, and all quantum circuits are executed via noise‑free classical simulation rather than on physical hardware.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-019]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that differentially private QML can protect sensitive information without significantly reducing model accuracy, successfully classifying 2D datasets and binary MNIST under various privacy levels. On the 2D "circles" task, the differentially private VQC is reported as 14% more accurate than the differentially private neural network, and in some cases differential privacy slightly improves classical accuracy. For binary MNIST, the private VQC exceeds 90% test accuracy, with accuracy for both VQCs and neural networks declining as the privacy parameter ε decreases. The authors also emphasize that the VQC achieves better accuracy than the analogous classical neural network while using only about 28% of its parameters and that there exists at least one model–dataset pair where the quantum network is more powerful than its classical counterpart.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-031]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Throughout the experiments the VQC is directly compared against a classical neural network trained with the same differential privacy mechanism. On the 2D "circles" dataset, the quantum classifier is reported as 14% more accurate than the differentially private neural network, and for binary MNIST the quantum model achieves better accuracy despite having only about a quarter of the parameters. The authors note that the differentially private VQC outperforms the classical neural network for mid‑range privacy budgets (ε between 0.4 and 1.4), and they conclude that this provides an example where the quantum neural network is more powerful than the classical model.
    [codes: C-017, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-031]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that their study relies entirely on noise‑free simulation of VQCs, which does not capture the effects of decoherence and gate errors present on real NISQ hardware. They further note that executing high‑dimensional inputs such as MNIST on current cloud‑based quantum computers would take an extremely long time, highlighting scalability and practicality challenges for near‑term deployment.
    [codes: C-028, C-029]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work proposed by the authors includes running privacy‑preserving quantum optimization on noisy simulators or actual cloud‑based quantum devices to assess robustness under realistic noise. They also suggest extending the private QML framework to additional architectures and tasks, explicitly mentioning quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) and applications such as facial recognition, where training must use large collections of unprotected personal images.
    [codes: C-026, C-027, C-030]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to provide the first proof‑of‑principle demonstration of privacy‑preserving quantum machine learning, showing that a hybrid VQC trained with a differentially private classical optimizer can maintain competitive accuracy while offering formal privacy guarantees and potential implementability on near‑term NISQ devices.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-006, C-010]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work uses standard differential privacy machinery—gradient clipping and noise addition—to train VQCs, with the privacy budget ε determined implicitly by the noise standard deviation, clipping norm, and δ parameter as formalized in their privacy accounting (Eq. 14b). Experiments span multiple 2D benchmarks with increasingly nonlinear decision boundaries to probe model capacity, and binary MNIST is compressed to a 10‑qubit representation via zero‑padding to 1024 dimensions and amplitude loading. The authors emphasize that the privacy‑preserving training procedure is straightforward to deploy, as the DP mechanism is simply added to an existing gradient‑based optimizer.
    [codes: C-007, C-011, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-025]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper also claims that its NISQ‑oriented design demonstrates potential for efficient implementation on near‑term quantum devices, even though experiments are presently limited to simulation.
    [codes: C-003]

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum computing as a potential paradigmatic leap for economics that requires timely reflection on its impacts in highly uncertain domains such as economic and financial systems, identifying a specific research gap around the methodological and epistemological role of quantum logic in economic sciences and its implications for optimization, resource allocation, portfolio design, auctions, and dynamic pricing problems.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-026]

    [codes: C-006, C-023, C-024, C-044, C-046]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Several conceptual elements fall outside the other dimensions: the paper develops an analogy between quantum measurement and the creation (rather than revelation) of uncertainty, links the Hadamard-induced superposition to Knightian uncertainty, and elaborates quantum-inspired models of cognition, preference, and game theory in which preferences are superposed and equilibria are redefined via quantum correlations; it also argues that economic computation has become structurally central to knowledge production and that economic policy must increasingly consider the cognitive state architecture of agents and the broader political implications of uneven quantum capabilities.

=== PAPER 9be7c1fe15c2 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets stock price prediction and high-frequency trading (HFT), arguing that existing classical machine-learning models struggle to process large-scale, high‑dimensional financial data and to support millisecond‑level trading decisions in modern markets. The authors frame this as a need for better prediction accuracy, execution speed, and dynamic risk management in HFT, which they propose to address using quantum machine learning (QML) capable of handling complex market dynamics in (near) real time.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-007, C-012, C-025, C-028]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The proposed approach is a hybrid quantum‑classical framework that integrates Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs), Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVMs), and Quantum Annealing (QA) within a Quantum Hybrid Trading Predictor (QHTP) pipeline. Classical components (sentiment analysis, technical indicators, multi‑head attention, residual blocks) generate features that are encoded into a parameterized quantum circuit via angle mapping, processed by a QNN using entanglement and parameterized rotations, combined with QSVM‑based classification and QA‑based trade‑execution/optimization, and finally merged with classical outputs through a dense layer to generate price predictions and trading signals.
    [codes: C-004, C-009, C-010, C-016, C-021, C-022, C-026, C-027, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that their QML‑based HFT system achieves high performance across several metrics, including execution speed efficiency of 93.57%, risk‑management efficiency of 95.15%, HFT optimization levels above 97.74%, improved flexibility of 98.14%, and forecasting accuracy up to 99.14%. They state that the hybrid model with all quantum components attains 92.5% prediction accuracy with a large reported reduction (93.57%) in performance time, and that statistical tests (paired t‑test p=0.02 and ANOVA p=0.03) indicate significant improvements in execution speed and accuracy over comparison models. They also claim that QML‑driven HFT systems are more precise, faster in execution, and more adaptable to dynamic markets, and that their framework outperforms existing QSVM, QA, and PCA‑based methods in accuracy, speed, and risk management.
    [codes: C-003, C-005, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-056, C-057, C-058, C-059]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper contrasts its QML‑HFT framework with classical models and earlier quantum‑enhanced baselines, claiming that traditional machine‑learning and HFT methods, which rely on linear assumptions, perform poorly on large, complex, real‑time financial data. Quantitatively, the authors state that their hybrid quantum model achieves 92.5% accuracy and a 93.57% performance‑time reduction over unspecified ‘classical models’, with component‑level ablations showing QSVM alone at 85.4% accuracy and QNN alone at 90.1%. In comparison with prior QSVM, QA, and PCA‑based approaches, they report relative gains of about 7.1%, 9%, and 10.4% in prediction accuracy, along with execution‑speed improvements of 52.37%, 35.77%, and 29.27%, and risk‑management efficiency gains of 51.56%, 31.36%, and 11%. They further argue that classical finance models are typically linear and struggle with complex, high‑dimensional market behavior, while QML and even quantum‑inspired models can enhance classical performance in related tasks such as churn prediction and credit risk assessment cited in their related‑work discussion.
    [codes: C-002, C-012, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-046, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053, C-056, C-057, C-058, C-059]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge multiple limitations for current QML approaches in finance and HFT. Beyond hardware, they emphasize that QML models are computationally costly to train and require specialized quantum computing environments and expertise, limiting practical adoption in industry. === PAPER 9c8acfa3bc72 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles financial regime detection in the U.S. market by formulating it as a multi‑class (and in some experiments effectively binary) classification problem and embedding it in a hybrid quantum–classical SVM framework. The quantum component is explicitly positioned as a complementary subsystem to conventional models rather than a full replacement, aiming to exploit quantum feature spaces for regime identification.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-008]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The quantum approach is a Quantum Support Vector Classifier implemented with Qiskit Machine Learning, using the Fidelity Statevector Kernel on a noiseless simulator and a six‑qubit ZZFeatureMap with three repetitions and full entanglement. Financial features are reduced via PCA to six components before being encoded into a six‑qubit Hilbert space, which the authors argue offers richer representational capacity than classical feature spaces.
    [codes: C-005, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The quantum SVM exhibits an 85.3% training accuracy but only 66.0% test accuracy, indicating an overfitting gap of about 19 percentage points and very weak minority‑class performance (Bullish regime F1 ≈ 0.20) that plateaus even when training data increase. Hybrid quantum–classical ensembles substantially improve generalization over the standalone quantum model, achieving test accuracies around 75–76% (e.g., 75.9% for a 50–50 ensemble) and minority‑class F1 scores of roughly 0.53–0.56, close to the classical SVM’s 80.43% accuracy. The study reports that classical and quantum components agree on about 62% of predictions, and that hybrid architectures maintain near‑linear training costs while avoiding the heavy runtime burden of the fully quantum kernel construction, which requires roughly one hour of training on the simulator.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-023, C-024, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical baselines include Random Forest, XGBoost, and an RBF‑kernel SVM, with XGBoost reaching about 71.8% accuracy and the classical SVM achieving the highest test accuracy of 80.43% (F1 ≈ 0.70). All classical models train in under one minute on standard CPU hardware, in stark contrast to the roughly one‑hour training time for the full QSVC pipeline. Hybrid ensembles recover more than 90% of the classical SVM’s accuracy while using fewer quantum resources and improving minority‑class detection relative to the pure quantum model, positioning hybrids as an efficient compromise rather than a clear improvement over strong classical baselines.
    [codes: C-007, C-013, C-029, C-030, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-037]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that all quantum components are run on noiseless simulated backends rather than physical quantum processors, which limits the realism of the performance and efficiency claims and leaves hardware‑specific noise and resource constraints unaddressed. They further note that quantum training incurs substantial runtime and quadratic kernel construction cost, which forces them to restrict quantum training set size and contributes to scalability concerns, though these aspects are framed mainly through observed runtimes rather than a full resource accounting.
    [codes: C-022, C-023, C-039]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future research, the paper suggests exploring adaptive weighting schemes between classical and quantum components within the hybrid ensemble, going beyond the fixed 50–50, 60–40, and related configurations studied in this work.
    [codes: C-026, C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is framed as an empirical evaluation of a hybrid quantum–classical SVM architecture for financial regime detection, where the quantum model is used as a complementary subsystem rather than a replacement, and as evidence that such hybrids can approach classical accuracy while improving minority‑regime recall and offering a more favorable accuracy–efficiency trade‑off than a purely quantum SVM. The authors also position the work conceptually by arguing that quantum‑enhanced models leverage exponentially large Hilbert‑space embeddings and by interpreting hybridization as a pragmatic intermediate frontier between conventional and quantum machine learning in finance.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-006, C-033, C-035, C-037, C-038, C-005]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses a multi‑asset macro‑financial dataset spanning the U.S. market from February 2006 to October 2025 and applies a unified transformation pipeline that includes return and volatility engineering, winsorization at the 1st and 99th percentiles, and standardized scaling for cross‑domain comparability. The experimental design employs chronological (non‑random) train–test splits to avoid information leakage and mimic forecasting conditions, macro‑averaged metrics for the three‑class structure, PCA reduction to six components before quantum encoding, SMOTE for minority‑class balancing, and a systematic multi‑metric comparison across classical, quantum, and multiple hybrid weighting configurations using deterministic weighted voting. These choices collectively support a relatively rigorous and finance‑aware evaluation, albeit on simulated quantum backends.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper reiterates the theoretical motivation that quantum‑enhanced models can embed financial data into exponentially large Hilbert spaces, which underpins but extends beyond the concrete experiments reported. It also characterizes hybridization in general terms as a pragmatic intermediate stage between fully classical and fully quantum machine learning for finance, framing the work more as a step in an ongoing methodological continuum than as a final solution.
    [codes: C-005, C-038]

=== PAPER 9fd619b02b3e (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames insurance and actuarial work as fundamentally about modeling and evaluating random risky events, and notes that growing data size and model complexity in insurance create computational challenges that motivate new approaches. Within this context, it systematically organizes insurance problems into stochastic modeling, optimization, and machine-learning-based tasks, covering non-life (e.g., policy excess, IBNR), life (e.g., contract valuation, Lee–Carter mortality forecasting, multi-period optimization), and risk management tasks (e.g., VaR, cVaR, reinsurance allocation).
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-029]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a general quantum framework where probability distributions are encoded via quantum state preparation, risk processes are analyzed with quantum stochastic simulation, collective risks are addressed with quantum optimization, and data-driven models use quantum machine learning, distinguishing NISQ-era variational methods from fault-tolerant linear-algebra-based approaches. Concretely, they discuss quantum stochastic modeling with amplitude encoding and quantum Monte Carlo, QUBO-to-Ising mappings for optimization solvable via quantum annealing and QAOA-like methods, and implement specific algorithms: a discrete quantum excess evaluation circuit using n+2 qubits, a reinsurance variance-minimization Hamiltonian optimized with a constraint-preserving ansatz and measurement-based error mitigation, and a Lee–Carter mortality solver based on quantum singular value decomposition on 4 qubits with real mortality data.
    [codes: C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper claims that quantum stochastic modeling using amplitude encoding and quantum Monte Carlo could yield exponential memory savings with a further quadratic speedup, though this is a theoretical result. In numerical simulations of the quantum excess evaluation algorithm, the estimated excess payment converges toward the truncated reference value as the number of qubits increases. On real hardware, the reinsurance allocation experiment shows the loss function decreasing during variational optimization, and the Lee–Carter QSVD experiment similarly reports decreasing loss and improved fit over optimization steps. The authors further assert that solving the Lee–Carter mortality forecasting model on a quantum processor with real mortality data constitutes the first implementation of an insurance-specific quantum algorithm on a quantum processor using real datasets and, more broadly, the first time an insurance-specific real-world data problem is experimentally solved on real quantum computers.
    [codes: C-023, C-028, C-033, C-036, C-010, C-037]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors conceptually compare their quantum stochastic modeling approach to classical Monte Carlo, asserting that amplitude encoding combined with quantum Monte Carlo can provide exponential savings in state space and a quadratic speedup over classical sampling-based methods. For the excess evaluation case, they benchmark convergence of the discrete quantum estimate toward a classically truncated integral, implying consistency with classical theoretical and truncated values, but they do not report explicit runtime benchmarks or detailed performance comparisons beyond these high-level claims.
    [codes: C-023, C-026, C-028]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges that in the NISQ era, both the number of available qubits and the allowable circuit depth are limited by noise, constraining the scale of feasible insurance computations on current hardware. It also explicitly notes that preparing quantum states corresponding to general probability distributions may require exponential resources, highlighting state preparation as a major bottleneck. Additionally, the authors point out that single-shot readout, where each shot yields only one n-bit string, greatly limits efficiency in extracting information from quantum states.
    [codes: C-038, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors outline a staged timetable for quantum computational insurance, distinguishing what may be achievable in the NISQ era versus fault-tolerant quantum computing, and express the belief that both theoretical and experimental breakthroughs in quantum insurance and actuarial science will be achieved. To mitigate current bottlenecks in encoding and readout, they suggest future use of Quantum Random Access Memory and more advanced encoding strategies to enable more efficient state preparation and data handling.

Specifically, they highlight solving the Lee–Carter mortality forecasting model as the first implementation of an insurance-specific quantum algorithm on a quantum processor with real data, and more broadly as the first time an insurance-specific real-world data problem has been experimentally solved on actual quantum hardware.

=== PAPER a052f266d945 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets accurate and efficient estimation of carbon market risk, focusing on value-at-risk (VaR) and conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) for the volatile EU emissions trading market, where price fluctuations driven by supply–demand, policy, and macroeconomic factors amplify financial risk exposure. It frames VaR and CVaR as preferred risk measures over simpler volatility or beta because they emphasize potential extreme losses in the carbon market context, and positions the task as estimating the future loss-rate distribution without strong parametric assumptions. This is motivated in part by limitations of traditional Monte Carlo methods, which require many simulations and rely on often-unrealistic distributional assumptions.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a hybrid quantum framework, QCGAN-QAE, which combines a quantum conditional generative adversarial network (QCGAN) with quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) to model and measure the distribution of future loss rates in the carbon market. In the QCGAN, a parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) generator encodes conditional information (past N-day loss rates) as an input quantum state and outputs a quantum state representing generated samples, while a discriminator distinguishes between real and generated samples; circuit expressiveness is enhanced by reordering entanglement and rotation layers and adding a quantum fully connected (QFC) layer to achieve full qubit connectivity. For measurement, QAE is used to estimate amplitudes whose squares correspond to probabilities, and a binary search procedure over the ordered, basis-encoded state space is integrated into QAE to locate the VaR-related quantum state and then to identify all states in the tail for CVaR computation, with CVaR calculated via discrete summation over those tail states.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-016, C-017, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-041]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On EU ETS (ECX) carbon price data, the authors report that the proposed QCGAN-QAE framework markedly improves the efficiency and precision of VaR and CVaR estimation relative to the original methods considered, with backtesting showing that the modified QCGAN circuits yield significantly higher estimation accuracy than the original QCGAN. The paper attributes improved performance to several components: placing entanglement before rotation in the generator circuit is claimed to enhance efficiency and expressiveness; adding the QFC layer improves VaR and CVaR accuracy at 90% and 95% confidence levels; and introducing QAE (instead of direct measurement) further improves estimation accuracy. They also report that integrating binary search into QAE leads to logarithmic-time VaR search and significant time-efficiency gains, particularly at lower confidence levels, and that QCGAN-QAE converges in far fewer training epochs than CGAN, while model performance appears relatively insensitive to circuit depth within the tested range.
    [codes: C-008, C-029, C-032, C-044, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-054, C-056]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum framework is compared against classical baselines including historical simulation and a classical CGAN model for carbon market VaR/CVaR estimation. The authors state that traditional Monte Carlo-style approaches require many simulations and rely on pre-assumed probability distributions, whereas their QCGAN-QAE avoids such strong assumptions and, in their experiments, generally delivers the best overall accuracy and efficiency across methods. They also highlight that QCGAN-QAE can achieve comparable or better VaR/CVaR accuracy than classical CGAN while requiring dramatically fewer training epochs and, under their time-cost model derived from circuit depth, an empirically large runtime reduction versus CGAN when implemented on a modeled quantum computer.
    [codes: C-011, C-013, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-044, C-046, C-047]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations and caveats. Conceptually, it notes that most existing quantum risk studies, including precursors, rely on pre-assumed data-generating distributions, which the authors seek to move beyond but still recognize as a broader limitation in the literature. At the model level, they find that the original QCGAN architecture performs poorly—its likelihood ratio statistics are too large and it fails the Kupiec VaR backtest at all three confidence levels—necessitating circuit redesign. Even for the improved QCGAN-QAE, the authors concede that performance at the 99% confidence level remains limited and that the framework has certain limitations when facing extreme market risks. Methodologically, they emphasize that encoding continuity is crucial; discontinuities in the binary encoding of loss rates can lead to discontinuous and inaccurate estimated CDFs and thus inaccurate VaR and CVaR, highlighting a sensitivity to the chosen encoding scheme. They also point out that a previously used weakly fully connected topology, with only one-direction connections between qubits, may reduce learning ability, and that increasing circuit depth, while potentially more expressive, raises risks of overfitting and susceptibility to noise. Finally, for the QAE-plus-binary-search measurement scheme, they report that the acceleration effect from binary search is more pronounced at lower confidence levels, but at particularly high confidence levels QAE with binary search may offer little benefit or even be only as good as the non-accelerated method, implying reduced speed advantages in the extreme-tail regime.
    [codes: C-013, C-031, C-034, C-042, C-043, C-045, C-053, C-055]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose two main directions for future work: refining the quantum data encoding by exploring angular rotation encoding, which they expect could significantly improve how classical loss-rate information is embedded into quantum states; and systematically fine-tuning the algorithmic parameters of the QCGAN-QAE framework to further enhance risk-estimation performance.
    [codes: C-057, C-058]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to be among the first applications of quantum computing to carbon market risk estimation, specifically for VaR and CVaR in the EU ETS context, and positions its QCGAN-QAE framework as a novel quantum computing-based approach that significantly advances carbon market risk estimation practices. It further argues that using QCGAN for real-world distribution simulation, rather than relying on pre-assumed parametric models, and integrating QAE with a binary search procedure for efficient VaR and CVaR measurement together constitute key contributions beyond prior quantum risk studies.
    [codes: C-012, C-014, C-015, C-056]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses real EU ETS carbon price data from the European Climate Exchange over 2015–2020, reflecting the third phase of the EU carbon market, and applies a chronological 80/20 train–test split without shuffling to respect the time-series structure. Risk is modeled on loss rates (negative returns) rather than prices, with daily loss rates min-max normalized, discretized, and binary encoded into qubits; the model conditions on the past N days of loss rates as inputs. For model evaluation, the authors employ standard backtesting procedures: Kupiec tests for VaR and a DLC-based test for CVaR, and they analyze computational time cost via a unified time model derived from quantum circuit depth and gate times. To improve GAN training stability and mitigate mode collapse, they use Minibatch Discrimination and an adaptive GAN approach, simultaneously training ten distinct CGANs or QCGANs. They also conduct an ablation on circuit structure (including swapping entanglement and rotation stages and adding QFC), a comparison of QAE versus direct measurement, and a parameter sensitivity analysis on circuit depth, indicating an effort toward systematic evaluation, though all experiments are performed on quantum simulators rather than physical hardware.
    [codes: C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-054]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Several codes provide definitional context or high-level framing that underpins but does not substantially add to the other dimensions: the definitions and interpretations of VaR and CVaR as measures of maximum potential loss and expected loss beyond VaR, respectively, and explicit emphasis that CVaR better captures extreme losses; the statement that encoding continuity is crucial further highlights the technical subtlety of mapping continuous loss-rate distributions into discrete quantum states. These elements collectively support the financial and technical background for the proposed quantum risk estimation framework.
    [codes: C-018, C-019, C-033]

=== PAPER a254eea1f1d3 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames financial markets as uncertain systems whose complex return and price distributions need to be represented as quantum states for simulation and derivative pricing. It focuses on modeling short‑term price formation and daily return distributions via a quantum-walk-based multi‑agent representation of investor sentiment, and on preparing target distributions (including log‑normal for European option pricing) as quantum states. The authors argue that efficient quantum state preparation of such probability distributions is critical for achieving any quantum advantage in financial applications.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-022, C-025, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a multi‑Split‑Steps Quantum Walk (multi‑SSQW) implemented as a parameterized quantum circuit combined with a classical optimizer (a variational quantum algorithm). The scheme extends one‑dimensional discrete‑time split‑step quantum walks by introducing multiple walkers (representing multiple investors) and an ancilla coin space that controls position-space amplitudes, thereby generating target probability distributions and serving as a state-preparation mechanism. The coin operators are parameterized unitaries (e.g., U3‑type) whose angles encode investor optimism and pessimism, the evolution is split into two half‑steps using conditional shift operators, and COBYLA iteratively minimizes MSE/KL divergence between trained and target distributions over successive PQC evaluations.
    [codes: C-002, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that multi‑SSQW can closely approximate intricate financial distributions such as daily stock/index return histograms, binomial distributions with varying numbers of trials, and a log‑normal distribution used for European call option pricing. For real market data, simulations of assets like JNJ and indices such as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq‑100 show visually close alignment between simulated and empirical distributions, with four walkers giving a particularly strong match for JNJ and fewer walkers sufficing for the S&P 500; more walkers generally reduce MSE and KL divergence. For synthetic benchmarks, the authors demonstrate that binomial distributions with p = 0.3 and 31, 63, and 127 trials can be approximated by tuning walker counts and control steps, and that increasing the number of walkers reduces approximation error. In the option‑pricing example, a trained multi‑SSQW distribution with three walkers and four steps approximates a log‑normal target, and the authors note that more accurate distribution training yields more favorable pricing outcomes. Overall, they characterize multi‑SSQW as flexible, rapidly convergent, and capable of stable convergence across these tasks.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-015, C-025, C-032, C-034, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-043, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper primarily compares its quantum-generated distributions against classical target distributions rather than against classical algorithms’ computational performance. For option pricing, the log‑normal distribution and Black–Scholes model are used as analytical benchmarks, and the expected payoff from the trained distribution is compared to that implied by the target distribution. The discussion acknowledges that inefficient state preparation could negate quantum advantage and cites Grover‑style ancilla‑rotation schemes as prior classical‑inspired quantum approaches, but no explicit runtime or accuracy comparison against concrete classical numerical methods (e.g., Monte Carlo or PDE solvers) is provided.
    [codes: C-013, C-014, C-015, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-045]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors note that some assets, such as Apple and Microsoft, exhibit return distributions that deviate from normality, which increases the complexity of their simulation within the proposed framework. They also explicitly recognize an inherent trade‑off in variational quantum algorithms between quantum circuit complexity and optimizer efficiency, implying practical constraints on scaling multi‑SSQW to larger or more intricate financial models.
    [codes: C-036, C-049]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work is planned to enhance forecasting of stock price trends by incorporating macroeconomic data into the model and by exploiting entanglement to capture interactions between different stocks, with the goal of constructing joint probability distributions for multi‑asset financial systems.
    [codes: C-050]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The core novelty claimed is the introduction of the multi‑Split‑Steps Quantum Walk (multi‑SSQW), which extends the traditional single split‑step quantum walk to a multi‑agent setting for financial market modeling and simultaneously provides a new method for quantum state preparation of complex probability distributions. This approach uses an ancilla coin space to control position‑space amplitudes, maps investor sentiments into configurable coin operators, and is presented as a flexible, stably convergent, and rapidly computable tool for financial simulation and probability distribution loading in quantum circuits.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-011, C-012, C-016, C-017, C-022, C-024, C-046, C-047]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work employs a hybrid PQC‑plus‑COBYLA variational loop, iterating until convergence to target distributions measured via MSE and KL divergence. The empirical evaluation uses real daily price data from Yahoo Finance for several large‑cap stocks and indices over a three‑month window, discretized into 16 return bins, and runs simulations 100 times while varying the number of walkers from 1 to 10, with results summarized through metrics and boxplots. Additional controlled tests on analytically defined binomial and log‑normal distributions illustrate how walker count and step parameters affect approximation quality. While this provides a multi‑dataset, multi‑task demonstration, the reporting remains predominantly qualitative (e.g., visual matching and trends in errors) and does not detail full resource counts or classical baselines, which has implications for reproducibility and for assessing practical quantum advantage.
    [codes: C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-043, C-045, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper draws conceptual parallels between financial and quantum uncertainty and uses random walk theory from classical finance as a baseline analogy. It also provides qualitative interpretations of fitted distributions in terms of investor behavior, such as reading JNJ’s match with four walkers as consistent with a stable, less sentiment‑driven investor base, interpreting the S&P 500’s convergence with fewer walkers as reflecting a relatively homogeneous investor population, and associating Nasdaq‑100’s characteristics with more sentiment‑driven investors due to innovation‑driven uncertainty.
    [codes: C-006, C-008, C-033, C-034, C-035]

The conclusion reiterates that moving to an implementation stage is still necessary for genuine global gold price prediction, underscoring that the current study is methodological and illustrative rather than a completed predictive system.

=== PAPER a4c29a22413b (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as using quantum machine learning as an alternative to classical differential machine learning for option pricing and sensitivity (Greeks) estimation in financial risk management, considering both learning in parametric space (e.g., European options and Bermudan swaptions) and in sample space (e.g., basket options). It positions this within the broader context of near‑term classical–quantum hybrid approaches and contrasts its focus on both parametric and sample-space learning with prior work that considered sample space only.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-009, C-027]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose "quantum differential machine learning" (QDML), a quantum analogue of classical differential machine learning, built on parameterized quantum circuits and the parameter‑shift rule to compute exact gradients with respect to both circuit parameters and market variables, enabling analytic sensitivities. They design specific circuit architectures and input encodings for each product: a two‑qubit, 15‑parameter circuit with tanh and angle encoding for European options; higher‑qubit, overparameterized circuits with compressed volatility encodings for Bermudan swaptions; and a six‑qubit circuit that feeds all input variables into all qubits for basket options, often training prices and derivatives jointly via loss functions that include derivative terms.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: For European options, the two‑qubit QDML model achieves very low test errors, with mean relative errors of 0.069% for price and 0.258% for delta, and the authors note that two qubits appear sufficient to reach this accuracy. They observe that adding delta terms to the loss for European options and basket options does not markedly improve price accuracy but does help for delta estimation, while for the more complex Bermudan swaption, including vega in the optimization and using an overparameterized circuit significantly reduce vega errors (e.g., from 6.2% to 4.6% when moving from non‑overparameterized to overparameterized), supporting their claim that QDML can be used for option pricing and sensitivity calculation in risk management.
    [codes: C-005, C-010, C-018, C-019, C-026, C-032]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum models are benchmarked against classical methods implicitly: European option data and deltas are generated from standard pricing formulas, while Bermudan swaption vegas are compared against finite‑difference approximations, and basket option learning follows the classical differential ML setup. The authors highlight that the parameter‑shift rule provides exact derivatives, contrasting with finite‑difference methods used classically for sensitivities and noting that classical DML suffers high Monte Carlo cost in preparing training labels, which QDML is intended to mitigate.
    [codes: C-007, C-013, C-024, C-027]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations. First, preparing training sets for differential machine learning remains costly because generating true prices via Monte Carlo requires many sample paths per exotic option, motivating but not eliminating data cost issues for QDML. Second, the authors find it difficult to learn Bermudan swaption prices due to their strong nonlinearity, indicating challenges for complex payoffs. They also emphasize that optimal construction of input encoders U_in is still an open design issue affecting efficiency and performance. Finally, all experiments are run on simulators rather than real quantum hardware, and the authors explicitly state the need to study QDML on high‑dimensional real market data and real quantum devices.
    [codes: C-007, C-011, C-035, C-037]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions include improving input encoding schemes, which the authors identify as a key issue, and exploring parallel execution strategies where multiple quantum circuits are used to compute many sensitivities (e.g., deltas) simultaneously to reduce computational cost. They also call for testing QDML on high‑dimensional real market data and evaluating its effectiveness on real quantum computers beyond simulators.
    [codes: C-034, C-035, C-036, C-038]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim novelty in defining and demonstrating "quantum differential machine learning" as a quantum analogue of classical differential ML, leveraging parameter‑shift rules in variational circuits to learn option prices jointly with exact analytic sensitivities across both parametric‑space and sample‑space settings. They position this as a step toward applying quantum machine learning to option pricing and Greeks for financial risk management on near‑term hybrid quantum devices.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-009]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study systematically covers several instrument types—European options, Bermudan swaptions, and basket options—to probe both parametric and sample‑space learning regimes. It reports numerical accuracy metrics such as mean relative errors for price and Greeks, explores the effect of including derivative terms in the loss functions, and investigates overparameterization by using more circuit parameters than training samples for the Bermudan case. However, the work relies entirely on simulator‑based experiments and synthetic or model‑generated data rather than real market data or hardware, and the authors themselves stress that better input encodings and real‑world validation remain to be addressed.
    [codes: C-004, C-009, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-035, C-037]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Beyond methodological and technical aspects, the authors suggest that using QDML could contribute to reducing electrical energy consumption and associated CO₂ emissions in the financial industry, framing an environmental motivation for pursuing more efficient quantum approaches to risk management computations.
    [codes: C-039]

=== PAPER a5b68f8e6d90 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames financial fraud as deceptive behavior for gain and focuses specifically on credit fraud, motivating the need for accurate and fast detection systems. It formulates fraud detection as a binary classification problem on the BankSim credit-fraud dataset, treating anomaly detection as integral to identifying fraudulent vs non-fraudulent transactions. The task is set up for quantum machine learning as supervised classification of balanced fraud/non-fraud samples using selected features such as age, gender, category, and amount.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-014, C-028, C-030, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study conducts a comparative analysis of four quantum machine learning models for fraud detection: a Quantum Support Vector Classifier (QSVC), a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC), an Estimator Quantum Neural Network (EQNN), and a Sampler Quantum Neural Network (SQNN), all implemented in Qiskit and executed on the Aer QasmSimulator. Data are encoded into quantum states using three feature maps—ZZFeatureMap (second-order Pauli-Z evolution), PauliFeatureMap (Pauli expansion), and ZFeatureMap (first-order Pauli-Z evolution)—with QSVC relying critically on the choice of kernel, VQC and EQNN implemented as hybrid variational architectures optimized via COBYLA with up to 200 iterations, and SQNN using a quantum sampler to draw states from complex distributions.
    [codes: C-001, C-013, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across the four QML models tested on the BankSim subset, QSVC with the ZFeatureMap is reported as the top performer, achieving F1 scores of 0.98 for both fraud and non-fraud classes and 0.98 accuracy. VQC attains an F1 score of about 0.90 and a best loss of 0.5 with the ZFeatureMap, but shows higher losses (0.95) with PauliFeatureMap and ZZFeatureMap; EQNN reaches an accuracy of 0.78 and an F1 score around 0.78 with ZFeatureMap, while SQNN performs worst with an accuracy of about 0.58 and F1 scores around 0.57–0.64. Exploratory analysis on the underlying data indicates that fraudulent transactions are typically of higher monetary amount, more common among individuals aged 26–35 and females, and concentrated in certain merchant categories such as “sports & toys” and “health,” with “amount” identified as the most influential feature.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-036, C-044, C-045, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-051, C-054, C-055]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors position QML as potentially more efficient than classical machine learning by enabling new algorithms and quantum parallelisation that could handle larger, real-time datasets, and they note prior work where quantum fraud detection was found superior to classical approaches. However, in this study they do not report explicit experimental comparisons against classical baselines (e.g., classical SVM or neural networks), nor provide runtime or complexity benchmarks—so the relative performance vs classical methods remains speculative and supported only by cited literature.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-016]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations. At a high level, they note the need for more efficient quantum algorithms and for larger, more complex datasets to fully realize quantum fraud detection, implying that current results are constrained by algorithmic maturity and data scale. Methodologically, they report optimization challenges for EQNN, where the training process struggled to reach an optimal solution and reduced its accuracy. For SQNN, they explicitly state that its lower accuracy may stem from inherent limitations in handling continuous and high-dimensional data like their BankSim-derived feature space, and they also indicate that SQNN is better suited to combinatorial optimization and constraint problems rather than this classification task. More generally, they suggest that the choice of quantum circuits and data encoding substantially affects EQNN and SQNN performance, indicating sensitivity to circuit design. Finally, all experiments are conducted on a small, balanced subset (200 records) of a much larger, highly imbalanced synthetic dataset, which implicitly limits the realism and scalability of the reported performance.
    [codes: C-005, C-050, C-052, C-053, C-057, C-029, C-030, C-038]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors point to refining the VQC training process as a promising avenue to further improve its performance beyond the reported F1 score of 0.90, and more broadly imply the need to develop more efficient quantum algorithms and to test on larger, more complex datasets as the field and hardware mature.
    [codes: C-005, C-056]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s contribution is framed as a comparative study of four different QML models—QSVC, VQC, EQNN, and SQNN—on a credit fraud detection task using the BankSim dataset, systematically examining how different quantum feature maps and hybrid architectures impact fraud classification performance. They also emphasize how feature selection and quantum data encoding choices (e.g., ZFeatureMap vs Pauli-based maps) critically affect model accuracy, particularly highlighting the strong performance of QSVC with a simple ZFeatureMap.
    [codes: C-001, C-013, C-017, C-019, C-022, C-024, C-044, C-054, C-057]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study carefully preprocesses the synthetic BankSim dataset by cleaning age values with regular expressions, label-encoding categorical variables (e.g., category and gender), and performing PCA-based dimensionality reduction plus domain reasoning to select four informative features—age, gender, category, and amount—for modeling. From the original 594,643-record, heavily imbalanced dataset (7,200 fraud vs 587,443 non-fraud), they construct a balanced subset of 200 records (100 fraud, 100 non-fraud), then apply a train–test split and evaluate using standard metrics such as precision, recall, F1, loss, and accuracy. All quantum models are implemented in Qiskit using the Aer QasmSimulator backend, with VQC, EQNN, and SQNN trained via the COBYLA optimizer capped at 200 iterations. The authors explicitly discuss how kernel choice and feature maps influence QSVC performance, and they present exploratory descriptive statistics and demographics to justify feature importance, but they do not provide code or classical baselines, and they simulate ideal (noise-free) quantum hardware, which affects external validity and reproducibility.
    [codes: C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-051]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors reiterate that fraud detection is closely related to anomaly detection and that the QSVC model differs conceptually from classical machine learning models by not employing a standard loss function, instead relying on its quantum kernel structure for classification. They also underscore that quantum approaches may, in the post-NISQ era, enable faster analysis of large-scale, real-time transactional data via parallelisation, though these points are positioned as broader context rather than empirically validated in this work.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-046]

=== PAPER a934c86420c1 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets time-series anomaly detection in settings where anomalies are scarce and only normal data are available for training, formulating the task as unsupervised detection via quantum autoencoders that highlight deviations either through reconstruction error or latent-space behavior. The authors motivate the work by emphasizing the multifaceted challenges of anomaly detection, particularly the scarcity of anomalous examples in training data and the presence of a single anomaly per test series in the UCR benchmark used. Anomalies are defined operationally as time steps whose reconstructed or latent representation deviates sufficiently from patterns learned on benign windows.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-010, C-011, C-026]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study employs quantum autoencoders for time-series windows, using amplitude encoding to map fixed-size windows into a logarithmic number of qubits, with deterministic state preparation followed by a variational encoding circuit and either reconstruction-based or Swap-Test-based anomaly scoring. Preprocessing converts time series into sliding windows of size 2^K (128 in experiments), with no prior normalization since normalization occurs during state preparation; amplitude encoding is chosen for qubit efficiency, requiring only log(N) qubits for N data points. The authors also propose a Swap-Test-only anomaly detection variant that trains the autoencoder to minimize the number of measured ones on benign data, and they implement both simulated and real-hardware versions, with the hardware setting using quasi-amplitude encoding to mitigate transpilation overhead while approximately preserving window shape and restricting the hardware experiment to a single configuration on IBM Torino.
    [codes: C-001, C-010, C-011, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: In simulation, the authors report that quantum autoencoders consistently outperform classical deep-learning autoencoders across all employed UCR time-series anomaly datasets, while using 60–230× fewer trainable parameters and requiring five times fewer training iterations. Performance varies substantially across datasets and ansatz choices, with some datasets (e.g., 28 and 99) particularly difficult and anomaly detection success depending on both low training loss and the selected ansatz (e.g., only RealAmplitudes with SCA entanglement detects the anomaly in dataset 28). They find that Swap-Test-based anomaly detection is more robust when training loss remains high, whereas MSE-based reconstruction is superior when loss is low, and they observe that training loss tends to increase with the number of ansatz parameters, a trend noted as counterintuitive. On real IBM hardware, all tested quantum autoencoders—trained either on a simulator or directly on IBM Torino—successfully identify the anomaly with detection performance comparable to simulation, though simulator-trained models show faster loss reduction than hardware-trained ones.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-006, C-014, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-041, C-042, C-044, C-045, C-047, C-048, C-051]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum autoencoders are compared against a classical deep-learning autoencoder baseline implemented in PyTorch, with experiments indicating that the quantum models outperform this baseline on every evaluated dataset. The reported advantage is framed in terms of both detection performance and efficiency: quantum models achieve superior anomaly detection while using 60–230 times fewer parameters and five times fewer training iterations than the classical autoencoder. The authors reiterate in the discussion that quantum autoencoders consistently outperform classical autoencoders across all tested datasets, positioning this as a central comparative finding.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-014, C-028, C-037, C-051]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper highlights several limitations. First, exact amplitude encoding is characterized as hardware-inefficient on current NISQ devices because transpiled circuits require substantially more operations than the logical design, constraining practical deployment on real hardware. As a workaround, quasi-amplitude encoding is used, but the authors stress that this approximation is only feasible for relatively small quantum systems and does not exactly reproduce the original series, limiting scalability and fidelity. They also acknowledge that the hardware demonstration is narrowed to a single dataset and a single quantum autoencoder configuration, and that training on real hardware is costly and time-consuming: each epoch takes about 11 minutes, summing to roughly 21 hours of quantum computing time and an estimated cost of around 120,960 USD for the reported study. Methodologically, they note a counterintuitive trend where training loss increases with the number of ansatz parameters, suggesting this may be due to factors such as the chosen optimizer (COBYLA), thereby casting some uncertainty on how well more expressive circuits can be exploited in practice.
    [codes: C-033, C-035, C-046, C-049, C-050, C-054, C-055]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose several future research directions, including designing more efficient ansatz architectures and scalable data encoding techniques to alleviate current hardware and scalability constraints. They suggest extending their quantum autoencoder framework to multivariate time series to better reflect richer real-world anomaly detection scenarios, and exploring models that process data at multiple resolutions simultaneously as another potential improvement in capturing complex temporal patterns.
    [codes: C-056, C-057, C-058]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims as its main contributions: establishing a framework for applying quantum autoencoders to time-series anomaly detection, proposing both reconstruction-error-based and latent (Swap-Test) anomaly classification techniques, and demonstrating empirically that quantum autoencoders can outperform classical deep-learning autoencoders on a UCR benchmark with significantly fewer parameters and training iterations. Additionally, the authors present what they describe as a successful real-hardware implementation of a quantum autoencoder for anomaly detection on IBM Torino, attaining performance comparable to simulation despite NISQ noise, and they position amplitude encoding as a qubit-efficient encoding method in this context, while also introducing a quasi-amplitude encoding variant tailored to hardware constraints.
    [codes: C-002, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-021, C-052]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses a standard public benchmark (UCR Time Series Anomaly Archive) where training data are anomaly-free and each test set contains a single labeled anomaly, with preprocessing via sliding windows of fixed length 128 and stride 1 to define inputs consistently across quantum and classical models. The quantum simulations are run with a statevector simulator using COBYLA for 45 iterations and evaluate multiple ansatz families and parameterizations, while anomaly decisions are made through moving-average-smoothed reconstruction or Swap-Test scores thresholded by a predefined rule. The hardware experiment is explicitly scoped down to one dataset and one configuration, uses quasi-amplitude encoding per Nakaji et al. to keep circuits hardware-feasible, and reports detailed runtime and cost metrics, underscoring the experimental burden of NISQ runs. The authors also analyze trends such as variability across datasets and ansatz choice, the relationship between training loss and detection performance, and a counterintuitive increase in loss with more parameters, suggesting some reflective engagement with robustness and optimization issues.
    [codes: C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-042, C-045, C-046, C-048, C-049, C-050]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors emphasize that amplitude encoding, while qubit-efficient in principle, faces practical constraints on NISQ hardware, and that quantum autoencoder performance is highly dependent on the chosen ansatz, reinforcing the importance of circuit design in future studies.
    [codes: C-052, C-053]

=== PAPER af45ea1743f6 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as efficiently loading arbitrary (including non-lognormal) asset price distributions into quantum states in order to perform option pricing on a quantum computer, including end-to-end pipelines that estimate expected option payoffs via amplitude estimation. It targets classical terminal-price distributions (synthetic, model-based, and real-option implied) and reformulates them as quantum states suitable for a three-step quantum pricing workflow that culminates in expected payoff estimation.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-005, C-014, C-015, C-033, C-035, C-038]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a hybrid quantum Wasserstein GAN where a quantum generator prepares probability amplitudes on n qubits and a classical discriminator operates directly on classical samples, thereby avoiding input encoding. This distribution loader is integrated into a three-step option-pricing workflow that (I) loads the distribution with the hybrid qWGAN, and (III) applies Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE), chosen over QPE-based QAE for improved NISQ implementability, to estimate expected payoffs. The qGAN-style loading channel is emphasized as using O(poly(n)) gates instead of O(2^n), and the Wasserstein objective is explicitly formulated with corresponding adjustments to the discriminator architecture typical for WGANs.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-011, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that the hybrid qWGAN substantially improves the efficiency and accuracy of loading arbitrary classical distributions into quantum states, achieving close fits for lognormal, Heston-model, and real implied distributions, as quantified by small relative entropy and Wasserstein distances. Within the option-pricing context, the Wasserstein-loss setup yields an almost perfect fit compared to a BCE setup and produces option price estimates that are closer to the target distribution payoff, including for a digital payoff where the estimate is about 1% (0.1 cent) below the true value. The authors also assert a quadratic enhancement in error scaling for the pricing step through IQAE and highlight that the hybrid approach offers broader distribution coverage and flexibility beyond the standard lognormal case, including real-market data.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-006, C-012, C-013, C-015, C-018, C-022, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-034, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors compare their hybrid qWGAN against fully quantum generative models conceptually and claim superior performance and stability when the target distribution is classical. Quantitatively, they contrast a Wasserstein-loss setup with a Binary Cross Entropy setup for the same task, showing that the Wasserstein formulation yields lower relative entropy and Wasserstein distance and more accurate option payoff estimates relative to the classical target distribution. They further emphasize that using QAE/IQAE in the pricing step theoretically provides quadratic error scaling compared to classical Monte Carlo methods, although this is presented as a known algorithmic advantage rather than as an empirically benchmarked runtime comparison.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-006, C-010, C-018, C-022, C-028, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations. On the hardware side, current quantum devices are described as very sensitive and prone to noise and errors, which affects the reliability of real-hardware experiments. Algorithmically, the authors note that quantum GAN training difficulties worsen as system size grows, with significant issues appearing already for a few qubits, and they highlight the barren plateau phenomenon whereby gradients in quantum neural networks become exponentially small as the number of qubits increases, threatening trainability at larger scales. They also point out that Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE), which underpins some QAE variants, requires deep circuits with many gates and is thus error-prone on NISQ devices, motivating their shift to IQAE. In the real-market data experiment, they explicitly caution that terminal price distributions are not directly observable and must be approximated from implied volatility and option prices, introducing approximation error and data-estimation uncertainty into their empirical results.
    [codes: C-010, C-016, C-017, C-020, C-036]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Not addressed in this paper.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim as their main contribution the development and implementation of a novel hybrid quantum Wasserstein GAN architecture specifically designed for efficiently loading arbitrary classical distributions into quantum states, with a focus on option-pricing applications. They position this hybrid qWGAN loading module—combining a quantum generator, classical discriminator, and Wasserstein loss—as the central innovation that improves stability, reduces gate complexity from O(2^n) to O(poly(n)), eliminates encoding/decoding errors for classical data, and constitutes a significant advancement over prior qGAN-based distribution loaders and fully quantum GANs.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-008, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-022, C-038]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper emphasizes GAN training stability by choosing a Wasserstein loss, arguing it is continuous and almost everywhere differentiable and thus better behaved than KL or JS divergences in terms of convergence. They adopt standard WGAN practices such as modifying the discriminator architecture (e.g., linear output layer) to match the Wasserstein objective, while also explicitly noting the need for a classical discriminator when the data are classical, consistent with their hybrid design. The experiments are structured around clear synthetic (lognormal), model-based (Heston), and real-market (option-implied) distributions, with discretization to a finite grid and quantitative evaluation via relative entropy and Wasserstein distance; the authors explicitly highlight close fits on both synthetic and real data. They further stress that many promising quantum algorithms require efficient distribution loading, suggesting their methodology is intended to be broadly applicable beyond finance, and they provide an end-to-end workflow (including IQAE) that is implemented both in simulation and on real hardware, though the codes indicate awareness of noise and scalability issues.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper underscores that its efficient distribution-loading approach has relevance beyond option pricing, as many quantum algorithms need mechanisms for loading arbitrary distributions into quantum states, suggesting broader cross-domain applicability.

=== PAPER b253d747bcc9 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets credit card fraud detection in financial transactions, framing it as an anomaly (outlier) detection task in a heavily imbalanced dataset dominated by genuine samples. Fraud detection is explicitly cast as identifying anomalous transactions within a Kaggle credit card dataset described by 28 anonymized features and a very small minority of fraud cases.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-010, C-011]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors employ quantum kernel methods built from quantum feature maps that embed classical transaction data into N‑qubit states, focusing on instantaneous quantum polynomial (IQP) circuits with data re-uploading. Data is angle-encoded into a quantum state |φ(x)⟩ on an N‑qubit register using IQP-style circuits, and kernels are defined via state overlaps κ(x,x′)=|⟨ψ(x)|ψ(x′)⟩|², estimated through return-probability measurements; in experiments they concentrate on IQP circuits re-uploaded three times with features scaled by a factor η=0.1.
    [codes: C-005, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the subsampled credit card dataset, quantum kernels based on IQP circuits with re-uploading achieve higher average precision than classical baselines as the feature/qubit count grows, with a reported quantum–classical separation of about 15% AP at 20 qubits. The quantum anomaly detection setup (unsupervised) attains average precision around 0.7 with IQP kernels, while the best classical OC‑SVM baseline saturates around AP≈0.55; in supervised settings, quantum kernels also show improved AP and appear less prone to overfitting at higher feature dimensions.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-015, C-021, C-023, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-049]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical benchmarks include supervised logistic regression and RBF-kernel SVC, as well as an unsupervised OC‑SVM with RBF kernel, all trained and tuned using standard ML practices. The authors report that SVC slightly outperforms logistic regression for medium feature counts, but both supervised methods deteriorate in average precision at higher dimensionality due to overfitting, while the OC‑SVM AP increases with feature count before saturating around 15 features at AP≈0.55. In contrast, quantum kernels—especially IQP circuits with re‑uploading—exhibit improved AP and ultimately outperform classical RBF kernels at larger feature spaces, with a quantum–classical AP separation of roughly 15% at 20 qubits/features.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-031, C-033, C-034, C-049]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors emphasize that the extreme class imbalance in the original dataset makes accuracy a misleading metric and motivates the use of average precision instead. They acknowledge significant scalability limitations of kernel-based quantum fraud detection: full Gram matrix estimation scales quadratically in the number of samples, making training computationally expensive for large datasets (~100,000 samples), and real-time detection may be infeasible if per-test latency is high. Reliable kernel estimation requires at least 10³ measurement shots, which further inflates training times; for large datasets, forming full Gram matrices on near-term hardware is described as extremely costly, with brute-force evaluations on slow platforms such as trapped ions becoming practically infeasible (e.g., 30-year estimates). They also note that photonic systems, despite high potential clock rates, currently lack established deterministic optical gate implementations, posing another significant practical barrier.
    [codes: C-012, C-037, C-039, C-042, C-043, C-046, C-048]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For practical deployment, the authors argue that future work must clarify operational requirements by defining realistic timescales and precision targets for both training and real-time inference, then matching these to available and anticipated quantum hardware resources. They suggest exploring randomized protocols and adaptive detection schemes to infer only parts of the Gram matrix, thereby reducing the O(Ns²) training cost, and they state that demonstrating a strong quantum advantage in fraud detection will require scaling beyond the 20‑qubit simulations to approximately 50–100 qubits.
    [codes: C-036, C-044, C-050]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is framed as developing quantum anomaly detection protocols for credit card fraud detection using quantum kernels, and systematically comparing them against classical supervised and unsupervised baselines under realistic, highly imbalanced data conditions. The paper claims that quantum kernels, particularly IQP circuits with data re-uploading, can challenge and eventually outperform classical RBF-based protocols as feature dimensionality increases, offering up to a 15% gain in average precision—an improvement the authors argue could have nontrivial industrial impact.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-049]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses a public Kaggle credit card fraud dataset with 28 anonymized features and a strongly imbalanced class distribution, but subsamples 500 transactions with 25 fraud cases for the main near-term simulations. Preprocessing includes feature-wise standard scaling, PCA retaining only the first N principal components, and exploratory t‑SNE visualization, with the authors noting that t‑SNE shows only partial nominal–fraud separation. Models are evaluated primarily via average precision due to imbalance, and classical baselines undergo hyperparameter tuning by random search with cross-validation AP as the objective; similar PCA-scaled features (with an additional η=0.1 factor for quantum encoding) are then used to construct both classical and quantum kernels, supporting a reasonably controlled comparison.
    [codes: C-003, C-010, C-011, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-024, C-030]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors discuss the broader feasibility of deploying quantum fraud detection across different hardware platforms: superconducting circuits, which can support microsecond-scale circuit evaluations and MHz repetition rates; trapped-ion systems, which trade higher gate fidelity for slower clock rates; and photonic systems, which promise the fastest hypothetical clock rates but lack mature deterministic gate technologies. They also stress that even modest percentage improvements in average precision for fraud detection could translate into multi-million-dollar savings in an industrial setting.
    [codes: C-035, C-041, C-043, C-045, C-047]
